rows.title: Architecture — The sources
rows.summary: software factory (ADR-developer-0002), `nuclear-agents/roles/<role>/skills/step-<step>.md` with the front matter `prompt: agent.<step>` (`{{name}}` filled by `Workbench.prompt`, a `## ` section all of whose values are empty dropped whole; the list is `roles/README.md`), over the use-case guides…
body: **The prompts are files**, never strings in the code: every prompt a model reads is a skill of a role of the
software factory (ADR-developer-0002), `nuclear-agents/roles/<role>/skills/step-<step>.md` with the front matter
`prompt: agent.<step>` (`{{name}}` filled by `Workbench.prompt`, a `## ` section all of whose values are empty
dropped whole; the list is [`roles/README.md`](../../../roles/README.md)), over the use-case guides (the skills with
`prompt: <use case>`). The graph serves them (`ingest` makes its `prompts` collection from the skills), so the
graphs read them as before.

rows.title: Architecture — What an agent reads
rows.summary: Not a search over documents: the graph is a library of cards (`ADR-graph-0001`).
body: Not a search over documents: the graph is a library of cards (`ADR-graph-0001`).
| Who | Asks the graph for |
| The coder | `kind:<platform>.<kind>` by its id, the pitfalls whose `kinds` list has that kind, solved tasks and an example file of that kind |
| A repair | `error:<code>` of each code the compiler named |
| The assistant | every shelf with the question, each card with the rows it links to; and the exact facts of a question with one right answer |
| The diagnoser | the cards of the codes in a log and the closest known failures |
**What the agents may read.** Only Nuclear and the platform (`backend`, `mobile`, `web`): a row the agents read
has no target-language code (the build of the knowledge base refuses one that has), a failing test reaches them
told in `.nuc` terms, a piece's errors are given by line, and the diagnoser's prompt forbids speaking of the
generated code. They check with `nuclear check --platform`.
**What it knows** is the knowledge base of the Smart Graph
([`nuclear-graph-storage/data`](../../../../nuclear-graph-storage/data/README.md)); the agents read every row but
the ones about the target languages and the dialects underneath (`agents: false`).

rows.title: The strategy of a request, and the analyst — Limits
rows.summary: (the platform binds a repository to its entity by its name, so an entity renamed alone compiles and fails when it runs).
body: - `refactor-move-extract`, `remove` and `beyond` need a lead: the local agents do their mechanical steps only.
- A rename by the tool covers a declaration's name and the declarations built from it by a word before or after
(the platform binds a repository to its entity by its name, so an entity renamed alone compiles and fails when
it runs). That also takes a declaration that only starts with the name (`OrderLine` with `Order`): the analysis
lists every name it changes. A field or a method is renamed by hand (the same word may be another declaration's
member); the file of a renamed declaration keeps its path; a plural (`ListBooks`) and an alias of the facade
stay. A rename runs no security review: it writes no new logic.
- A bug whose failure names only its test stops at *Verification*: where the cause is needs a lead or the user.
- The Builder writes files and never deletes one.
- Still by hand or by a model, with no generator: relations in a stored resource, the tests of a backend resource
over another API, what a screen shows of a use case added with `gen usecase` (mobile, web).

rows.title: The strategy of a request, and the analyst — The analyst
rows.summary: `components/developer/ai/analyst.nuc`, `POST /developer/analyze`.
body: `components/developer/ai/analyst.nuc`, `POST /developer/analyze`. It runs before anything is generated or planned,
in fixed steps:
1. The project's files say which names of the request exist.
2. The graph gives the strategy (by the request's exact signs, then its meaning, and by which of its names the
project has).
3. The strategy gives the stages that run, the source of the pieces and the facts it needs.
4. **A model is asked for one thing only**: the resources a request in plain words describes
(`component | Name | fields | source | actions`). Each line becomes a `nuclear gen resource` call and is kept
only if its `--dry-run` accepts it.
5. A fact the request lacks is a question for the user and stops the run: nothing is guessed.
It answers the strategy and why, the stages, the generator calls, the pieces the tools already gave (the files that
declare what changes; every file of a rename, rewritten) and the questions.
A model asked about a request that lists no field invents them. So it is asked only when the request lists some,
and its answer is held to that list: the number of fields must be the request's, it is asked once more when it is
not, and left out (the fields are then asked to the user) when the second answer fails too. Types it reads from
words (`total` as `double`) are shown in the *Generate* step of the run, to be checked there.

rows.title: The strategy of a request, and the analyst — The kinds of request
rows.summary: The kinds of request
body: | Family | Strategies | In words |

| create | `system`, `project`, `component`, `resource-api`, `resource-db`, `client-of-backend`, `interface`, `repository`, `usecase`, `endpoint`, `declaration` | a whole system, a project, a component, a resource of another API, a stored resource, the app of a backend, only an interface, a repository, a use case, a route, one declaration |

| change | `member`, `refactor-rename`, `refactor-move-extract`, `refactor-architecture`, `data-migration`, `configuration`, `remove` | one more field, method or action; a rename; a move or an extraction; a break of the architecture's rules; the database's schema; the configuration; taking something out |

| fix | `bug-compile`, `bug-failing-test`, `bug-behaviour`, `bug-runtime`, `bug-data-contract`, `bug-interface`, `bug-environment` | it does not compile; a test fails; it does the wrong thing; it fails while running; the data does not match; a screen shows the wrong thing; the machine or a service fails |
| verify and explain | `tests`, `security-review`, `document`, `question`, `operate` | tests for what exists; a security review; documentation; a question; building, running and shipping |
| beyond | `beyond` | what NuclearLang or the local agents cannot do: said before anything is written |

rows.title: The strategy of a request, and the analyst
rows.summary: A whole system, one screen, a rename and a failing test are not done the same way.
body: A whole system, one screen, a rename and a failing test are not done the same way. The knowledge base holds a
**strategy** for each kind of request a user makes (31 rows, `strategy:<name>`, on the `playbooks` shelf of the
Smart Graph): how the kind is recognised, its plan step by step with the tool of every step, and what it asks of a
run. Changing how a kind of request is handled is changing a row, never code. Why: `ADR-developer-0001`.

rows.title: The strategy of a request, and the analyst — Tools before models
rows.summary: In every strategy: `nuclear gen resource suppliers Supplier --fields "name:string phone:string" --source db --actions create,delete,update`, shown before it runs.
body: In every strategy:
- A generator writes what is standard. "Suppliers with a name and a phone: add, change and remove them" becomes
`nuclear gen resource suppliers Supplier --fields "name:string phone:string" --source db --actions
create,delete,update`, shown before it runs.
- The compiler's exact fixes (`nuclear fix`) come before any repair.
- A rename is done by a tool and no model writes (`Workspace.renamed`): every file that writes the name as a word,
with the new one in its place, and with it the project's names built from it (`NewBook` and `BookRepository` for
`Book`).
- The files a change starts in are found by the project's declarations, not planned.
- A generator finishes what it starts on a resource that exists: `nuclear gen resource` with a new action adds
the repository's method and the controller's route too (merged member by member). It refuses a search of a
stored resource, because which column is searched is a decision (a query of the repository, wired with
`nuclear gen usecase --calls`).
A model writes only a piece of one file that no tool can write.

rows.title: The strategy of a request, and the analyst — What a run does with it
rows.summary: The Builder follows the strategy (the project `extensions/` has the pipeline): the analysis is the last step of the *Specification* stage; the stages the strategy has no use for are skipped; and asks the planner only when the strategy's pieces come from a plan; *Code* writes a piece a tool already…
body: The Builder follows the strategy (the project [`extensions/`](../../../../extensions/AGENTS.md) has the pipeline):
the analysis is the last step of the *Specification* stage; the stages the strategy has no use for are skipped;
*Generate* runs the spec's own resources and the calls the analysis derived; *Plan* takes the pieces the tools gave
and asks the planner only when the strategy's pieces come from a plan; *Code* writes a piece a tool already wrote
as it is, and afterwards wires each use case the coder wrote with `nuclear gen usecase` (its alias and, when the
spec's sentence gives it, its route); *Verification*, for a bug, repairs the file the failure names whoever wrote
it, and never the test. A Developer without an analyst leaves the run as it was: every stage. A lead model gets
the same routing and the same plans over MCP (`graph_strategy`).

rows.title: The strategy of a request, and the analyst — What a strategy row says
rows.summary: Besides its card for people and lead models: Which strategy a request gets is chosen by the graph, without a model (the selection).
body: Besides its card for people and lead models:
| Field | Meaning |
| `data.signals` | regular expressions over the request: its exact signs (a diagnostic code, a test's output, `rename A to B`, a `GET <url>` line) |
| `meta.triggers` | the words that point to it |
| `data.target` | `existing`: the request names a declaration the project has; `new`: one it has not |
| `asks` | how people ask for it, in English and Spanish: found by meaning |
| `data.mode` | `write`, `repair` (the compiler's errors drive), `fix` (a failing test drives), `review`, `answer`, `commands`, `lead` |
| `data.stages` | the stages of the Builder it runs; empty: this kind of request is not a run |

| `data.pieces` | where its pieces come from: `plan` (the planner splits what is left), `declaring` (the files that declare what the request names), `naming` (every file that writes a name: a rename), `none` |
| `data.generators` | the generators it calls |
| `data.needs` | the facts it cannot start without, each with its question for the user |

collection (a feature as one example per file). The 18 `test` tasks are held out: their answers never reach the
graph, so the test score measures what the graph teaches, not what it copied.
3. `local`: the local coder answers every task through the Developer. An answer passes when `nuclear check` reports
no errors and it has every acceptance text. The local developer is **equivalent** to Sonnet on a task when both
pass.

new round.

rows.title: The Nuclear Developer — From a frontier model, over MCP
rows.summary: Claude Code, Codex or Cursor with the MCP server `nuclear-mcp` (its guide): The lead's loop is: generators first, `developer_task` for what they leave, validate and correct, then `developer_review`.
body: Claude Code, Codex or Cursor with the MCP server `nuclear-mcp`
([its guide](../../../../tools/mcp/docs/08-guides/mcp.md)):
| MCP tool | When |

| `developer_task(project, title, description, criteria, use_case)` | **first**, for every task that writes `.nuc`: the local agents do the whole task in the project and answer the run's journal. `use_case`: `feature`, `bug`, `refactor`, `test` |
| `developer_retry(project, run, from_stage, from_step, scratch)` | after a failure: from the step that failed (every step that passed is kept), from a stage, from one step, or from scratch |
| `developer_review(project, run, notes, files)` | **last**: what the lead corrected and why; each corrected file becomes an example in the graph, so the junior gets it right next time |
| `developer_code`, `developer_test`, `developer_security` | one `.nuc` file, the tests of a piece of code, or its security findings, outside a task |
The lead's loop is: generators first, `developer_task` for what they leave, validate and correct, then
`developer_review`.

(`nuclear-graph connect nuclear-developer --scopes read,write`).

The Developer listens on `127.0.0.1:7879`. By hand, the settings (`CODER_MODEL`, `ASSISTANT_MODEL`, `OLLAMA_URL`,
`CONTEXT_TOKENS`, `NUCLEAR_GRAPH_URL`) and what to do when it fails: [run it](../06-runbooks/run.md).

rows.title: The Nuclear Developer
rows.summary: The Nuclear Developer is a team of small local agents (at most 3B parameters, on Ollama) that work as the junior developer of a frontier model.
body: The Nuclear Developer is a team of small local agents (at most 3B parameters, on Ollama) that work as **the junior
developer of a frontier model**. A lead (Claude, another frontier model, or you) makes the decisions: the plan, the
names, the review. The local agents write each piece. What a small model cannot hold in its head comes from the
[Smart Graph](../../../../nuclear-graph-storage/docs/08-guides/README.md); what it writes is checked by the Nuclear
compiler before it answers. Your code stays on your machine, and the lead spends tokens only on leading and
correcting.
**Tools before models.** A product is made with the platform's tools
([ADR-platform-0004](../../../../docs/03-adr/0004-products-are-made-with-the-tools.md)): `nuclear new`, `gen` and
`make` write what is standard, `nuclear fix` applies the compiler's exact fixes, a rename is done by a tool. The
Developer writes only what those leave, and only in Nuclear: it names a platform (`backend`, `mobile`, `web`),
never a dialect, and never writes target code.

rows.title: The Nuclear Developer — What a task goes through
rows.summary: A task (a spec) is a run of the Builder with the local agents: 1. Analysis.
body: A task (a spec) is a run of the Builder with the local agents:
1. **Analysis.** Which kind of request it is (a resource, a screen, a rename, a failing test...), which generator
calls cover it, and what the platform cannot do yet. It asks you when the request lacks a name or a field.
2. **Plan.** The planner splits the spec into pieces, one file each, and says what is beyond the agents (`limits`).
3. **Tests first.** The tester writes the Nuclear tests.
4. **Code.** The coder writes each piece, checks it with `nuclear check` and repairs it with the card of each error
(at most three attempts), and with the failing tests told in Nuclear (`nuclear explain`).
5. **Verification.** The project is checked and its tests run.
6. **Security.** The security reviewer reads each new file.
7. **Journal.** The documenter writes what was built, how it was checked and what is left. When a stage fails, the
diagnoser says why (transient, environment, code, test, spec) and what to do next.
Every run is written to `.nuclear/builder/runs/<id>.md` in the project, beside a `.json` with every log whole; a
lead's review is `<id>.review.md`.

rows.title: The Nuclear Developer — What it cannot do yet
rows.summary: From the roadmap: `gen resource --source db`, a search of a stored resource, a field added to a resource that exists, tests for a backend REST resource, what a screen shows of a use case.
body: From [the roadmap](../01-product/roadmap.md):
- It does not choose names, data or architecture: the order gives them.
- Some requests still need a model or your hand because no tool covers them yet: relations in
`gen resource --source db`, a search of a stored resource, a field added to a resource that exists, tests for a
backend REST resource, what a screen shows of a use case. The Builder never deletes or moves a file, and a rename
covers declarations, not fields or methods.
- The security reviewer stops a backend run that changes data with a "missing authorization check" the platform
cannot express yet.
- A spec in plain words plans worse than one written with the platform's words (`use case`, `repository`...).
- The strategies ran end to end only on a `fastapi` project: never on a mobile or web project, never with
`nestjs`, never led by Claude.
- When a model enters an answer without end, every call waits: restart the Developer
([run it](../06-runbooks/run.md#when-it-fails)).

rows.title: The roles of the software factory — A role's folder
rows.summary: A role's folder
body: | File | What it is |
| `role.md` | front matter `id`, `title`, `stations`, `default` (the default assignment: `kind`, `provider`, `model`); the body: Mission, Inputs, Outputs, Definition of done, Never, Skills |
| `skills/*.md` | the how-tos the role may use; front matter `name`, `description`, `title_es` and `description_es` (below), and `prompt` when the skill is a prompt the Smart Graph serves |
| `templates/*.md` | the documents its stations write in the spec's folder (`specs/<id>/`); `{{name}}` is filled by the engine or the agent |

| `checks.toml` | the checks it proposes: `[[check]]` with `id`, `title`, `title_es`, `station`, `on`, `by` (`role` or `user`), and a `command` (a key of the `commands` of `.nuclear/builder.json`) or a `prompt` |

| `roster/en.json`, `roster/es.json` | the 40 employees the user can hire for the role: `role`, `stats` (the six stat names, once), `employees` (below); the same ids, genders, temperaments, years, recommenders and numbers in both languages, English the source |
| `roster/faces/<id>.webp` | each employee's portrait, painted by `faces.nuc` (below); never edited by hand |
| `roster/faces/thumb/<id>.webp` | its thumbnail, 128 × 128 WebP of quality 70 (about 3 KB), made by `faces.nuc` from the portrait: what the editors' tiles, cards, rows and chat avatars draw |

rows.title: The roles of the software factory — Localization
rows.summary: English is the source; what the screens read has its Spanish beside its English, in the same file, as the field's name with `_es`: skill's name in words).
body: English is the source; what the screens read has its Spanish **beside its English, in the same file**, as the field's
name with `_es`:
- a skill a member can switch on: `title_es` and `description_es` in its front matter (the English title is the
skill's name in words). A prompt of a local agent's step (`prompt: agent.<step>`) is never shown and has none;
- a check: `title_es` in `checks.toml`;
- the rosters are whole files per language (`roster/en.json`, `roster/es.json`) and the temperaments carry
`name` and `description` as `{ en, es }`: they were made per language from the start.
`nuclear-builder team roster --lang es` gives each skill's `skillTexts` in that language; a run's checks keep the
`title_es` and the screens show the one of their language. The text a model reads (a skill's body, a check's prompt,
a temperament's `voice`) stays English. `tests/test_roster.nuc` fails when a skill or a check the screens show has no
Spanish.

rows.title: The roles of the software factory — The tool and the model (outside the repository)
rows.summary: `--only <id>` remakes one face with the seed `faces.json` keeps (or `--seed <n>`, a new one, then kept); a change to the prompts takes `--force`, or `--only` for the faces it concerns.
body: `--only <id>` remakes one face with the seed `faces.json` keeps (or `--seed <n>`, a new one, then kept); a change
to the prompts takes `--force`, or `--only` for the faces it concerns. Look at every new face before it is checked
in: broken anatomy, text, a cartoon look or a face that does not match the gender or the temperament is made again.
`tests/test_roster.nuc` checks that the compendium has its temperaments with both names, a description, a voice and
a look; that every employee has a gender and a valid temperament (the same in both languages) and the profile's
fields, recommended by employees who exist; the spread of the genders per role; that every face is a WebP of at most
100 KB with its seed and prompt in `faces.json` and a thumbnail, a WebP of at most 10 KB, and no drawn face is left; and that a prompt is the same each time.

rows.title: The roles of the software factory — The tool and the model (outside the repository)
rows.summary: It runs 4 steps of Euler without guidance (FLUX.1-schnell's; the negative prompt kept in `faces.json` is not read by it), the diffusion model on the GPU and the text encoder on the processor.
body: It runs 4 steps of Euler without guidance (FLUX.1-schnell's; the negative prompt kept in `faces.json` is not read
by it), the diffusion model on the GPU and the text encoder on the processor. On an AMD Radeon 890M (integrated,
Vulkan, 28 GB of shared memory) one face takes 30 to 70 s, the first one about two minutes (the 200 in about two and a half hours).
```sh
nuclear check . --json && nuclear build .                         # the generator and its tests, into build/
cd build && python3 -c "from nuclear_roles.faces import main; main()"                      # the faces not yet made
python3 -c "from nuclear_roles.faces import main; main(['--only', 'dev-003', '--seed', '7'])"  # one again, another seed
python3 -c "from nuclear_roles.faces import main; main(['--force'])"                        # all again (after a prompt change)
python3 -c "from nuclear_roles.faces import main; main(['--thumbs'])"                       # only the thumbnails (no model)
cd .. && python3 -m pytest -q && (cd build && npx -y pyright nuclear_roles)   # the checks below; their types

body: - **`team-names.json`**: the word lists of the new-team wizard's *Suggest a name* (`nuclear-builder team
name-suggest`), per language: `{ "en" | "es": { "patterns", "adj", "noun", "thing", "suffix" } }`. A pattern names
lists in braces (`"The {adj} {noun} of {thing}"`), each filled at random; `{topic}` is a word of the team's purpose,
and a pattern with it is used only when there is one. Satirical, a cyberpunk office's dark humour; a Spanish pattern
agrees with its words (masculine plural nouns and adjectives).
- **`temperaments.json`**: the compendium of 25 workplace personalities, each `{ id, name: { en, es }, description:
{ en, es }, voice, look }`: `extrovert`, `introvert`, `shy`, `nerd`, `sarcastic`, `optimistic`, `grumpy`,
`perfectionist`, `chaotic`, `formal`, `joker`, `arrogant`, `paranoid`, `passive-aggressive`, `burnt-out` (the
burnt-out veteran), `micromanager`, `people-pleaser`, `know-it-all`, `workaholic`, `slacker`, `mentor`, `dramatic`
(the drama queen), `conspiracist`, `zen`, `overconfident` (the overconfident junior). The `description` is one
sentence for people (the screens); the `voice` is the text a member's prompt carries (how long they write, their
tone, their emoji and GIFs, and that the temperament never changes what is true); the `look` is how the portrait

rows.summary: shows it (expression, pose, styling).
body: shows it (expression, pose, styling). Each employee's `temperament` fits their bio; a team may give a member
another one (`personality.temperament` of the team file).
- **The faces**: a painted, lifelike cyberpunk bust portrait per employee, 512 × 512 WebP of quality 80 (20 to 40
KB), made on the developer's machine by an image model and checked in: nobody needs the model to use them.
`faces.nuc` (this folder is a small Nuclear project, `python` dialect, `nuclear.toml`) writes each employee's
prompt from the card (the role's neon as the rim light, the gender, the age the card says or one the dice pick,
the temperament's `look`, a detail of the bio such as a coffee cup) and a style shared by the whole set; the dice
(a seed from the id) pick the origin, the hair, two implants and the jacket. It runs the model once per employee
(a process), converts its PNG with ImageMagick (`magick`), and records the prompt and seed in
`roster/faces/faces.json`. It skips the faces already made, so a stopped run goes on where it was. Then it makes
each face's thumbnail (`roster/faces/thumb/<id>.webp`: `magick -resize 128x128 -quality 70`) where there is none or
the face is newer; `--thumbs` makes only the thumbnails, from the portraits already there, without the model. The

rows.summary: A skill whose front matter has `prompt:` is a prompt of the Smart Graph: `nuclear-graph ingest` puts the text after its front matter in the graph's `prompts` collection, served by `GET /v1/prompts/<prompt>` (the Developer's `Workbench`, the MCP server's `graph_prompt`).
body: A skill whose front matter has `prompt:` is a prompt of the Smart Graph: `nuclear-graph ingest` puts the text after
its front matter in the graph's `prompts` collection, served by `GET /v1/prompts/<prompt>` (the Developer's
`Workbench`, the MCP server's `graph_prompt`). Two kinds:
- **A use case** (`prompt: feature`): the validated guide of a kind of work, for a frontier model or as the
`{{guide}}` of a step.
- **An agent's step** (`prompt: agent.<step>`, the files `skills/step-<step>.md`): the whole prompt one step of a
Nuclear Developer agent sends to its model. `{{name}}` is filled by the agent (`Workbench.prompt`); a `## `
section all of whose values are empty is dropped whole, with the words written around them, so a prompt never shows
an empty heading nor says what to do with rows it lacks.

rows.title: The roles of the software factory
rows.summary: Every spec goes through six stations, each owned by a role (spec 011, ADR-platform-0005).
body: Every spec goes through six stations, each owned by a role (spec 011, ADR-platform-0005). A role is a folder of
files, the one source of what the role is: the local agents of the [Nuclear Developer](../nuclear_developer/AGENTS.md),
a provider's agent (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode) and a provider's model through an API all read the
same files (ADR-developer-0002). Nothing of a role is repeated in code.
| # | Station (`id`) | Role | Folder |
| 1 | Analysis (`analysis`) | Analyst | [`analyst/`](analyst/role.md) |
| 2 | Design (`design`) | Architect | [`architect/`](architect/role.md) |
| 3 | Tests first (`tests`) | Developer | [`developer/`](developer/role.md) |
| 4 | Code (`code`) | Developer | [`developer/`](developer/role.md) |
| 5 | Quality (`quality`) | QA | [`qa/`](qa/role.md) |
| 6 | Delivery (`delivery`) | DevOps | [`devops/`](devops/role.md) |
DevOps (`devops`) is the infrastructure (CI/CD, deployments and environments, containers, monitoring, secrets) and
the delivery (the definition of done, the documents, the user stories, the pull request after the user's approval,
never a merge). Its role id was `delivery` before spec 011's amendment: the engine reads that id as `devops` in a
team, a run and a command (`roles.nuc`'s `OLD_ROLES`), and its employees keep their ids (`del-NNN`).

rows.title: Analyst
rows.summary: The product owner: the owner of the product in the factory.
rows.body: The product owner: the owner of the product in the factory. The first station of every spec.

rows.title: Analyst — Definition of done
rows.summary: "fast" or "nice" left without a number or an example.
body: - Every acceptance criterion says what is checked and how (a test, a command, a person's look), with no "should",
"fast" or "nice" left without a number or an example.
- Every fact names its source (the client, a URL, a row of the Smart Graph); nothing is invented.
- Every open question is in `questions.md` with its default; the run stops at the gate after the analysis when one
is not answered and has no safe default.
- The resources a request describes are named in English, whatever language the request is in.

rows.title: Analyst — Inputs
rows.summary: Inputs
body: - The spec as the user wrote it (`specs/<id>/spec.md`: title, description, acceptance criteria, platform).
- The project card (`.nuclear/project.json`: platform, components, declarations) and the project's documents.
- The Smart Graph: its strategy for the request (`graph_strategy`), the playbooks, the capabilities and limits.
- The user's answers to the questions of a previous gate.

rows.title: Analyst — Mission
rows.summary: Understand what the user asks before anyone designs or writes it: ask the questions that change the answer, gather the facts from the client, the internet and the Smart Graph, and turn the request into acceptance criteria that a test or a person can check.
body: Understand what the user asks before anyone designs or writes it: ask the questions that change the answer, gather
the facts from the client, the internet and the Smart Graph, and turn the request into acceptance criteria that a
test or a person can check.

rows.title: Analyst — Never
rows.summary: Never
body: - Designs the solution, chooses components or writes code: that is the Architect's and the Developer's work.
- Invents a requirement, a field or a rule the user did not ask for; an assumption is written as a question.
- Names a dialect or a target language: the request is for a platform (`backend`, `mobile`, `web`).
- Changes the user's spec: it writes its own documents next to it.

rows.title: Analyst — Outputs
rows.summary: request, the facts and their sources, the resources, the acceptance criteria made checkable, what is out of scope.
body: - `specs/<id>/analysis.md` from [`templates/analysis.md`](templates/analysis.md): the request understood, the kind of
request, the facts and their sources, the resources, the acceptance criteria made checkable, what is out of scope.
- `specs/<id>/questions.md` from [`templates/questions.md`](templates/questions.md): the questions for the user, each
with why it matters and the default the run takes when it is not answered.
- The checks of the station, from [`checks.toml`](checks.toml), in the run's list.

rows.title: Analyst — Skills
rows.summary: guessing.
body: - [`skills/ask-the-client.md`](skills/ask-the-client.md): the questions that change the answer, and only those.
- [`skills/read-the-graph.md`](skills/read-the-graph.md): what the Smart Graph knows about the request, before
guessing.
- [`skills/write-acceptance-criteria.md`](skills/write-acceptance-criteria.md): criteria a test can check.
- [`skills/answer-a-question.md`](skills/answer-a-question.md) (prompt `chat`): answer the developer's question from
the facts given only.
- [`skills/step-chat.md`](skills/step-chat.md) (prompt `agent.chat`): the local assistant's whole prompt.
- [`skills/step-analyze.md`](skills/step-analyze.md) (prompt `agent.analyze`): the local analyst's resources table.

rows.title: Architect
rows.summary: The solutions architect and planner.
rows.body: The solutions architect and planner. The second station: from the analysis to the design and the plan.

rows.title: Architect — Definition of done
rows.summary: piece only uses pieces before it.
body: - Every acceptance criterion is served by at least one piece of the plan, and every piece by a criterion.
- What a generator can write is a generator call in the plan, never a piece for a model.
- Every piece names its path (from the platform's layout), its kind, every name it declares and what it uses; a
piece only uses pieces before it.
- The design follows the project's ADRs; a decision that departs from one is a proposed ADR, never a silent change.
- The diagrams use the names of the code and say what flows on every arrow.

rows.title: Architect — Inputs
rows.summary: standard (`nuclear gen inspect`).
body: - `specs/<id>/analysis.md` and the user's answers in `questions.md`.
- The project card (`.nuclear/project.json`), the project's `docs/02-architecture/` and `docs/03-adr/`.
- The Smart Graph: the platform's kinds and layout, the strategy of the request, the generators that write what is
standard (`nuclear gen inspect`).

rows.title: Architect — Mission
rows.summary: Decide how the accepted request is built on the platform: the components and their relations, the data model, the diagrams, the decisions (the ADRs of the project it follows, and the ones it proposes), and a plan the Developer can follow piece by piece, the generators first.
body: Decide how the accepted request is built on the platform: the components and their relations, the data model,
the diagrams, the decisions (the ADRs of the project it follows, and the ones it proposes), and a plan the Developer
can follow piece by piece, the generators first. Every choice is checked against the Smart Graph and the project.

rows.title: Architect — Never
rows.summary: Never
body: - Writes the code or the tests: it plans them.
- Changes an accepted ADR: a new one replaces it.
- Adds a component, a layer or a library the criteria do not need.
- Names a dialect or a target language in the design of a platform project.

rows.title: Architect — Outputs
rows.summary: data model, the C4 diagrams in Mermaid, the ADRs it follows.
body: - `specs/<id>/design.md` from [`templates/design.md`](templates/design.md): the components, their relations, the
data model, the C4 diagrams in Mermaid, the ADRs it follows.

body: Every piece comes from the tools, never written by hand where a tool writes it
([ADR-platform-0004](../../../docs/03-adr/0004-products-are-made-with-the-tools.md)):
- **CI/CD**: the project's commands in its line (`nuclear-builder line set commands=…`), the CI file exported from it
(`nuclear-builder export github|gitlab|bitbucket`), each stage one `nuclear-builder ci <stage>` (check, test,
security, artifacts, deploy). A failed pipeline is read from its stage, fixed in the line, exported again.
- **Deployments and environments**: the `deploy` command of the line (and `seed`, `integration` before it), one per
environment the project names; production only from the default branch, after the user's approval.
- **Containers**: a container image only from what the platform builds (`nuclear build`); where the platform cannot
write it yet, say so and record the missing capability in the roadmap of the tool that should.
- **Monitoring**: a backend's traces and metrics through the platform's telemetry (`plugins(telemetry = true)` and a
`Datadog`, `NewRelic`, `Grafana` or `Otlp` connection in `config/`), its keys from `env(...)`.
- **Secrets**: in the environment (`env("NAME")` in the code, the CI's own secret store, `testEnv(...)` for the
tests' fake values) or the system's keyring (the Builder's vault); never in a file of the repository, a log, a
document or a commit.

rows.title: Accessibility — Checklist
rows.summary: Checklist
body: - [ ] Every interactive element is a native element or standard widget, or has a role and label.
- [ ] Every non-decorative image and icon button has a translated label.
- [ ] Text and essential icons meet the contrast ratios; state is never color alone.
- [ ] Targets are at least 48 dp (mobile) / 24 px (web).
- [ ] The main task works at 200 % text size, with a screen reader, and by keyboard on web.
- [ ] Reduce-motion is respected; dialogs return focus; `nuclear check .` reports 0 errors; `nuclear test` is green.

rows.title: Accessibility — Pitfalls
rows.summary: Pitfalls
body: - Tappable containers with no role or label; icon buttons read as "button".
- Placeholder-only fields; errors shown only in red.
- Fixed-height rows that clip text at large sizes.
- Custom dropdowns, tabs and dialogs on web without keyboard support or focus management.
- Labels that repeat the role ("button submit") or are in another language than the UI.
- Disabling zoom on web.

rows.title: Accessibility — Steps
rows.summary: reading order, a visible focus ring, every action reachable by keyboard, Escape closes dialogs, focus returns to the opener when a dialog closes, no keyboard trap.
body: reading order, a visible focus ring, every action reachable by keyboard, Escape closes dialogs, focus returns to
the opener when a dialog closes, no keyboard trap.
9. **Announce changes**: a toast, a loading result or a new chat message is announced to screen readers (a live
region on web, a semantics announcement on mobile); a spinner has a label ("Loading orders").
10. **Motion and time**: respect the OS "reduce motion" setting (no parallax, short fades), no flashing above 3 per
second, no time limit without a way to extend it (session timeouts warn first: `SessionManager(timeout)`).
11. **Headings and structure** on web: one `h1` per screen, ordered headings, landmarks (`main`, `nav`), lists as
lists, and a page title per route.
12. **Test it**: TalkBack (Android) and VoiceOver (iOS, macOS) through one full task; keyboard only on web; the OS
text size at maximum; a contrast checker on the theme colors. Write what you checked in the work log.

rows.title: Accessibility — Steps
rows.summary: 1. Use the native element or standard widget for its job: a button is a `button` (web) or a toolkit button (mobile), not a tappable `div` or a gesture on a text.
body: 1. **Use the native element or standard widget** for its job: a button is a `button` (web) or a toolkit button
(mobile), not a tappable `div` or a gesture on a text. You get the role, focus and keyboard for free.
2. **Every meaningful image and icon has a label**: `alt` on web, a semantics label on mobile; decorative ones are
hidden from screen readers (`alt = ""`). Icon-only buttons need a label ("Delete order", not "trash").
3. **Labels come from translations** (`"orders.delete.label".tr()`): screen-reader text is user-facing text
4. **Forms**: each field has a visible label (not only a placeholder), errors are text next to the field and
announced, required fields say so, and the submit error moves focus to the first invalid field.
5. **Contrast**: text 4.5:1 against its background (3:1 for large text and for icons, borders of inputs and focus
rings); never color alone to say a state (add an icon or text to "error" red).
6. **Touch and click targets** at least 48x48 dp on mobile (24x24 CSS px minimum on web, 44 recommended), with
space between them.
7. **Text scaling**: the layout survives the OS text size at 200 %: no fixed heights on text, wrap instead of
clip, scroll when needed. Never disable scaling.
8. **Focus and keyboard** (web, and mobile with a keyboard or switch access): logical focus order following the

rows.title: Accessibility — The platform's tools
rows.summary: `nuclear make widget <name>` for a shared accessible widget used everywhere.
body: - `nuclear make screen <component> <screen>` (mobile) and `nuclear make stateless <component> <Name>` (web) for views;
`nuclear make widget <name>` for a shared accessible widget used everywhere.
- `nuclear device <device>` to try text scaling and orientation; `nuclear run` on a phone with the screen reader on.
- `nuclear test`: `@widget` tests can find widgets by their label text, so a missing label fails a test.
- `nuclear check .` before handing over.

rows.title: Accessibility — What the platform has
rows.summary: standard widgets carry semantics for TalkBack and VoiceOver, and its semantics widget labels a custom one.
body: - **Mobile**: views are the UI toolkit's widgets written in Nuclear (`nuclear help flutter`, §5); the toolkit's
standard widgets carry semantics for TalkBack and VoiceOver, and its semantics widget labels a custom one. Forms
(`form`, `FormTextField(..., label = ...)`) give each field a label and its errors.
- **Web**: views are HTML element functions with the attributes as named arguments (`img(src = ..., alt = ...)`,
`button(onClick = ..., children = ...)`; `nuclear help web`, §3.1): native elements bring their roles and
keyboard behaviour.
- **Not yet**: an accessibility check in the platform's tests (the framework's roadmap mentions `meetsGuideline`);
check by hand and with the OS's tools until then.

rows.title: Accessibility — When to use
rows.summary: Every screen, form and custom widget, on both UI platforms.
rows.body: Every screen, form and custom widget, on both UI platforms. The target is WCAG 2.2 level AA.

rows.title: Analytics events — Checklist
rows.summary: Checklist
body: - [ ] Every event is in the tracking plan with a question it answers.
- [ ] Names follow `object_action`, past tense, snake_case; each has a typed model.
- [ ] No personal data in any property (review the models).

rows.summary: Pitfalls
body: - Tracking before consent; ignoring a withdrawal.
- Event names that drift (`OrderComplete`, `order-completed`, `orderCompleted`) and split the data.
- Personal data in properties or in URLs sent as properties.
- One request per event: battery and data use; lost events when offline.
- Client clocks for ordering; no `eventId`, so retries double-count.
- Measuring revenue from client events instead of the backend's facts.

6. **One tracking service per app**: `nuclear make service analytics Tracker` with `track(event)`. It checks
consent, adds the common fields, and queues. Screens and state managers call a use case, not a provider SDK.
7. **Batch and retry**: keep events in a local table (mobile: a model with `@primary`), send in batches (every 30 s

rows.title: Audit logging — Checklist
rows.summary: Checklist
body: - [ ] Audited actions are listed in the spec; each writes an entry with actor, action, target, outcome, time.
- [ ] Entries are written inside the action's transaction; a test shows a rolled-back action leaves none.
- [ ] No route or repository method updates or deletes entries.
- [ ] The hash chain verifies; a test alters one row and the verification fails at it.
- [ ] Secrets are masked and personal data minimised in `changes`.
- [ ] Retention per action type is written down; `nuclear check .` reports 0 errors; `nuclear test` is green.

rows.title: Audit logging — Pitfalls
rows.summary: did not happen).
body: - Writing the audit entry after the transaction commits (lost on a crash) or before it (a record of something that
did not happen).
- An update or delete route on the audit table, or the app's database user able to rewrite it.
- Logging the whole request body (passwords, card data, personal data).
- Local times without a zone; the client's clock as `occurredAt`.
- Free-text `action` names that drift; no `requestId` to tie entries of one request together.
- Auditing only successes: denied attempts matter most in an investigation.

rows.title: Audit logging — Steps
rows.summary: 1. List the audited actions in the spec, each with its name (`account.frozen`, `role.granted`, `payment.refunded`, `profile.exported`).
body: 1. **List the audited actions** in the spec, each with its name (`account.frozen`, `role.granted`,
`payment.refunded`, `profile.exported`). Not every read: the sensitive ones.
2. **The entry** (`nuclear gen resource audit AuditEntry --source db --actions list,get --fields "..."`):
`id`, `occurredAt` (UTC, `@created`), `actorType` (`user` | `service` | `system`), `actorId`, `action`,
`targetType`, `targetId`, `outcome` (`success` | `denied` | `failed`), `reason?`, `changes` (the fields that
changed, before and after), `requestId`, `ip?`, `userAgent?`, `prevHash`, `hash`. **No create, update or
delete route**: only `list` and `get`, behind an auditor guard.
3. **Write it in the same transaction** as the action: the use case is `@transactional` and saves the entry with
the change, so an action never happens without its record (and a rolled-back action leaves none). For
`denied` outcomes (an `@acl` refusal, a 403) write the entry outside the failed transaction.
4. **One place builds entries**: an aggregate (`nuclear make aggregate audit Auditor`) used by the use cases, so
the fields and the hashing are written once. Listeners can audit events that are already facts
(`@consumer("payments.event")`), but the critical ones belong in the transaction.
5. **Append-only**: the repository has no update or delete method; in production the database user of the app

rows.title: Audit logging — Steps
rows.summary: gets INSERT and SELECT only on the table (in the migration or the database's grants).
body: gets INSERT and SELECT only on the table (in the migration or the database's grants).
6. **Tamper evidence**: `hash = sha256(prevHash + canonical JSON of the entry)`, chained in insert order (one
writer, or a per-day chain); a verification use case walks the chain and reports the first broken link.
Periodically copy the latest hash somewhere the app cannot rewrite (write-once storage, a signed export).
7. **Minimise what is stored**: `changes` lists field names and values, but masks secrets (passwords, tokens) and
keeps personal data only as needed (`privacy-gdpr`): an id instead of a name where possible.
8. **Retention**: keep as long as law or contract says (often 1-10 years per action type), then archive or delete
by whole periods; erasure requests usually do not apply to legal audit records, but the personal data inside
them must be the minimum (document the legal basis).
9. **Search**: index `(targetType, targetId)`, `actorId`, `occurredAt`, `action`; paginate (`paginate`) with
filters (see `search`). Exports for auditors are themselves audited.

rows.title: Authentication and sessions — Checklist
rows.summary: Checklist
body: - [ ] Passwords hashed with argon2id or bcrypt; no hash field in any answer model.
- [ ] Login and reset answer the same message for unknown and known emails.
- [ ] Refresh tokens are stored hashed, rotate on use, and reuse revokes the family.
- [ ] Lockout after N failures and a rate limit per IP; tests for both.
- [ ] Every protected route and screen is checked by a test without a session (401 / forward to login).
- [ ] Secrets come from `env(...)`; `nuclear check .` reports 0 errors; `nuclear test` is green.

rows.title: Authentication and sessions — Pitfalls
rows.summary: Pitfalls
body: - Saying "unknown email" vs "wrong password": account enumeration.
- Tokens in URLs or query strings (they reach access logs; the guards read only headers for this reason).
- Long-lived access tokens with no refresh rotation; refresh tokens stored in plain text.
- Keeping the token anywhere but `SessionManager` on the device (it uses the secure storage).
- Logging passwords or tokens: `Log` masks `password` and `token` keys in maps, but not inside a message string.
- A signing secret in code instead of `env(...)`.

rows.title: Authentication and sessions — Steps
rows.summary: 5. Refresh with rotation: each refresh revokes the used token and issues a new one in the same family; a reused (already revoked) token revokes the whole family (it was stolen).
body: 5. **Refresh with rotation**: each refresh revokes the used token and issues a new one in the same family; a reused
(already revoked) token revokes the whole family (it was stolen).
6. **Lockout**: increment `failedLogins`; after N (5-10) set `lockedUntil` with a growing wait; reset on success.
Rate-limit by IP too, so one attacker cannot lock every account.
7. **Logout** revokes the refresh token; "log out everywhere" revokes every token of the user.
8. **Password reset**: a single-use token (hash stored, 15-60 min), the same answer for unknown emails, and every
refresh token revoked after the change.
9. **Checking a token on a route**: until the platform has a guard kind for it, the use case receives the token's
claims through its parameters and checks them; never trust a user id sent in the body.
10. **Apps**: `nuclear make component session`, a login screen (`nuclear make screen session login`), a form with
`@email` and `@required`, and a `LoginUseCase` that calls the backend and `~session.start(auth, token =
auth.token, roles = auth.roles, expiresAt = ...)`. Protected screens use `loggedIn = { forward: LoginScreen }`;
a 401 ends the session by itself. Logout calls the backend, then `~session.destroy()`.

rows.title: Authentication and sessions — Steps
rows.summary: 1. Users (`nuclear gen resource users User --source db --fields "..."`): `id`, `email` (unique, stored lower case), `passwordHash`, `status` (`unverified` | `active` | `locked` | `disabled`), `failedLogins: int`, `lockedUntil: DateTime?`, `roles`, `createdAt`.
body: 1. **Users** (`nuclear gen resource users User --source db --fields "..."`): `id`, `email` (unique, stored lower
case), `passwordHash`, `status` (`unverified` | `active` | `locked` | `disabled`), `failedLogins: int`,
`lockedUntil: DateTime?`, `roles`, `createdAt`. The answer model never carries `passwordHash`.
2. **Hash passwords** with a slow, salted algorithm (argon2id, or bcrypt with cost >= 12) in a service. Nuclear's
standard library has no password hash: add the dialect's package with `nuclear add <package>` (this ties the
service to the dialect; keep it in that one service) and record the missing portable word in the platform's
roadmap. Never a plain or fast hash (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256 alone).
3. **Sign-up**: model with `@email`, `@minLength(12)` on the password; check it against a breached-password list if
possible; answer the same message whether the email exists or not; send a verification link with a single-use,
expiring token (store its hash, not the token).
4. **Login** use case: find by email, compare the hash in constant time, then issue a short **access token** (5-15
min) and a long **refresh token** (days). Store only the refresh token's hash, with `userId`, `expiresAt`,
`revokedAt?`, `familyId`. Every failure answers the same `Unauthorized("wrong email or password")`.

rows.title: Bank accounts and transfers — Checklist
rows.summary: Checklist
body: - [ ] No edited balance column; the balance is a sum of entries (or a snapshot written with them).
- [ ] Every `LedgerTransaction` has entries that sum to 0 (a test checks it after each use case).
- [ ] IBAN check digits are validated; a test with a valid and a mistyped IBAN.
- [ ] `CreateTransfer` is `@transactional`, idempotent by key, and refuses over-limit and insufficient funds.
- [ ] A test runs two transfers that together exceed the balance: only one passes.
- [ ] Only `active` accounts send money; KYC changes come from the provider.
- [ ] `nuclear check .` reports 0 errors and `nuclear test` is green.

rows.title: Bank accounts and transfers — Pitfalls
rows.summary: Pitfalls
body: - A mutable `balance` column updated with `balance = balance - x`: lost updates and no history.
- Entries that do not sum to zero; a transfer that writes the debit and fails before the credit (no transaction).
- Mixing currencies in one sum; converting without storing the rate used.
- Checking the balance outside the transaction, then writing: two transfers overdraw the account.
- Trusting the client for the source account: check that the session's user owns `fromAccountId`.
- Validating an IBAN with a regex only (no mod-97), or storing it with spaces (duplicates).
- Deleting a ledger row to "fix" it.

rows.title: CI pipelines — Checklist
rows.summary: Checklist
body: - [ ] `.nuclear/builder.json` holds the project's commands and is committed.
- [ ] `nuclear-builder ci check test security` passes locally.
- [ ] The CI file was produced by `nuclear-builder export ...` after the last change of the line.
- [ ] The pipeline runs `nuclear check . --json`, `nuclear fmt --check .` and `nuclear test`.
- [ ] No secret appears in the line or the CI file.
- [ ] The project's docs say how its CI runs and what each stage does.

rows.title: CI pipelines — Pitfalls
rows.summary: tool as a `security` command run inside `build/` (it names a dialect's tool, so say so in the project's docs), or record the gap.
body: - Editing the exported YAML by hand: the next export overwrites it. Change the line, export again.
- The default `security` stage only re-runs the check: the platform has no dependency audit. Add the target's audit
tool as a `security` command run inside `build/` (it names a dialect's tool, so say so in the project's docs), or
record the gap.
- `nuclear fmt --check` is not in the defaults: add it, or formatting drifts.
- A mobile project's stages need Flutter on the runner; confirm the exported file provides it before relying on it.
- Secrets for `deploy` belong in the CI service's secret store, read as environment variables; never in
`.nuclear/builder.json`, which is committed.
- The agent stations of the software factory run on your machine; the server only checks their result.

rows.title: CI pipelines — Steps
rows.summary: 1. See the line: `nuclear-builder line show`.
body: 1. **See the line**: `nuclear-builder line show`. The defaults come from the platform: `check`
(`nuclear check . --json`), `build` (`nuclear build`, plus `nuclear install` on backend and web), `test`
(`nuclear test`), `security` (empty: the check runs again), `artifacts` (`nuclear build`; `nuclear build web` on
mobile), `seed`, `integration`, `deploy` (empty).
2. **Run it locally first**: `nuclear-builder ci check test security` runs those stages where you are, exactly as
the server will.
3. **Add what the project needs** with `nuclear-builder line set KEY=<json>`; `commands` is merged with the
defaults:
`nuclear-builder line set 'commands={"security":["nuclear check . --json","nuclear fmt --check ."]}'`.
`branches` picks the branches the CI runs on (default `main` and `feature/**`).
4. **Export the CI file**: `nuclear-builder export github` (`.github/workflows/nuclear-builder.yml`),
`nuclear-builder export gitlab` (`.gitlab-ci.yml`) or `nuclear-builder export bitbucket`
(`bitbucket-pipelines.yml`). Each job installs NuclearLang and runs the stage's commands; `artifacts` uploads
`build/`. Export again after every change of the line.
5. **Read the file** before committing it, and commit it with `.nuclear/builder.json`.
6. **When a stage fails**, run the same stage locally (`nuclear-builder ci test`), fix the `.nuc`, never the CI file.

rows.title: CI pipelines — The stages and their order
rows.summary: The stages and their order
body: | Stage | Runs (defaults) | Fails when |
| `check` | `nuclear check . --json` | any compiler or architecture error |
| `test` | the `build` commands, then `nuclear test` | a build or a test fails |
| `security` | the `security` commands, else the check again | a command exits non-zero |
| `artifacts` | `nuclear build` (mobile: `nuclear build web`), uploads `build/` | the build fails |
| `deploy` | `seed`, `integration`, `deploy` commands | any of them fails |

rows.title: Clean architecture with components — Checklist
rows.summary: Checklist
body: - [ ] Each component maps to one business capability and has its facade.

- [ ] Every file sits where `nuclear help layout --platform

` says its kind goes.
- [ ] Rules live in use cases (or services/aggregates they call), never in controllers or views.
- [ ] Other components use only the facade and the public kinds; no N0301/N0302.

rows.title: Clean architecture with components — Pitfalls
rows.summary: write them.
body: - Interfaces or classes that only pass data around: the layers exist in the generated code; in Nuclear you do not
write them.
- Rules in a controller, a view or a state manager: move them into a use case.
- A "utils" or "common" component everyone calls: put shared models in `shared/`, shared logic in a service of its
owning component, and cross-component calls through facades.
- One component reaching into another's repository to save a step: N0302, and the coupling the rule prevents.
- `test/` may use any declaration: do not copy a test's shortcut into production code.
- Moving files by hand between components: the kind follows the folder; re-run `nuclear check` after any move.

Generate, do not lay out by hand: `nuclear gen resource` writes models, repository, use cases, facade aliases and the controller or screen at their places; `nuclear make <kind> <component> <Name>` (backend, web) or the mobile `nuclear make usecase|repository|service|aggregate <component>…
body: 4. **Generate, do not lay out by hand**: `nuclear gen resource` writes models, repository, use cases, facade aliases
and the controller or screen at their places; `nuclear make <kind> <component> <Name>` (backend, web) or the
mobile `nuclear make usecase|repository|service|aggregate <component> <name>` for the rest;
`nuclear gen usecase` wires a use case into the facade (and a route on the backend).
5. **Respect the dependency rules** (checked by `nuclear check`): a use case is used only from the facade (N0301); a
service only from a use case or an aggregate; an aggregate only from a use case; a repository only from a use
case or an aggregate (or a `tools` on the backend). From another component only its facade and its public kinds
are visible (N0302): backend `appcomponent`, `model`, `entity`, `tools`, `agent`, `state`, `graph`; mobile and web
the `appcomponent`, models, events, global components, guards and screens.
6. **Cross-component work** goes through facades or events: component A calls `B`'s facade, or publishes an event
(`~publish` on the backend, `Events.publish` on mobile and web) that B listens to.
7. **Dependencies are typed parameters of the header**, injected by type: never construct a repository or a
connection by hand.
8. `nuclear check . --json` must print `[]`; `nuclear test`.

rows.title: Clean architecture with components — Steps
rows.summary: 1. See the layout: `nuclear help layout --platform backend|mobile|web` prints where each kind's file goes.
body: 1. **See the layout**: `nuclear help layout --platform backend|mobile|web` prints where each kind's file goes.
Backend: `components/<c>/data/entities/`, `data/repositories/`, `domain/models/`, `domain/usecases/`,
`domain/services/`, `domain/aggregates/`, `api/` (controllers), `events/` (listeners), `ai/`. Mobile and web:
`data/` (repositories), `domain/models/`, `domain/usecases/`, `presentation/<screen>/` with `managers/` and
`state_models/`. Shared pieces in `shared/`; app configuration in `config/project_config.nuc`.
2. **One component per business capability** (orders, payments, catalog), not per technical layer. Create it with
`nuclear gen component <component>` (its facade and config), or let `nuclear gen resource` create it.
3. **Place each piece by its job**:
- `repository`: the data of one entity or one API; queries only;
- `usecase`: one business operation, one `exec` returning `Result`; the rules live here;
- `service`: helpers several use cases share (mapping, calculations without state);
- `aggregate`: rules several use cases share that compose repositories or services (a cart with its totals);
- `appcomponent`: the facade, one alias per use case (`create() = CreateTask.exec`);
- backend `controller`: routes calling the facade; mobile/web `statemanager`: states from the facade; views
show states.

rows.title: Code review — Checklist
rows.summary: Checklist
body: - [ ] `nuclear check . --json` prints `[]`, `nuclear fmt --check .` lists nothing, `nuclear test` is green.
- [ ] Standard code came from `gen`/`make`; nothing under `build/` or `contracts/` was edited.
- [ ] No target-language file or target library name was added to platform code.
- [ ] Layers and component boundaries are respected; logic sits in its kind.
- [ ] Each criterion and error path has a test; no test was weakened.
- [ ] The project's docs and roadmap changed with the code.
- [ ] Every comment names a file, a line and a concrete fix.

rows.title: Code review — Pitfalls
rows.summary: Pitfalls
body: - Approving because the check is green: the check proves the code compiles, not that it does what the spec asks.
- Reviewing the generated target code instead of the `.nuc`.
- Accepting a word that "looks right": Nuclear is not TypeScript, Dart or Python; look it up.
- Asking for an abstraction, option or wrapper nobody needs: the golden rule is minimal readable Nuclear.
- Letting docs slide to a later change: the rule is the same change.

rows.title: Code review — Steps
rows.summary: 1. Let the tools speak first.
body: 1. **Let the tools speak first.** In the project: `nuclear check . --json` (must print `[]`), `nuclear fmt --check .`
(must list nothing), `nuclear test` (green). Or the whole line: `nuclear-builder ci check test security`. A red
tool is the first comment; the rest waits.
2. **Was it made with the tools?** Each new resource, screen, use case and kind should come from `nuclear gen` or
`nuclear make` (`nuclear gen inspect` shows what the project has). Hand-written CRUD, repositories that duplicate
a contract's, or skeletons written by hand are a request to regenerate.
3. **Generated code untouched.** No change under `build/`, no edit of `contracts/<name>/*.nuc`, no `.py`, `.ts`,
`.dart` written for a feature. Migrations in `migrations/` are reviewed as code: a drop that should be a rename
loses data.
4. **Architecture.** A use case is called only from the facade; a service from a use case or an aggregate; a
repository from a use case, an aggregate (or a `tools` on the backend); another component only through its
`appcomponent` (N0301/N0302 catch most; read for logic placed in the wrong layer: rules in a controller or a
view, queries in a use case instead of the repository).
5. **The platform's words, not the target's.** Platform code names Nuclear's standard library only (`nuclear help

rows.title: Code review — Steps
rows.summary: library`); a React, Flutter, FastAPI or npm/pub/PyPI name in platform code is a bug, unless the file is meant to use that package's definitions and the docs say so.
body: library`); a React, Flutter, FastAPI or npm/pub/PyPI name in platform code is a bug, unless the file is meant to
use that package's definitions and the docs say so. Names are camelCase in the `.nuc`, whatever the dialect.
6. **Behaviour and errors.** Use cases return `Result` with the platform's errors (`NotFound`, `Invalid`,
`Unauthorized`, `Forbidden`, `Conflict`); edge cases (empty, repeated, unauthorised, concurrent) have tests;
writes spanning several rows are `@transactional`.
7. **Tests.** Every acceptance criterion has a `@test`; no test deleted or weakened; mocks only at the repository.
8. **Security and performance** at a glance: secrets from `env(...)`, guards on private routes, no list without
pagination, no awaited call in a loop (skills `security-review-owasp`, `performance-load`).
9. **Docs in the same change.** The project's `AGENTS.md`, `docs/`, roadmap (a done item deleted, half-done work
recorded). For a compiler or dialect change: a new diagnostic documented in
`nuclearlang/docs/07-reference/diagnostics.md`, every dialect word in its `docs.toml`, goldens regenerated and
their diff read, and the parser unchanged per dialect.
10. **Write the review**: each comment with file and line, what is wrong, why, and the fix (a command to run or the
Nuclear to change). Separate blocking from optional.

- `nuclear help <word> --dialect <d>` to confirm a word exists before accepting it.
- `nuclear-builder run show <id>`, `nuclear-builder run journal <id>`, `nuclear-builder checks <id>` for a factory run.
- MCP: `nuclear_check`, `developer_review` (keeps the lead's corrections as examples for the local developer).

rows.title: File uploads — Checklist
rows.summary: Checklist
body: - [ ] Type allow-list and size limit per purpose, checked on request and again on completion.
- [ ] Storage keys are server-made UUID paths; no user file name in a key.
- [ ] Presigned URLs expire in minutes; downloads check the caller's right first.
- [ ] Only `ready` files are visible; a test covers a rejected file.
- [ ] Orphan `pending` uploads and files of deleted accounts are removed.
- [ ] Keys come from `env(...)`; `nuclear check .` reports 0 errors; `nuclear test` is green.

rows.title: File uploads — Pitfalls
rows.summary: Pitfalls
body: - Trusting the client's content type or file extension; serving uploads from the app's own domain as HTML (XSS).
- Using the user's file name in the storage key (path traversal, collisions).
- Presigned URLs that last hours, or that do not pin type and size.
- Showing a file before the scan finished.
- Base64 files inside JSON bodies: three times the memory, request size limits.
- Leaving GPS coordinates in photo metadata.

rows.title: File uploads — Steps
rows.summary: 1. The metadata (`nuclear gen resource files StoredFile --source db --fields "..."`): `id` (UUID), `ownerId`, `purpose` (`avatar` | `receipt` | `attachment`), `key` (the object's path in the bucket, made by the server: `<purpose>/<ownerId>/<uuid>`), `contentType`, `size: int` (bytes), `checksum?`,…
body: 1. **The metadata** (`nuclear gen resource files StoredFile --source db --fields "..."`): `id` (UUID), `ownerId`,
`purpose` (`avatar` | `receipt` | `attachment`), `key` (the object's path in the bucket, made by the server:
`<purpose>/<ownerId>/<uuid>`), `contentType`, `size: int` (bytes), `checksum?`, `status`: `pending` →
`uploaded` → `scanning` → `ready` | `rejected`, `createdAt`.
2. **Limits per purpose**, in one service: allowed types (`image/jpeg`, `image/png`, `image/webp` for an avatar;
`application/pdf` for a receipt) and a maximum size (5 MB, 20 MB). Allow-list, never deny-list.
3. **Ask for an upload** (`POST files/uploads` with `purpose`, `contentType`, `size`, the file name for display):
validate the limits, save the row `pending`, and answer a presigned PUT URL that expires in minutes and fixes
the content type and the maximum length. The storage API (S3-compatible or another) is an HTTP repository or a
target package (`nuclear add <package>`, which ties that service to the dialect); its keys come from `env(...)`.
4. **The client uploads** the bytes with a PUT to that URL, showing progress, with retries on network failures
and a cancel button; large files use the storage's multipart upload.
5. **Confirm**: `POST files/{id}/complete`; the backend checks the object exists, its real size and type (read the

rows.title: File uploads — Steps
rows.summary: first bytes: magic numbers, not the extension), then `scanning`.
body: first bytes: magic numbers, not the extension), then `scanning`.
6. **Scan** with an antivirus service (an HTTP repository) and set `ready` or `rejected`; only `ready` files are
linked or shown. Images: strip EXIF metadata (location!) and make the resized copies the app shows.
7. **Download**: private files are served by short-lived presigned GET URLs made after checking the caller may
read that file; public files (avatars) through a CDN URL.
8. **Clean up**: `pending` rows older than a day and their objects; the old avatar when a new one is ready; every
file of a deleted account (`privacy-gdpr`).
9. **Mobile**: picking a file or a photo needs the dialect's picker package (`nuclear add <package>`); ask the
camera or photos permission only when the user taps "add photo". Compress images before uploading.

- `nuclear gen usecase files RequestUpload --route "POST files/uploads"`, `nuclear gen usecase files CompleteUpload --route "POST files/{id}/complete"`

(a model, a path or query value), with no multipart body. So the file never goes through the API: the client

rows.title: Translations and localization — Checklist
rows.summary: Checklist
body: - [ ] No user-facing literal text in views; every text is a key in the component's dictionary.
- [ ] Every locale has the same keys (a check fails on a missing one).
- [ ] Arguments are named placeholders; no concatenated sentences.
- [ ] Dates, numbers and money are formatted with the current locale.
- [ ] One screen is checked in an RTL locale and with long translations.
- [ ] `nuclear check .` reports 0 errors and `nuclear test` is green.

rows.title: Translations and localization — Pitfalls
rows.summary: Pitfalls
body: - Concatenated sentences and text inside images.
- `count == 1 ? "item" : "items"`: wrong in most languages.
- Hard-coded date formats (`dd/MM/yyyy`) and decimal separators.
- Left/right paddings that do not mirror in RTL.
- Keys renamed in one locale only; the fallback hiding a missing translation in development.
- Translating backend error messages on the server with the server's locale instead of the user's.

rows.title: Translations and localization — Steps
rows.summary: 1. No literal user-facing text in views.
body: 1. **No literal user-facing text in views.** Every text on screen is a key: `Text("orders.list.empty".tr())`.
Name keys by meaning and place (`orders.checkout.pay_button`), not by the English words.
2. **One dictionary per component**: `assets/i18n/en/orders.json`, `assets/i18n/es/orders.json`, same keys in
both; deleting the component deletes its texts. Shared words in `shared.json`.
3. **Arguments, never concatenation**: `"Hi {name}"` with `tr({ "name": ... })`; word order changes between
languages, so `"Hi " + name` breaks.
4. **Plurals** until the platform has them: separate keys chosen in code (`orders.count.zero`, `.one`, `.other`)
and pass the number as an argument. Remember some languages have more forms (Arabic six, Polish three): keep
the choice in one helper so it can move to the platform's word later.
5. **Locale formats**: dates, times, numbers and money are formatted with the locale (`Translations.locale`), never
by hand: `1,234.50` vs `1.234,50`, day/month order, 24 h clocks, the currency symbol's side. Store dates in UTC
and amounts as minor units; format only at display.
6. **Right to left**: with an RTL locale the toolkit mirrors the layout when its delegates and the locale are
passed (`main.nuc` above). Use start/end paddings and alignments instead of left/right; mirror directional

rows.title: Translations and localization — Steps
rows.summary: icons (back arrows), not logos or media controls; test a screen in Arabic.
body: icons (back arrows), not logos or media controls; test a screen in Arabic.
7. **Text expansion**: German and Finnish are ~30 % longer; leave room, allow wrapping, test with long strings.
8. **The language picker** lists each language in its own name ("Español", "English") and calls
`~Translations.use(code)`; save the choice in the user's profile too (`user-profiles`) so emails match.
9. **Check the dictionaries**: a test (or a script in the project's checks) compares the key sets of every locale
and fails on a missing key; review translations with a native speaker.

rows.title: Translations and localization — The platform's tools
rows.summary: new dictionary owner.
body: - `Translations(...)` in `appConfig` `globals`; `.tr()`; `~Translations.use(...)`; `~Translations.refresh()`.
- `nuclear new <name> -p mobile` gives the project layout with `assets/`; `nuclear make component <component>` for a
new dictionary owner.
- `nuclear help example/clean-flutter-project` shows translations used in screens and forms.
- `nuclear run`, `nuclear device` to see each locale; `nuclear test` for the key checks.

body: server-rendered texts (emails) in templates per locale chosen from the user's profile.
- **Not yet**: plurals in `tr` (an idea in the mobile roadmap), a warning for a missing key.

rows.title: Translations and localization — What the platform has
rows.summary: `Translations(locales = ["en", "es"], fallback = "en")` in the `globals` of `appConfig`.
body: - **Mobile** (`nuclear help flutter`, §6.16; example: `nuclear help example/clean-flutter-project`):
`Translations(locales = ["en", "es"], fallback = "en")` in the `globals` of `appConfig`. Texts are JSON
dictionaries, **one per component and per locale**, in `assets/i18n/<locale>/<component>.json` (`shared.json`
for the whole app). A key is `<file>.<path inside the file>`: `"session.login.title".tr()`, with arguments
`"session.login.hi".tr({ "name": auth.name })` for `"Hi {name}"`. The language is the stored one, else the
device's, else `fallback`; `~Translations.use("es")` changes it, remembers it and rebuilds the app keeping its
state. `main.nuc` passes `Translations.locale`, `Translations.supportedLocales` and `Translations.delegates` to
the app widget. A missing key falls back to `fallback`, then Synapsis's own texts, then shows the key.
`remote = RemoteDictionaries(url = ...)` updates texts without a release (versioned `manifest.json`, downloaded
in the background, used only when complete).
- **Web**: translations are **not in this version** (the web platform's roadmap); they will come with the mobile
platform's words. Until then keep texts in one place per component and do not invent a mechanism.
- **Backend**: no translations word. Answer stable error codes and let the client translate them, or keep

rows.title: Translations and localization — When to use
rows.summary: A second language, a language picker, dates, numbers and prices that follow the user's locale, an Arabic or Hebrew version.
body: A second language, a language picker, dates, numbers and prices that follow the user's locale, an Arabic or
Hebrew version.

rows.title: Maps and geolocation — Checklist
rows.summary: Checklist
body: - [ ] The precision needed is written in the spec; the lowest that works is requested.
- [ ] Permission is asked in context; denied, denied forever and services-off paths work (tests).
- [ ] Tracking stops when not visible and uses a distance filter.
- [ ] Coordinates are validated on the backend; nearby queries use an indexed bounding box.
- [ ] Provider keys live on the backend in `env(...)`; attribution is shown.
- [ ] Location retention and precision follow `privacy-gdpr`; `nuclear check .` reports 0 errors; `nuclear test` is green.

rows.title: Maps and geolocation — Pitfalls
rows.summary: Pitfalls
body: - Asking for location at first launch with no context: most users deny, and many forever.
- Requesting "always" when "while in use" is enough (store rejection, user distrust).
- A continuous GPS stream left running in the background: battery drain.
- `ORDER BY distance` over the whole table with no bounding box.
- The geocoding key inside the app binary.
- Storing precise histories "just in case".

rows.title: Maps and geolocation — Steps
rows.summary: 6. Geocoding: the provider (an HTTP repository, key from `env(...)`) is called from the backend, not the app, so the key stays secret and answers can be cached (`~cacheSet` with plugin `redis`, or a table).
body: 6. **Geocoding**: the provider (an HTTP repository, key from `env(...)`) is called from the backend, not the app,
so the key stays secret and answers can be cached (`~cacheSet` with plugin `redis`, or a table). Respect the
provider's terms on caching and attribution. Debounce address autocomplete (see `search`).
7. **Maps on the client**: the map widget in one `stateful` of the component; markers from the use case's models;
cluster many markers; show the provider's attribution.
8. **Privacy**: location is personal data (`privacy-gdpr`). Store the least: a rounded position or the city when
the exact one is not needed; keep tracks only as long as the purpose needs; never log raw coordinates; show
other users an approximate position unless they chose to share it.
9. **Tests**: the position service behind a use case lets a test mock it (`@mock([...])` on mobile); test denied
permission and services off, not only success.

rows.title: Maps and geolocation — Steps
rows.summary: 1. Ask why before asking where.
body: 1. **Ask why before asking where.** Decide the precision the feature needs: city (coarse, ~km) for "events near
you", street (~100 m) for a store finder, precise (~10 m) only for navigation or delivery. Ask for the
coarsest that works.
2. **Permissions**: ask "while in use" when the user taps the feature, after a screen that says why; "always"
(background) only for a feature that truly needs it, with its own explanation (the stores review it).
Handle every answer: granted, denied, denied forever (send to the system settings), location services off,
approximate only (iOS, Android 12+). The feature must still work with a typed city or a map pick.
3. **Battery**: one position for a one-off lookup, not a stream; for tracking, a distance filter (move > 50 m) and
a time interval, stop when the screen closes, and lower accuracy when precision is not needed.
4. **Coordinates**: `latitude` and `longitude` as `double` in WGS84 degrees, with `accuracy` in meters and the
`capturedAt` time. Validate ranges on the backend (`@min(-90) @max(90)`, `@min(-180) @max(180)`).
5. **Nearby queries** on the backend: a bounding box first (`between` on latitude and longitude, both indexed with
`@column(index = true)`), then the exact haversine distance in a service, sorted and limited. For large sets,
the database's geo index (PostGIS) written in the migration file.

rows.title: Maps and geolocation — The platform's tools
rows.summary: The platform's tools
body: - `nuclear add <package>` (mobile: the position and map packages of the dialect); `nuclear remove <package>`.
- `nuclear make service places Position`, `nuclear make stateful <name>` (mobile, the map widget).
- `nuclear gen resource places Geocode --source rest:<provider base url> --actions get` (backend).
- `nuclear gen resource places Place --source db --fields "name:string latitude:double longitude:double"`
- `nuclear migrate make "place indexes"`; `nuclear device` to try it in a phone window; `nuclear test`.

rows.title: Maps and geolocation — What the platform has
rows.summary: No location, map or geocoding word in any platform yet.
body: No location, map or geocoding word in any platform yet. On mobile, the device position and the map widget come
from the dialect's packages through `nuclear add <package>`; that code is tied to the dialect, so keep it in one
service (position) and one widget (map), and record the missing portable words in the mobile platform's roadmap.
Geocoding and routing are other APIs: HTTP repositories with `--source rest:<url>`.
