rows.body: "Near me" lists, a map with markers, delivery or ride tracking, address autocomplete, check-ins.

rows.title: Notifications — Checklist
rows.summary: Checklist
body: - [ ] Business components only publish events; the notifications component decides and sends.
- [ ] `dedupeKey` is unique; a test delivers the same event twice and gets one notification.
- [ ] Preferences and quiet hours are checked per channel, in the user's time zone; tests for both.
- [ ] Mandatory types cannot be disabled; marketing needs opt-in.
- [ ] Invalid device tokens and bounced addresses are removed.
- [ ] Provider keys come from `env(...)`; `nuclear check .` reports 0 errors; `nuclear test` is green.

rows.title: Notifications — Pitfalls
rows.summary: Pitfalls
body: - Sending from inside the business use case: a slow email provider slows the order; a failure rolls it back.
- No dedupe: at-least-once event delivery sends the same push twice.
- Quiet hours computed in UTC; preferences ignored for one channel.
- Stale device tokens never cleaned; tokens kept after logout (another user gets the push).
- Personal or sensitive data in push text (it shows on the lock screen).
- Building the deep link from untrusted data without checking the user can open it.

rows.title: Notifications — Steps
rows.summary: 1. One event in, many channels out.
body: 1. **One event in, many channels out.** The component where the thing happens only publishes a domain event
(`~publish("orders.shipped", {...})`). A `notifications` component has a `listener` with `@consumer` per topic
that decides who is told, by which channel, and writes a `Notification` row. Business code never sends an email.
2. **The notification** (`nuclear gen resource notifications Notification --source db --fields "..."`): `id`,
`userId`, `type` (`"order.shipped"`), `title`, `body` (or a template key + data, rendered in the user's
locale), `data` (ids for the deep link), `dedupeKey` (unique), `createdAt`, `readAt?`.
3. **Deliveries**: one row per channel (`notificationId`, `channel`: `push` | `email` | `inapp`, `status`:
`queued` → `sent` | `failed` | `skipped`, `attempts`, `lastError?`, `sentAt?`). Retry `failed` with growing
waits up to a limit; a permanent error (invalid token, bounced address) stops and cleans up.
4. **Preferences** (`NotificationPreference`: `userId`, `type`, `channel`, `enabled`): defaults per type, editable by
the user. Security and legal messages (password changed, receipts) cannot be turned off; marketing is off until
the user opts in (`privacy-gdpr`).
5. **Quiet hours**: `quietStart`, `quietEnd` and the IANA `timeZone` of the user's profile. A non-urgent push inside

rows.title: Notifications — Steps
rows.summary: reason), and a global `component` with `@on(...)` reacts.
body: reason), and a global `component` with `@on(...)` reacts. Ask the OS permission at a meaningful moment, not at
first launch.

rows.title: Notifications — Steps
rows.summary: them is delayed to the end (or folded into the in-app inbox); urgent types (security) go through.
body: them is delayed to the end (or folded into the in-app inbox); urgent types (security) go through. Compute in
the user's time zone, not the server's.
6. **Deduplicate and group**: `dedupeKey` (`"order.shipped:<orderId>"`) stops repeats when an event is delivered
twice; group bursts ("3 new messages") within a short window.
7. **Device tokens** (`DeviceToken`: `userId`, `token` unique, `platform`, `lastSeenAt`): registered after login,
refreshed when the push service rotates it, deleted on logout and when the service says it is invalid.
8. **Providers**: email (an SMTP relay or an email API) and push (the platform's push service) are other APIs:
HTTP repositories (`--source rest:<url>`) with keys from `env(...)`. Respect rate limits; batch where the API
allows.
9. **In-app**: a `GET notifications` paginated (`paginate(page, size)`), `POST notifications/{id}/read`, an unread
count. With the app's WebSocket (`WebSocketServer`, plugin `websocket`) the backend pushes new ones by topic;
the web app listens with `@on("notifications.${userId}")` on a repository method returning `Stream<T>`.
10. **Mobile**: receiving pushes needs the dialect's push package (`nuclear add <package>`, which ties that code to

rows.title: Offline-first sync — Checklist
rows.summary: Checklist
body: - [ ] Offline-writable models have client UUIDs, a version and a tombstone field.
- [ ] Every write goes to the local table and the pending queue; the UI reads the local table.
- [ ] A test group with `@offline` creates, edits and deletes, then syncs with the network back.
- [ ] Each queued change carries an idempotency key; a retried change is applied once on the backend.
- [ ] A 409 follows the conflict rule written for that model; a test covers it.
- [ ] Logout clears personal local data; `nuclear check .` reports 0 errors; `nuclear test` is green.

rows.title: Offline-first sync — Pitfalls
rows.summary: Pitfalls
body: - Server-generated ids for offline creates: the app cannot reference the row until it syncs.
- Hard deletes: the other devices never learn the row is gone. Use tombstones and purge later.
- Sending changes out of order (an update before its create).
- Retrying a POST without an idempotency key: duplicates.
- Clock skew: never decide conflicts with the device's clock; use server versions.
- Changing `encrypted` after the first run: the tables must be cleared (a table is read with its cipher).
- `WebSocket` on mobile uses `dart:io` and does not work on the web build.

rows.title: Offline-first sync — Steps
rows.summary: entry and store the server's version; on a transient failure stop and retry later with growing waits; on a permanent 4xx mark it failed and show it to the user.
body: entry and store the server's version; on a transient failure stop and retry later with growing waits; on a
permanent 4xx mark it failed and show it to the user.
6. **Conflicts**: the backend compares `baseVersion` with the row's version and answers 409 when they differ.
Choose per model and write it down: last-writer-wins (simple, loses data), server-wins (the device takes the
server's row), field-level merge, or ask the user. Never resolve silently for money or legal data.
7. **Pull**: `GET <resource>?since=<cursor>` returns rows changed after the cursor, tombstones included; save them
with `saveAll`, then store the new cursor. Pull after pushing.
8. **Session end**: `~session.destroy()` empties the response cache; clear the local tables of personal data too
(`local<Model>().clear()`), after warning if pending changes would be lost.

rows.title: Offline-first sync — Steps
rows.summary: 1. Pick what works offline, per screen: read-only (cached rows), or read-write (queued changes).

small: each offline-writable model costs a queue and conflict rules.
2. **Give every row a client id**: `@primary` `id: string`, a UUID made on the device, so a row created offline
has its final id before the server sees it. Add `version: int` (or `updatedAt` from the server) and
`deleted: boolean` (a tombstone instead of removing it).
3. **Reads**: the repository with `saveLocal = true`; the use case calls the request and, on `HttpError.offline`
or `Err`, falls back to `<method>AsLocal()`. The screen shows that the data may be stale (last synced time).
4. **Writes**: the use case writes the row to the local table **and** an entry to a `PendingChange` table
(`id`, `entity`, `entityId`, `operation`: `create` | `update` | `delete`, `payload`, `baseVersion`,
`attempts`, `createdAt`), in that order, then returns `Ok` at once. The UI reads the local table.

by a pull-to-refresh) sends the pending changes **in order**, one at a time or in a batch endpoint, each with
an idempotency key (the change's id) so a retry after a timeout does not duplicate it. On success, delete the

body: - **The local database** (ADR-mobile-0006): a model with `@primary` has a local table, encrypted by default
(`LocalDatabase(encrypted = true)` in `appConfig` or a component's `config`). `local<Model>()` gives
`find`, `findAll`, `save`, `saveAll`, `remove`, `clear` and the backend's queries (`where`, `orderBy`,
`limit`, `paginate`, `count`, `exists`, `update`, `delete`).
- `@repository(saveLocal = true)` (or `@get(local = true)`) keeps what each GET answered and gives
`<method>AsLocal()`, the same answer from the device without a request.
- `NetworkManager()` in `globals`, `@requires(internet = true)` on a use case, `HttpError.offline`,
`NetworkWrapper(offline = ...)` in the app's builder, `@offline` on a test group.
- Retries: GET, PUT and DELETE retry transient failures twice; POST and PATCH only with `retry = n`.
- **Not in the platform**: a sync queue, conflict resolution, background sync. They are built as below. The web
platform has no local database yet.

rows.title: Importing an API — Checklist
rows.summary: Checklist
body: - [ ] Each resource came from `nuclear gen resource` with `--from-json`, `--from-spec` or `--fields`.
- [ ] The example answers used are kept under `specs/` so the generation can be repeated.

rows.title: Importing an API — Pitfalls
rows.summary: rules are not read from the document: the example answer decides the types.
body: - Polymorphic schemas (`oneOf`, `anyOf`, discriminators), enums, formats (`date-time`, `uuid`) and required/optional
rules are not read from the document: the example answer decides the types. A field absent from the example is
absent from the model; a `null` in the example gives no type. Pick an example with every field filled, or fix the
model by hand (`T?` for optional).
- Authentication schemes (OAuth flows, signed requests) are not generated: only static `headers` on the connection.
- A backend resource over `rest` gets no tests, and an `Http` connection takes no fake transport in backend tests
(roadmap): test the use cases on models built by hand.
- An error answer becomes an `Err` by status (404 `NotFound`, 400/422 `Invalid`, 401, 403, 409); a provider's error
body is not modelled.
- Never translate the vendor's SDK or a generated client into Nuclear by hand, and never write target code for it.
A vendor SDK needed on a device is `nuclear add <package>`, which ties that code to the dialect.

repositories. The platform exports OpenAPI (a backend's build writes `.nuclear/openapi.json`); it does not import

- **What exists**: `nuclear gen resource` builds a whole resource from **one example answer** (`--from-json <file|url>`)

rows.title: Payments — Checklist
rows.summary: Checklist
body: - [ ] No card number, CVC or full PAN in any entity, model, log or test fixture.
- [ ] Every amount is an `int` in minor units next to its `currency`.
- [ ] `idempotencyKey`, `providerId` and `providerEventId` are unique columns; a repeated request answers the first result.
- [ ] The webhook route acts only on a verified event (signature or fetched back), refuses an old one, and ignores a repeat.
- [ ] Status changes only through the allowed transitions; a test tries an illegal one.
- [ ] Refunds can never exceed the captured amount (a test with two refunds).
- [ ] Secrets come from `env(...)`; `testEnv(...)` in `config.nuc` holds test values only.
- [ ] `nuclear check .` reports 0 errors and `nuclear test` is green.

rows.title: Payments — Pitfalls
rows.summary: Pitfalls
body: - Floats for money (`19.99 * 3`): rounding errors. Integers in minor units, always with the currency.
- Trusting the client's "payment succeeded" redirect: only the verified webhook (or a server fetch) changes status.
- Retrying a POST to the provider without the same idempotency key: a double charge.
- Acting on a webhook before verifying it, or verifying a re-serialized body instead of the raw one.
- Logging the full provider answer or headers: secrets and personal data in the logs.
- One currency hard-coded; converting currencies at display time with a stale rate.
- Refunding more than was captured through two concurrent refund requests: check inside the transaction.

- `providerId: string` (the provider's payment id, `unique`), `idempotencyKey: string` (`unique`),
`failureCode: string?`, `createdAt`, `updatedAt` (`@created`, `@updated`).

4. **Charge with an idempotency key.** The use case `CreatePayment` (`@transactional`) takes the order id and the
client's idempotency key: if a payment with that key exists, answer it as it is (no second charge); otherwise
save it `pending`, call the provider with the same key, store `providerId` and the status. Compute the amount
on the server from the order, never from the client's body.
5. **Webhooks are the truth.** A controller route receives the provider's events. Verify the signature header
against the raw body with the webhook secret (`env("PAYMENTS_WEBHOOK_SECRET")`) before reading anything;
refuse an old timestamp (replay). A controller parameter is a parsed model, and the platform documents no raw
body nor request headers for a route: until it does, verify by fetching the event back from the provider by id
(an HTTP repository call) and record the missing raw-body access in the backend roadmap. Store the event by `providerEventId` and ignore a repeat (the provider retries);
answer 2xx fast and do the work in a listener (`~publish("payments.event", ...)` + `@consumer`).

rows.title: Performance and load — Checklist
rows.summary: Checklist
body: - [ ] A monitored run before and after the change, with the hot spot named.
- [ ] No `async calls in a loop` or `many connections` hot spot left on the changed path.
- [ ] Lists that grow are paginated; relations used in a loop are loaded with `relations(...)`.
- [ ] Filtered and sorted columns on large tables are indexed, with a migration.
- [ ] The shipped build has no `--monitor`.
- [ ] `nuclear check . --json` prints `[]` and `nuclear test` is green after the change.

rows.title: Performance and load — Pitfalls
rows.summary: desktop run.
body: - Optimising without a measurement, or measuring a build with the monitor and shipping it.
- A save in the editor rebuilds without the monitor: measure, then edit.
- A phone or browser tab cannot write the report to the project folder yet (roadmap): measure the backend, or a
desktop run.
- `exists()` and `count()` replaced by loading every row and checking the list's length.
- Load testing against SQLite in a temp file and concluding about PostgreSQL.
- Caching data that must be fresh (balances, stock) without an expiry or an invalidation.

rows.title: Performance and load — Steps
rows.summary: 1. Measure.
body: 1. **Measure.** A backend: `nuclear run --monitor`. Another program: `nuclear build --monitor` and run it your usual
way. Use it: call the slow routes, open the slow screens. The report lands in `.nuclear/monitor/report.json`.
2. **Read the hot spots**: `nuclear monitor` (or `--json`; in VS Code *Nuclear: Open Monitor*; MCP
`project_monitor`):
- `slow`: its own time is a fifth or more of the whole call;
- `async calls in a loop`: five or more awaited calls one after another inside one call;
- `many connections`: ten or more new connections per call;
- `much memory`: 10 MB or more grown per call.
3. **Fix the cause in Nuclear**, by hot spot:
- **async calls in a loop** → start them together: `~awaitAll([a(), b()])`; on a list of ids, one repository query
with the `oneOf` filter of `where` (`nuclear help backend` §2.2) instead of one `find` per id;
- **N+1 over relations** → load them in the same query with `relations("tasks")`; an unloaded relation is never a
hidden query, so a loop that fetches each one is yours to remove;
- **big lists** → `paginate(page, size)` (`Page<T>`) instead of `findAll()`; `limit` on feeds;
- **slow filters or sorts** → `@column(index = true)` on the column, then `nuclear migrate make "index ..."`;
- **repeated reads** → backend `plugins(redis = true)` with `~cacheGet(key)` / `~cacheSet(key, value, seconds =

rows.title: Performance and load — Steps

body: 60)`; mobile and web repositories `@get(cache = true, ttl = ...)`;
- **many connections** → connections belong to the configuration (opened once at start), never made per call;
- **slow work in a request** → publish an event and do it in a `listener`.
4. **Measure again** with the same steps; keep the change only if the hot spot shrank.
5. **Build again without `--monitor`** before shipping: the monitor is for finding problems, not for production.
6. **Load test** (the platform has no load tool): run the built app (`nuclear build`, `nuclear install`,
`nuclear run`, without the monitor) against a database with realistic volume, and drive it with an external

rows.summary: 1. component's facade (`appcomponent`), as JSON, and delivers it through a short-lived download link
(`file-uploads`). Verify identity again before exporting; audit the export (`audit-logging`).

rows.title: Chat and real time over WebSockets — Checklist
rows.summary: Checklist
body: - [ ] Messages have a server `seq` per room and a sender `clientId`; a retried send stores one message.
- [ ] Membership is checked on subscribe and on every send; a test with a non-member gets 403.
- [ ] After a reconnect the client fetches `afterSeq` and shows no gap or duplicate.
- [ ] Receipts are batched up to a `seq`; typing is throttled; presence expires.
- [ ] A socket test (`~app.socket`, `subscribe`, `next`) sees the pushed message.
- [ ] `nuclear check .` reports 0 errors and `nuclear test` is green.

rows.title: Chat and real time over WebSockets — Pitfalls
rows.summary: Pitfalls
body: - Ordering by `createdAt` from the client's clock; two messages with the same timestamp.
- Trusting a socket message to say who the sender is: take it from the guarded request.
- Missing messages after a reconnect because the client only listens for new pushes.
- Several backend instances with Kafka: pushes reach only the clients of the publishing process.
- Storing typing and presence in the database (write storms).
- Using mobile `WebSocket` in a Flutter web build.

rows.title: Chat and real time over WebSockets — Steps
rows.summary: 1. Messages are data first.
body: 1. **Messages are data first.** `nuclear gen resource chat Message --source db --fields "..."`: `id`, `roomId`,
`senderId`, `clientId` (a UUID made by the sender, unique per sender: dedupe on retry), `body` (`@maxLength`),
`seq: int` (per room, given by the server), `createdAt`, `editedAt?`, `deletedAt?`. Plus `Room`
(`id`, `kind`: direct | group) and `Membership` (`roomId`, `userId`, `role`, `lastReadSeq`, `lastDeliveredSeq`).
2. **Send over the socket as a normal request** (`POST rooms/{id}/messages`). The use case (`@transactional`)
checks membership, assigns the next `seq` for the room, saves, then `~publish("rooms.${roomId}", message)`.
A repeated `clientId` answers the stored message.
3. **Ordering**: clients sort by `seq`, never by their clock. A gap in `seq` means missed messages: fetch them
with `GET rooms/{id}/messages?afterSeq=<n>`.
4. **Reconnect**: after the socket comes back (web does it by itself), fetch everything after the last `seq` seen,
then rely on pushes again. Messages typed while offline stay `sending` and are retried with their `clientId`.
5. **Receipts**: the client reports `delivered` and `read` up to a `seq` (one request, not one per message); the
server stores `lastDeliveredSeq`/`lastReadSeq` and publishes a small receipt event to the room.

rows.title: Chat and real time over WebSockets — Steps
rows.summary: 6. Presence and typing are ephemeral: keep them in memory or Redis (`~cacheSet(key, value, seconds = 30)`), refreshed by a heartbeat; publish changes, throttle typing events (one per 3 s), never store them in tables.
body: 6. **Presence and typing** are ephemeral: keep them in memory or Redis (`~cacheSet(key, value, seconds = 30)`),
refreshed by a heartbeat; publish changes, throttle typing events (one per 3 s), never store them in tables.
7. **Authorization**: a topic per room; subscribe only after checking membership, and check it again on every
send. Do not put private data in a topic everyone can subscribe to.
8. **History**: paginate backwards by `seq` (`where({ "seq": lt(before) })`, `orderBy("seq", desc = true)`,
`limit(50)`); index `(roomId, seq)`.
9. **Moderation and limits**: rate-limit sends per user, cap message size, soft-delete (`deletedAt`) so receipts and
order stay consistent.

- `nuclear gen resource chat Message --source db --fields "roomId:int senderId:int clientId:string body:string seq:int"`
- `nuclear gen usecase chat SendMessage --route "POST rooms/{id}/messages"`

rows.title: Chat and real time over WebSockets — What the platform has (ADR-synapsis-0008)
rows.summary: its same controllers over one socket and pushes what it publishes: `~publish("topic", value)` reaches the clients subscribed to the topic.
body: - **Backend**: `WebSocketServer(path = "ws")` in the connections (plugins `websocket` and `events`). The app answers
its same controllers over one socket and pushes what it publishes: `~publish("topic", value)` reaches the
clients subscribed to the topic. Frames: requests `{"id", "method", "path", "headers", "body"}`, answers
`{"id", "status", "body"}`, `{"subscribe": topic}`, `{"event": topic, "data"}`. The upgrade passes the app's
guards.
- **Web**: `WebSocket(url, headers, timeout, interceptors)` connection; repositories bound to it work as they are;
a method without a body with `@on("topic")` returning `Stream<T>` receives pushes (the topic may use the method's
parameters). The socket reconnects with growing waits and subscribes again by itself. Example:
`nuclear help example/tasks_live`.
- **Mobile**: `WebSocket(connectionName, uri, headers, protocols, pingInterval, interceptors)`; it uses `dart:io`
and does not work on the web build.
- **Tests**: `appClient()` and `~app.socket("/ws", headers = ...)` with `subscribe`, `request`, `next`, `close`.
- **Limits** (backend roadmap): with Kafka a socket gets only what its own process publishes, so several instances
need the events fanned out; no wildcard topics.

rows.title: REST APIs and contracts — Checklist
rows.summary: Checklist
body: - [ ] Every route came from `gen resource` or `gen usecase --route`, or is a controller method calling the facade.
- [ ] Each route returns a `Result`, and each error is one of the platform's with the right status.
- [ ] Every body is a model with validation decorators; a test sends an invalid body and gets a 4xx.
- [ ] `appClient()` tests assert the status of the success and of each error path.
- [ ] The app declares the contract, its connection has the same name, and `nuclear contracts list` shows it current.
- [ ] No hand-written repository duplicates a generated one in the app.

rows.title: REST APIs and contracts — Pitfalls
rows.summary: and the diff would not show the API change.
body: - Editing `contracts/<name>/*.nuc`: they are generated and overwritten. Change the backend and rebuild.
- Forgetting to commit `contracts/<name>/contract.json` of a URL contract: the app's build would need the network
and the diff would not show the API change.
- A route reached by a parameter by mistake: `{id}` never takes `page`, but two parameter routes at the same depth
are ambiguous; give one a fixed segment.
- A token in the query string: guards read only headers, so it would fail and leak into logs.
- The web client gets no `@primary` and no rules from the contract until the web platform has forms and a local
database.
- The OpenAPI document does not list the guards' headers yet (the contract does).
- No CORS setting: a browser on another origin cannot call the API (roadmap).

rows.title: REST APIs and contracts — Steps
rows.summary: 1. Routes come from the tools.
body: 1. **Routes come from the tools.** `nuclear gen resource <component> <Name>` writes the controller with a route per
action (`GET /names`, `GET /names/{id}`, `POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE`). Another route:
`nuclear gen usecase <component> <Name> --route "POST orders/{id}/cancel"` (the controller of the first segment
gets it, created when missing).
2. **Paths are segments**: `@controller("tasks")` is the prefix; `@get()` the prefix itself, `@get("{id}")` binds
`{id}`, `@post("plan")` adds a segment; no leading slash. A fixed segment wins over a parameter.
3. **Where parameters go**: a model parameter is the JSON body, a name in the path is a path parameter, any other
is a query parameter (optional when `T?` or defaulted).
4. **Status codes**: `@post` answers 201, the others 200; `@status(201)` changes the success status. A `Result`
answer becomes the value, or its error's status: `NotFound` 404, `Invalid` 400, `Unauthorized` 401, `Forbidden`
403, `Conflict` 409. Return the error from the use case (`Err(Conflict("..."))`), never a 200 with an error
inside.
5. **Validation lives on the model**: `@required`, `@minLength(n)`, `@maxLength(n)`, `@min(n)`, `@max(n)`,
`@pattern(r"...")`, `@email`, `@url`. An invalid body is refused with the reasons before the use case runs.

rows.title: REST APIs and contracts — Steps
rows.summary: 6. Build the backend: `nuclear build` writes `.nuclear/contract.json` and `.nuclear/openapi.json`; the running app serves both at `/.nuclear/contract.json` and `/.nuclear/openapi.json`.
body: 6. **Build the backend**: `nuclear build` writes `.nuclear/contract.json` and `.nuclear/openapi.json`; the running
app serves both at `/.nuclear/contract.json` and `/.nuclear/openapi.json`.
7. **Declare the backend in the app**: `contracts(tasks_api = "../tasks_api")` in its `config.nuc` (a path in the
same repository) or `contracts(tasks_api = "https://api.example.com")`, and a connection with that name:
`Http(connectionName = "tasks_api", baseUrl = "http://localhost:3000/")`.
8. **Generate the client**: a path is regenerated at every build; a URL with `nuclear contracts update [<name>]`.
`nuclear contracts list` shows each contract, its source and the version of the copy. The models (with their
validation rules and key) and one repository per controller land in `contracts/<name>/`.
9. **Write only the app's logic**: use cases over the generated repository (`~tasks.all(done = false)`), then
screens. `nuclear check --json` in both projects, `nuclear test`.

rows.title: Search, filters and pagination — Checklist
rows.summary: Checklist
body: - [ ] The searched columns, filters and sorts are written in the spec and nowhere wider.
- [ ] `size` has a maximum; `sort` accepts only known values; the text has `@maxLength`.
- [ ] Every filtered or sorted column has an index (a migration).
- [ ] Order is stable (an id tie-breaker); a test pages through and sees every row once.
- [ ] The client debounces and ignores stale answers; empty, loading and error states exist.
- [ ] `nuclear check .` reports 0 errors and `nuclear test` is green.

rows.title: Search, filters and pagination — Pitfalls
rows.summary: Pitfalls
body: - One request per keystroke and answers arriving out of order (old results overwrite new ones).
- No upper bound on `size`: one request dumps the table.
- Sorting without a unique tie-breaker: rows repeat or vanish between pages.
- `%` and `_` from the user acting as wildcards; unbounded text length.
- Counting the total on every page of a huge table: cache it or show "more" instead of a number.
- Searching private rows: the owner filter is part of the query, not applied after.

rows.title: Search, filters and pagination — Steps
rows.summary: "search indexes"`.
body: "search indexes"`. `ilike '%x%'` cannot use a normal index: for large tables use the database's full-text
search (PostgreSQL `tsvector`, a trigram index) written in the migration file, or an external search engine as
an HTTP repository. Measure with `nuclear run --monitor` and `nuclear monitor`.
6. **Deep pages**: `offset` gets slow and shifts when rows are inserted; for infinite scroll on big tables use a
cursor (`where({ "id": lt(lastId) })` + `orderBy("id", desc = true)` + `limit(size)`).
7. **Empty and edge results**: an empty text lists the default order (or nothing, for autocomplete); no match
answers an empty page (200), not 404; a page past the end answers empty items with the real `total`.
8. **The client**: `nuclear gen resource catalog Book --from-json <sample> --screen books` gives the repository
and a list screen; add a search use case and a state manager method. **Debounce** the text field (300-400 ms),
ignore texts shorter than 2-3 characters for autocomplete, and drop stale answers: keep the latest query and
ignore an answer for an older one. Show loading, empty, error and results states (a `statemodel`).
9. **Offline or small sets** on mobile: query the local table (`local<Book>().where(...)`) instead of the network.
10. **Remember the query** in the route (`/books?text=x&page=2`) on web so it can be shared and survives a reload.

rows.title: Search, filters and pagination — Steps
rows.summary: 1. Decide what is searched.
body: 1. **Decide what is searched.** `nuclear gen resource` gives a stored resource no `search` on purpose: which
columns are searched is a decision. Write it down: the text fields (`title`, `description`), the filters
(status, category, price range, date range), the sort orders, the page size.
2. **The query model** (`nuclear make model catalog BookQuery`): `text: string?` with `@maxLength(100)`,
each filter optional, `sort` limited to a known list, `page: int` with `@min(1)`, `size: int` with `@min(1)`
and `@max(100)` (default 20). Never accept a raw column name or an SQL fragment from the client.
3. **The repository method** builds one query: `where({...})` with `ilike` for a case-insensitive match
(`"%" + text + "%"`), `oneOf` for a set of categories, `between` for ranges, `gte`/`lte` for open ranges,
`orderBy(field, desc = ...)` with a **stable tie-breaker** (the id), and `paginate(page, size)` → `Page<T>`
(`items`, `page`, `size`, `total`, `pages`). Escape `%` and `_` in the user's text.
4. **Wire it**: `nuclear gen usecase catalog SearchBooks --calls BookRepository.search --route "GET books/search"`.
Extra rules (only published books for anonymous users) go in a hand-written use case.
5. **Indexes**: `@column(index = true)` on every filtered and sorted column; then `nuclear migrate make

rows.title: Security review (OWASP) — Checklist
rows.summary: Checklist
body: - [ ] Every route has a guard or is meant to be public, and the docs say which.
- [ ] Ownership is checked in the use case; a test tries another user's item.
- [ ] Every body is a validated model; a test sends an invalid one and gets a 4xx.
- [ ] No secret literal in `.nuc`, tests, docs or `.nuclear/builder.json`; all from `env(...)`.
- [ ] No base URL built from input; repositories use configured connections.
- [ ] Added packages are pinned and reviewed; the CI `security` stage runs something beyond the check.
- [ ] Each finding has a fix in Nuclear or a roadmap entry, and `nuclear test` is green.

rows.title: Security review (OWASP) — Pitfalls
rows.summary: Pitfalls
body: - Trusting `@acl` on a screen as protection: it hides UI; the backend decides.
- A token in a URL: it reaches access logs and the guard ignores it.
- `Token(value = env("X"))` with `X` unset: an empty value refuses every request (safe), but check deployment sets it.
- A browser cannot reach the API from another origin (no CORS setting): do not "fix" it by patching the generated app.
- Reporting a generated-code issue as fixed by editing `build/`: the next build undoes it.
- Findings without a reproducing test: write the test (skill `tdd`).

rows.title: Security review (OWASP) — Steps
rows.summary: server; state changes follow allowed transitions; writes that must not repeat are idempotent.
body: server; state changes follow allowed transitions; writes that must not repeat are idempotent.
5. **A05 Misconfiguration.** `createTables` off in production (migrations instead); a guarded app serves no docs
pages; plugins enabled only when used; no debug values in `config/project_config.nuc`.
6. **A06 Vulnerable components.** `nuclear add <package>@<version>` pins what enters `config.nuc`; review each added
package. The platform has no audit command: add the target's audit tool to the CI `security` stage (skill
`ci-pipelines`).
7. **A07 Authentication failures.** Tokens travel in headers only (guards never read the query). The backend has no
user/session kind yet: say so instead of inventing one in target code.
8. **A08 Integrity failures.** `build/` and `contracts/` untouched; migrations read before applying; the contract copy
committed.
9. **A09 Logging failures.** Errors return the platform's statuses without internals; nothing logs secrets or
personal data; with `plugins(telemetry = true)` use cases are traced.
10. **A10 SSRF.** HTTP repositories call a fixed `Http(baseUrl)` from the configuration; a parameter only fills a
`:name` segment or the query. Never build a base URL or a full URL from user input.

rows.title: Security review (OWASP) — Steps
rows.summary: Walk the change through each risk; each finding gets the file and line, the risk, and the fix in Nuclear.
rows.body: Walk the change through each risk; each finding gets the file and line, the risk, and the fix in Nuclear.

rows.title: Security review (OWASP) — Steps
rows.summary: 1. A01 Broken access control.
body: 1. **A01 Broken access control.** Every backend route is reachable only as intended: `guards` in `appConfig`
(`Token(value = env("..."))`, `NoOrigin()` for a local service) and per controller
(`@controller("x", guards = [...])`). A use case checks ownership (another user's item answers `Forbidden` or
`NotFound`). On mobile and web, `@acl(roles, permissions, guards)` and `@requires(session)` guard the UI only:
the backend must refuse too.
2. **A02 Cryptographic failures.** Secrets come from `env("VAR")`, never literals in `.nuc`, tests or docs;
`testEnv(...)` holds test values only. No password or token stored in a plain column. The mobile local database
is encrypted unless the config says `LocalDatabase(encrypted = false)`: question any such line.
3. **A03 Injection.** Queries use the repository chain (`where({ "title": t })`, `like`, `oneOf`...): the platform
has no raw SQL word, so there is nothing to concatenate. Every body is a model with validation decorators
(`@required`, `@minLength`, `@maxLength`, `@min`, `@max`, `@pattern(r"...")`, `@email`, `@url`). Text sent to a
model's prompt (an `agent`) is untrusted: its tools must check what they do.
4. **A04 Insecure design.** Rules live in use cases returning `Result`; limits (amounts, counts) are checked on the

rows.title: SQL databases — Checklist
rows.summary: Checklist
body: - [ ] The engine's plugin is enabled and the URL comes from `env(...)`.
- [ ] Every column queried by `where` or `orderBy` on a large table has `@column(index = true)` or is the key.
- [ ] Unique business keys carry `@column(unique = true)`, and the use case answers `Conflict` before saving.
- [ ] Use cases that write several rows carry `@transactional`; a test proves an `Err` rolls back.
- [ ] Lists are paginated; relations are loaded explicitly.
- [ ] A migration exists for every entity change, was read (no unintended drop) and applies with `nuclear migrate`.
- [ ] `nuclear check . --json` prints `[]` and `nuclear test` is green.

rows.title: SQL databases — Pitfalls
rows.summary: into a rename or the data is lost.
body: - A renamed table or column shows in a migration as a drop and an add: `make` warns of every drop; edit the file
into a rename or the data is lost.
- `make` compares the entities with the last migration, never with a live database: a database changed by hand
drifts silently.
- Migrations belong to the dialect they were made with; switching `fastapi` ↔ `nestjs` needs new ones.
- Only SQLite migrations have been run by the platform's tests; test against your real engine before shipping.
- An unloaded relation is absent from the JSON, never `null` and never a hidden query: load it with `relations(...)`
in the query that needs it, instead of one `find` per row (N+1).
- A resource from `--source db` has no relations and no search; which column is searched is a decision you write.
- `createTables = true` against a production database: tables appear but never change; use migrations.
- `findAll()` on a growing table: use `paginate(page, size)`.

rows.title: SQL databases — Steps
rows.summary: 1. Pick the engine with its plugin and connection: `sqlite` + `SQLite(file = env("DATABASE", "app.sqlite"))`, or `postgres` / `mysql` / `mariadb` + `Postgres(url = env("DATABASE_URL"))`, `MySQL(url = ...)`, `MariaDB(url = ...)`.
body: 1. **Pick the engine** with its plugin and connection: `sqlite` + `SQLite(file = env("DATABASE", "app.sqlite"))`,
or `postgres` / `mysql` / `mariadb` + `Postgres(url = env("DATABASE_URL"))`, `MySQL(url = ...)`,
`MariaDB(url = ...)`. The URL comes from `env(...)`, never a literal with a password.
2. **Generate the resource**: `nuclear gen resource orders Order --source db --fields "id:int total:double
status:string"` writes the entity, `NewOrder`, the repository with a paged query, a use case per action, the
controller and the tests over an in-memory database.
3. **Shape the entity** (`nuclear help entity --dialect fastapi`): `@entity("table")`, `@primary(generated = true)`,
`@column(length, unique, index, nullable, name)`, `@created`, `@updated`; `T?` is a nullable column and a
default is the column's default. Another table: `nuclear make entity <component> <Name>`.
4. **Relations** (by hand, the generator does not write them): `@manyToOne(inverse, onDelete)` on `x?: T` plus the
field `xId`; `@oneToMany(inverse)` on `xs?: T[]`; `@manyToMany(inverse)` with `@joinTable()` on one side;
`@oneToOne(inverse, onDelete)` with `@joinColumn()` on one side. N0308 checks them.
5. **Queries** are repository methods whose lines build one query: `where({...})` (equality, `gt`, `gte`, `lt`,

`relations("tasks")`; the last line runs it: `getOne()`, `getMany()`, `paginate(page, size)` (`Page<T>`),

an `Err` or an error rolls it back, an `Ok` commits.
7. **Migrations** once the data must be kept: `nuclear install` (once), `nuclear migrate make "<what changed>"`,
read the file in `migrations/`, then `nuclear migrate`; `nuclear migrate down` reverts the last one. Remove

rows.title: Subscriptions and billing — Checklist
rows.summary: Checklist
body: - [ ] Plan prices are `int` minor units with a currency; plans are never deleted.
- [ ] Code checks entitlements; the backend enforces them, not only the UI.
- [ ] Subscription state changes only from verified, deduplicated webhooks or store notifications.
- [ ] Store receipts are verified server-side; a test feeds a forged receipt and gets no access.
- [ ] Past-due grace, cancel at period end and downgrade at period end each have a test.
- [ ] `nuclear check .` reports 0 errors and `nuclear test` is green.

rows.title: Subscriptions and billing — Pitfalls
rows.summary: Pitfalls
body: - Checking `plan == "pro"` all over the code instead of entitlements.
- Granting access from the client's purchase callback without server verification.
- Ending access the moment a renewal fails (no grace period) or never ending it (no `past_due` handling).
- Computing proration yourself and disagreeing with the provider's invoice.
- Time zones and month lengths in period math: use the provider's period dates.
- Selling digital subscriptions in a mobile app through an outside payment link (store rejection).

rows.title: Subscriptions and billing — Steps
rows.summary: 5. Trials: one per customer (check by customer and payment fingerprint, not by email); remind before it ends; decide whether a card is needed upfront.
body: 5. **Trials**: one per customer (check by customer and payment fingerprint, not by email); remind before it ends;
decide whether a card is needed upfront.
6. **Upgrades and downgrades**: upgrade at once with proration (the provider computes the credit for unused time
and charges the difference); downgrade at period end, so paid features stay until then. Show the amount before
the user confirms.
7. **Dunning**: a failed renewal moves to `past_due`; the provider retries on a schedule; email the user with a link
to update the card (`notifications`); keep access during a grace period (e.g. 7 days), then restrict. Recovery
moves back to `active`.
8. **Cancel**: by default at period end (`cancelAtPeriodEnd = true`); access stays until `currentPeriodEnd`. Make
cancellation as easy as sign-up (consumer law in many countries).
9. **Store receipts on mobile**: in-app subscriptions must use the store's billing (store rules). The app buys
through the dialect's purchase package (`nuclear add <package>`, tied to the dialect), sends the receipt or
purchase token to the backend, and the backend **verifies it with the store's server API** and listens to the
store's server notifications for renewals, refunds and cancellations. Never unlock from the device's word.

rows.title: Subscriptions and billing — Steps
rows.summary: 1. Let a billing provider run the clock.
body: 1. **Let a billing provider run the clock.** Renewals, retries, taxes and invoices are hard; the provider (or the
store) is the source of truth, reached as HTTP repositories (`--source rest:<url>`, keys from `env(...)`).
Your backend mirrors its state from **verified webhooks** and decides entitlements.
2. **Plans** (`nuclear gen resource billing Plan --source db --fields "..."`): `id`, `code` (`"pro_monthly"`),
`priceAmount: int` (minor units), `currency`, `interval` (`month` | `year`), `trialDays: int`, `active`,
`providerPriceId`. Never delete a plan with subscribers; mark it inactive.
3. **Subscriptions**: `customerId`, `planId`, `status`: `trialing` → `active` → `past_due` → `canceled` |
`expired` (plus `paused` if offered), `currentPeriodStart`, `currentPeriodEnd`, `cancelAtPeriodEnd: boolean`,
`trialEnd?`, `providerSubscriptionId` (unique), `source` (`web` | `app_store` | `play_store`).
4. **Entitlements, not plan names, in code**: a table or a map from plan to features (`"export"`, `"seats:10"`);
use cases ask "has entitlement X" (an aggregate). Mobile and web hide or lock features with a `guard` whose
`canActivate` reads the entitlements, used in `@screen(acl = {...})` and `@acl(guards = [...])`; the backend
enforces the same rule, because a hidden button is not a check.

rows.title: Subscriptions and billing — Steps
rows.summary: 10. Webhooks: verify, store by event id (ignore repeats), apply in order of the provider's timestamps, and re-fetch the subscription from the provider when unsure.
body: 10. **Webhooks**: verify, store by event id (ignore repeats), apply in order of the provider's timestamps, and
re-fetch the subscription from the provider when unsure.

rows.title: Subscriptions and billing — The platform's tools
rows.summary: provider's webhooks, not from your own timers.
body: - `nuclear gen resource billing Subscription --source db --fields "customerId:int planId:int status:string providerSubscriptionId:string"`
- `nuclear gen resource billing ProviderSubscription --source rest:<provider base url> --actions get,create,update`
- `nuclear make aggregate billing Entitlements`, `nuclear make listener billing ProviderEvents` (backend).
- `nuclear make guard <name>` (mobile, web) for plan-gated screens; `nuclear add <package>` for a store SDK.
- `nuclear migrate make "billing"`, `nuclear migrate`; `nuclear test`.
- There is no billing kind and no background jobs in the backend platform: period ends and reminders come from the
provider's webhooks, not from your own timers.

rows.title: Synapsis backend — Checklist
rows.summary: Checklist
body: - [ ] Every file came from `nuclear new`, `gen` or `make`, or is Nuclear written for a rule no generator knows.
- [ ] `nuclear check . --json` prints `[]`.
- [ ] `nuclear install` ran, and `nuclear test` is green.
- [ ] No file under `build/` was edited; no `.py` or `.ts` was written for a feature.
- [ ] Every plugin used is enabled in `config.nuc`; secrets come from `env(...)`.
- [ ] A schema change has its reviewed migration in `migrations/`.
- [ ] The project's `AGENTS.md`, `docs/` and roadmap say what changed.

rows.title: Synapsis backend — Pitfalls
rows.summary: (`.venv/bin/python: No such file or directory`).
body: - `nuclear test` or `nuclear migrate` before `nuclear install`: the virtual environment is missing
(`.venv/bin/python: No such file or directory`). Install once after `new`, and after `nuclear add`.
- Calling a repository from a controller, or a use case from another component: N0301/N0302. Go through the
component's `appcomponent`.
- Editing `build/`: it is rewritten on every build. Change the `.nuc` and build again.
- Writing a resource's CRUD by hand when `gen resource` writes it finished and tested.
- A browser on another origin cannot call the API: the platform has no CORS setting yet (roadmap). Do not patch
the generated app; record the need.
- No user authentication kind yet (users, sessions, JWT): only header guards. Say so instead of improvising one in
target code.
- A stored resource gets no `search`: which column is searched is a decision; write the query, then
`nuclear gen usecase ... --calls`.

rows.title: Synapsis backend — Steps
rows.summary: 1. Read first.
body: 1. **Read first.** `nuclear spec --brief --dialect fastapi` (or `nestjs`), then `nuclear help backend` and
`nuclear help onboarding-backend`. Look a word up instead of guessing: `nuclear help <word> --dialect fastapi`.
2. **Create the project** (only for a new one): `nuclear new <name> -p backend` (`-d nestjs` for TypeScript;
`--websocket` adds the app's WebSocket, `--token <ENV_VAR>` its guards). It writes only `.nuc` files:
`config.nuc`, `config/project_config.nuc` (SQLite by default) and `test/app_test.nuc`.
3. **Inspect.** `nuclear gen inspect` lists the components and every declaration by kind: never declare a name twice.
4. **Generate the resource.** `nuclear gen resource <component> <Name> --fields "id:int title:string done:boolean"`
writes the entity, `New<Name>`, the repository, one use case per action, the facade's aliases, the controller and
the tests. The fields can come from `--from-json <file|url>` or `--from-spec <spec.md>`. Add `--dry-run` to see
the files first.
5. **Make the other pieces** where the platform puts them: `nuclear make <kind> <component> <Name>` with a kind of
`agent, aggregate, appcomponent, config, controller, entity, listener, model, repository, service, state, tests,
tools, usecase` (`nuclear help layout --platform backend` shows each folder).

rows.title: Synapsis backend — Steps
rows.summary: 6. Write only the rules.
body: 6. **Write only the rules.** A use case with rules of its own is written by hand in Nuclear, then wired:
`nuclear gen usecase <component> <Name> --route "POST orders/{id}/cancel"`. A use case that only calls a
repository method is written by the command: `--calls <Repository>.<method>`.
7. **Enable what you use** in `plugins(...)` of `config.nuc` (`sqlite`, `postgres`, `mysql`, `mariadb`, `redis`,
`kafka`, `events`, `websocket`, `ai`, `openai`, `ollama`, `chroma`, `telemetry`); a kind of a plugin not enabled
is N0304, with the line to add.
8. **Check**: `nuclear check . --json` must print `[]`; `nuclear fix .` applies the exact fixes.
9. **Build, install, test, run**: `nuclear build`, `nuclear install` (a venv or `npm install`), `nuclear test`,
`nuclear run` (FastAPI serves its docs at `/docs`).
10. **A database that keeps its data**: `nuclear migrate make "<message>"`, review the file, `nuclear migrate`;
leave `createTables` out of the connection once the project has migrations (skill `sql-databases`).
11. Update the project's `AGENTS.md`, `docs/` and roadmap in the same change.

rows.title: Synapsis mobile — Pitfalls
rows.summary: component's facade and a state manager.
body: - Editing `build/app` (Dart files): it is regenerated; change the `.nuc`.
- A use case or repository used from a view or from another component: N0301/N0302. Views go through the
component's facade and a state manager.
- The router or the UI context outside a `stateless` or `stateful`: N0301.
- A state manager method named like the runtime's own members (`emit`, `close`, `state`...): N0223.
- Naming the storage engine or a pub.dev class in platform code: the Nuclear never names the engine; a package's
names tie that file to the dialect (say so in the project's docs).
- Retries on writes: `@post` is not retried by default; keep it off for anything that must not happen twice.
- Mocks follow this platform's syntax (`when(() => X.method(...)).thenReturnAsync(...)`, `nuclear help flutter` §8),
which differs from the web's.

rows.title: Test-driven development — Checklist
rows.summary: Checklist
body: - [ ] The generators ran before the first hand-written test.
- [ ] Each new test was seen failing for the right reason before its code existed.
- [ ] Each criterion maps to at least one `@test` whose description says it.
- [ ] `nuclear check --json` prints `[]`, `nuclear fmt --check .` lists nothing, `nuclear test` is green.
- [ ] No test was deleted or weakened.
- [ ] The work log lists the commands, the files and any criterion left to QA.

rows.title: Test-driven development — Pitfalls
rows.summary: nothing.
body: - Writing the code first and the test after, then calling it TDD: the test was never seen failing, so it may test
nothing.
- A red test that is red because it does not compile: that proves nothing about behaviour.
- Writing by hand what a generator writes (a CRUD, its tests): wasted work and code the platform does not know.
- Big steps: several behaviours green at once hide which line made which test pass.
- Refactoring with a red test: the safety net is gone.
- Weakening an assertion, or deleting a test, to get green. Never.
- Testing the generated target code or `build/`: test behaviour, in Nuclear.

rows.title: Test-driven development — Steps
rows.summary: 1. Generators first.
body: 1. **Generators first.** Run the `nuclear gen resource`, `nuclear gen usecase` and `nuclear make` calls the plan
names. They write finished code and, often, its tests. Read what they wrote: what they cover is not written
again.
2. **List the behaviours** the generated tests do not cover: each acceptance criterion, each error path (skill
`find-the-edge-cases` of QA), the bug's reproduction.
3. **Red.** Write one `@test("<the criterion in words>")` in `test/<name>_test.nuc`, using exactly the names and
signatures the plan gives. Run `nuclear test`: it must **fail for the right reason** (the rule is missing or
wrong). A test that does not compile is not red: `nuclear check --json`, apply each `fix` (`nuclear fix .`), and
declare the missing piece's skeleton with `nuclear make` so the test compiles and fails on behaviour.
4. **Green.** Write the smallest Nuclear that makes that test pass, in the right kind and layer (a rule in a use
case, a calculation in a service, a query in the repository). `nuclear check --json` after each file; `nuclear
test` until green. Wire a new use case with `nuclear gen usecase`.
5. **Refactor.** With everything green: remove repetition, rename what reads badly, move logic to its layer.
`nuclear fmt .`, `nuclear check --json` and `nuclear test` after each step. Never change a test's meaning.

rows.title: Test-driven development — Steps
rows.summary: 6. Repeat for the next behaviour.
body: 6. **Repeat** for the next behaviour. One red test at a time.
7. **A bug**: first a test that reproduces it (red), then the fix (green). The test stays as the regression guard.
8. **Log**: the commands run and their results, the files written, what is left (a criterion no test can check is
said, for QA).

rows.title: Test-driven development — The platform's tools
rows.summary: plan of the run is `nuclear-builder checks <id>`.
body: - `nuclear test [-- <runner args>]`: one test by name with the runner's filter after `--`.
- `nuclear check --json`, `nuclear fix .`, `nuclear fmt .`, `nuclear explain` (a failure on its `.nuc` lines).
- `nuclear make <kind> ...`: the skeleton a red test needs to compile.
- Backend: `inject<X>()`, `appClient()`, `FakeModel([...])`; mobile and web: `@mock`, `@states`, `@widget`.
- MCP: `developer_task` runs the same cycle with the local agents (plan, tests first, code, verification, review).
- The software factory's *Tests first* station (`nuclear-builder run`) writes the red tests before *Code*; QA's
plan of the run is `nuclear-builder checks <id>`.

rows.title: Test-driven development — When to use
rows.summary: Every feature with acceptance criteria and every bug fix.
body: Every feature with acceptance criteria and every bug fix. The tests are Nuclear (skill `testing-in-nuclear`); the
cycle is the classic one, with one difference: the standard code and its tests come from the generators before the
first red test.

rows.title: Test-driven development — Where each test goes
rows.summary: Where each test goes
body: | What fails | The test |
| A rule of a use case | `@test` calling the facade through `inject<X>()` (backend) or the class (mobile, web) |
| A route's status or guard | backend `appClient()` with and without headers |
| The states of a screen | `@states("...", expect = [...])` on its manager |
| What a screen shows | `@widget` (mobile, web) |

- [ ] Tests run offline: mocks, `FakeModel`, in-memory databases.

rows.title: Testing in Nuclear — Pitfalls
rows.summary: built by hand (roadmap).
body: - The mock syntax differs between mobile and web; copy it from the platform's reference, not from the other one.
- Backend: `nuclear test` before `nuclear install` fails with a missing virtual environment.
- Backend: an `Http` connection takes no fake transport, so a use case calling another API is tested only on models
built by hand (roadmap).
- Backend (fastapi): listeners of one test receive the events of the next (roadmap); assert on counts with care.
- A user's real token in `testEnv`: only test values there.
- Deleting or weakening a test to make it pass. A failing test is a finding: fix the code, or say why the test is
wrong.
- Testing the generated target code, or snapshotting `build/`: test behaviour in Nuclear.

rows.title: Testing in Nuclear — Steps
rows.summary: 1. Let the generators write the first tests.
body: 1. **Let the generators write the first tests.** `nuclear gen resource` writes them (a database resource on the
backend; on mobile and web, a test with the repository mocked). A new file: `nuclear make tests <component>
<Name>` (backend, web) or `nuclear make test <component>` (mobile).
2. **Write one `@test("what it checks")` per behaviour**, the description saying the rule in words.
3. **Backend** (`nuclear help backend` §2.14): `tests Name`; the app runs with its connections and databases in

model; `appClient()` calls the app over HTTP and its WebSocket (`~app.get(path, headers = ...)`, `post`, `put`,
`patch`, `delete`, `~app.socket(...)`). `testEnv(NAME = "value")` in `config.nuc` sets the tests' environment.
4. **Mobile** (`nuclear help flutter` §8): a file is one group, no header word; `@mock([CharacterRepository])` on the

`isOk`, `isErr`, `isOkWith(v)`, `isErrWith(e)`; `@states("...", expect = [...])` tests a manager; `@widget` a
screen; `@offline` disconnects the network; `setUp()`/`tearDown()` hooks. Integration tests in

rows.summary: `integration_test/` (`nuclear make integration <name>`) run with `nuclear test --integration -- -d <device>`.

rows.title: User profiles — Checklist
rows.summary: Checklist
body: - [ ] Separate models for owner view, public view and changes; `ProfileChanges` has no privileged field.
- [ ] The caller's id comes from the session or token; a test edits another user's profile and gets 403/404.
- [ ] Validation rules are the same in the backend model and the app's form.
- [ ] Email change needs the new address confirmed; the old one is notified.
- [ ] Public answers carry only `PublicProfile` fields (a test reads another user's profile and finds no email).
- [ ] Phone numbers are stored in E.164 and verified before use.
- [ ] Account deletion revokes sessions and publishes an event other components handle.
- [ ] `nuclear check .` reports 0 errors and `nuclear test` is green.

rows.title: User profiles — Pitfalls
rows.summary: Pitfalls
body: - Mass assignment: saving the request body into the entity lets a user set `roles` or `status`.
- IDOR: `GET profiles/{id}` answering private fields for any id.
- Returning the full entity as the public answer (email, phone leak).
- Changing the email without verifying the new address (account takeover).
- Caching a public profile and serving it after the user made it private or deleted the account: purge on change.
- Avatars and display names shown to others without moderation or a report button where users meet strangers.
- Storing the time zone as an offset (`+01:00`): it breaks at daylight saving. Store the IANA name.

rows.title: User profiles — Steps
rows.summary: 5. Email change: never in `ProfileChanges`.
body: 5. **Email change**: never in `ProfileChanges`. A use case stores `pendingEmail` and sends a single-use link to the
new address and a notice to the old one; the change happens when the link is opened.
6. **Phone**: store it in E.164 (`+34600111222`) after validation; verify with a code before trusting it.
7. **Avatar**: the skill `file-uploads` (type and size limits, a resized copy, the URL stored, the old file removed).
8. **Locale and time zone** feed `i18n` and `notifications`; validate them against the supported lists.
9. **Delete the account**: a confirmation, then anonymise or erase as `privacy-gdpr` says, revoke every session,
and publish `users.deleted` (`~publish`) so other components clean up.
10. **Apps**: `nuclear gen resource profiles Profile --from-json <sample>` (or the backend's contract) gives the
repository, use cases and with `--screen` a screen; the edit screen is a `form` with the same rules as the
backend model and a `formmanager`. The use cases carry `@requires(session = true)`.

rows.title: User profiles — Steps
rows.summary: 1. Separate the profile from the credentials.
body: 1. **Separate the profile from the credentials.** The `User` (email, password hash, status) belongs to
authentication; a `Profile` entity holds what the user shows and edits: `userId` (unique), `displayName`,
`avatarUrl?`, `bio?`, `locale` (`"en"`), `timeZone` (`"Europe/Madrid"`), `updatedAt`. Generate it with
`nuclear gen resource profiles Profile --source db --fields "..."`.
2. **Three models, not one**: the stored entity, `ProfileView` (what the owner sees), `PublicProfile` (what others
see: no email, no phone, no time zone) and `ProfileChanges` with only the editable fields, all optional, with
their rules: `@minLength(1)`, `@maxLength(50)` on `displayName`, `@maxLength(500)` on `bio`, `@url` on links.
Fields like `roles`, `status`, `email` are never in `ProfileChanges`.
3. **Ownership**: the use case takes the caller's id from the session or token (per-user identity in the backend
is built as the skill `authentication` says: the platform has no users yet), never from the body or the path;
`PATCH profiles/me` instead of `PATCH profiles/{id}`. An admin route is a separate controller with its own guard.
4. **Partial update**: `PATCH` applies only the fields present; validate, then save; answer the new `ProfileView`.
Use `@updated` for `updatedAt` and, if two devices edit, refuse a change whose `updatedAt` is older (409).

rows.title: WebSocket connections — Checklist
rows.summary: Checklist
body: - [ ] `config.nuc` enables `events` and `websocket`; `WebSocketServer(path = ...)` is in the connections.
- [ ] Each change a client must see is published with a stable topic name, documented in the project's docs.
- [ ] The web connection is `WebSocket(...)` and each pushed topic is an `@on` method returning `Stream<T>`.
- [ ] A backend test opens the socket, subscribes, causes the change and receives the event.
- [ ] A guarded socket refuses a client without the token (a test).
- [ ] `nuclear check . --json` prints `[]` in both projects and `nuclear test` is green.

rows.title: WebSocket connections — Pitfalls
rows.summary: through a host page (the bridge); `headers` of the web connection go with every call, not with the upgrade.
body: - A browser sends no headers on the socket's upgrade: a backend whose guards check the upgrade is reached only
through a host page (the bridge); `headers` of the web connection go with every call, not with the upgrade.
- Listening to an `@on` stream over an `Http` connection is an error: it needs `WebSocket` or the bridge.
- The port differs by dialect: a fastapi app listens on 8000 (the generated URL), the `tasks_live` example points at
3000. Read the backend's `nuclear run` output.
- With Kafka and several instances, a socket receives only what its own process publishes (roadmap). Topics have no
wildcards yet.
- A request frame that does not parse closes the socket; the client reconnects with growing waits and subscribes
again, and a call during the reconnection fails like a network failure (the repository's retries cover it).
- A manager method named `listen` or `subscribe` clashes with the runtime: N0223.

rows.title: WebSocket connections — Steps
rows.summary: `nuclear gen usecase tasks WatchCreatedTasks --calls TaskRepository.created` writes the use case that passes the stream on, and its alias.
body: `nuclear gen usecase tasks WatchCreatedTasks --calls TaskRepository.created` writes the use case that passes the
stream on, and its alias.
5. **Show it.** In the state manager, `listen(tasks.watchCreatedTasks(), (created) => load())`: it runs until the
screen leaves. Read the whole example: `nuclear help example/tasks_live` (and its backend,
`nuclear help example/tasks_api`).
6. **Test the socket** from the backend's tests with `appClient()`: `~app.socket("/ws", headers = ...)`,
`~ws.subscribe(topic)`, `~ws.request("POST", "/tasks", body = {...})`, `~ws.next()` (the next pushed event or
`null`), `~ws.close()`. A guarded socket without the token is an `Err` with the guard's status.
7. `nuclear check . --json`, `nuclear test`, then run both apps (`nuclear run` in each) and watch the list change.

rows.title: WebSocket connections — Steps
rows.summary: 1. The backend.
body: 1. **The backend.** A new one: `nuclear new <name> -p backend --websocket [--token <ENV_VAR>]` writes
`plugins(sqlite = true, events = true, websocket = true)`, `WebSocketServer(path = "ws")` in
`config/project_config.nuc` and, with `--token`, the guards `NoOrigin()` and `Token(value = env("<ENV_VAR>"))`.
An existing one: enable `websocket` (it needs `events`) in `plugins(...)` and add `WebSocketServer(path = "ws")`
to the `appConfig` connections; `nuclear check . --json` says what is missing (N0304).
2. **Publish what changed.** In the use case that makes the change, `~publish("tasks.created", { "id": task.id,
"title": task.title })`. Every client subscribed to the topic gets `{"event": "tasks.created", "data": ...}`.
A `listener` with `@consumer("topic")` receives it inside the backend too.
3. **The web app.** A new one: `nuclear new <name> -p web --websocket` writes a `WebSocket(url = ..., timeout =
5000)` connection. An existing one: replace its `Http(...)` by `WebSocket(url = "ws://<host>:<port>/ws")`: the
repositories stay as they are and their calls travel over the socket.
4. **Listen to a topic.** Add to the repository a method without a body: `@on("tasks.created") created()
Stream<TaskCreated>` (and the model `TaskCreated` with `nuclear make model <component> TaskCreated`). Then

rows.title: Nuclear Chat (`nuclear-chat/`) — Rules
rows.summary: host's; the service only routes, keeps and tells.
body: - **The chat knows nothing of the factory.** What a member is, how they answer and what a button does are the
host's; the service only routes, keeps and tells.
- **Every rule in the service, in platform Nuclear**; `system/` only touches the machine (a file, a process, the
keyring) and holds no rule of the chat. What platform Nuclear cannot say is a finding in its project's roadmap.
- **Nothing written is rewritten**: a channel's file is appended; an edit or a reaction is a line that names its
message; a line cut by a crash is skipped. Only `channels.json` and `gifs.json` are replaced whole (atomically).
- **Events pass through one place**: `EventsAppComponent.emit` (the `EventLog` and the topic `chat.event`).
- **Local and private**: `127.0.0.1` only; a GIF service's key lives only in the keyring (a `0600` file of the chat's data
folder without one) and never reaches a file of the project, an answer or an event; a search leaves the machine only after the project said yes once.

rows.title: Nuclear Chat — Why it exists
rows.summary: do not understand, and every run tells its work in its team's channel.
body: - Work you take part in beats logs you read afterwards. You write to a team or to one member. They ask when they
do not understand, and every run tells its work in its team's channel.
- Each member answers as themselves: their profile is their character, and their provider is how they think. A
message to a team goes to its tech lead.
- Everything stays private: the history lives in your project (`.nuclear/chat/`). Nothing leaves the machine
unless you turn on a GIF service or put a paid provider on a member.
- Left out on purpose: several users, calls, files bigger than an image, and Slack itself (no account, no bridge).

| **tech lead** | the member who answers a message to the team: its channel without a member mentioned, `@<team>`, a thread of its channel; without `lead`, the team's first member |
| **channel** | `general`, one per team (its `team`, or its id is the team's), one the user made, or a direct message `dm-<member>` (kind `dm`) |
| **you**, **system** | the user's author id, and the author of the chat's own messages (a member that could not answer) |
| **message** | a line of a channel: `id`, `at`, `author`, `text`, `thread`, `gif`, `reactions`, `buttons`, `links`, `costUsd` |

rows.title: Vision — The problem
rows.summary: The software factory (spec 011) has teams the user builds, each member with a name and a personality.
body: The software factory (spec 011) has teams the user builds, each member with a name and a personality. Its work
was a log read afterwards and two separate chat boxes, one in the Builder and one in Atlas. The user is the head
of the company and wants to work with them as a company works in Slack: talk to a team or to one member, be asked
when something is unclear, polish a spec in a conversation, try a proof of concept, and see each run as it
happens.

rows.title: Vision — The users
rows.summary: and Nuclear Atlas (the local assistant as a member).
body: - **The hosts**: Nuclear Builder (teams as channels, a run as a thread, its questions as messages with buttons)
and Nuclear Atlas (the local assistant as a member).
- **The person** using a host's page, who never sees the service itself.

rows.title: Vision — What it does not do
rows.summary: is the host's.
body: - It does not know how a factory runs. A member's answer is the host's command (a responder); a button's action
is the host's.
- It has one user (the company is one person and their teams): no accounts, calls, notifications outside the
editor, or files bigger than an image.
- It is not Slack and has no bridge to it.

rows.title: Vision — Why each thing exists
rows.summary: conversation the user takes part in.
body: - **The workplace, not a prompt box.** A factory is people working together. The chat makes the work a
conversation the user takes part in.
- **Talk to who does the work.** A question about the tests goes to the team's QA by name. That member answers as
their role and through their provider, with what they did in front of them.
- **The tech lead answers for the team.** A message to the team (its channel, `@<team>`, a run's thread) goes to
its tech lead, who brings in a member when the question is theirs. A direct message or `@<member>` goes to that
member.
- **They ask, they do not guess.** A member that does not understand asks in the chat. The answer goes back to the
work (a responder's `ask`).
- **Character makes it readable.** A member speaks as their profile, so who said what is clear at a glance. A GIF
now and then says a failure or a success faster than a paragraph; it comes by their personality, never at random
on a re-read.
- **Local and private by default.** The history stays in the project. Nothing leaves the machine unless the user
turns on a GIF service (asked once) or puts a paid provider on a member (confirmed twice, by the responder).
- **One chat for every tool.** The Builder and Atlas are hosts of the same component; neither keeps its own.
- **Nothing is lost.** A channel's file only grows. A crash costs at most the line being written.

| `typing` | `{member, thread}` |

| `done` | `{member, thread, costUsd, error}`: after the answer, its GIF and a failure are posted |
| `agent.changed` | `{member, agent, model}`: a direct message's agent chosen |
| `action` | `{action: "button", message, button}` or `{action: "poc", what, message, thread}` |

rows.title: The API
rows.summary: The service on `127.0.0.1`, at the port the set-up chose (`NUCLEAR_CHAT_PORT` of `ai.env`, 7880 by default).
body: The service on `127.0.0.1`, at the port the set-up chose (`NUCLEAR_CHAT_PORT` of `ai.env`, 7880 by default). JSON
in and out. Every route needs the header `X-Chat-Token` with the service's token (401 without it or with another);
a request with an `Origin` header (a web page) is refused (403); there are no documentation pages. A host gets the
URL, the header and the token from `nuclear-chat connect --json` (ADR-synapsis-0007, `config/project_config.nuc`);
the token lives in the system's keyring, or in `~/.local/share/nuclear-chat/.token` (`0600`) on a machine without
one ([security.md](../05-standards/security.md)).
`nuclear_chat/test/api_test.nuc` checks the guards and the socket through the app (`appClient()`, with the test
token of `testEnv` in `config.nuc`, never the keyring's; ADR-synapsis-0010).
An error answers its status with `{"detail": "…"}`: 400 a body that is not valid or a name not in the workspace,
404 no workspace, channel, message or waiting question, 409 a channel's name taken.
A `Channel` carries `state` (`open`, `closed`, `archived`, kept in `channels.json`; a new message in a closed one opens
it again); a `Message` carries `deleted` (its time, 0 when it is not).
The fields of an answer have Nuclear's names (`lastRead`, `costUsd`), as the files on disk (ADR-synapsis-0012).

rows.title: The API — The GIF search
rows.summary: The pack first (every word a tag's start or in the title; no words, all).
body: The pack first (every word a tag's start or in the title; no words, all). When the workspace's `gifs` names a
service and `q` is not empty: no answer kept → the pack's results, `ask: "online"`, `service` (the page asks the
user, then `POST …/consent`); `false` → the pack's only; `true` → the key from the keyring (`no-key` in `note`
without one) and the service's results after the pack's (`note: "failed"` when it does not answer; its error is
never shown, since its URL holds the key). A pack GIF's `src` is `pack/<file>`: the page draws the `svg` of
`GET gifs/pack`.

rows.title: The API — The WebSocket (`/ws`, ADR-synapsis-0008)
rows.summary: The same routes and the events, over one socket.
body: The same routes and the events, over one socket. The upgrade needs the same header (`X-Chat-Token`) and no
`Origin`. Frames, JSON text: a request `{"id", "method", "path", "headers", "body"}` answered `{"id", "status",
"body"}`; `{"subscribe": "chat.<workspace>"}` (and `unsubscribe`), then each event of that workspace arrives as
`{"event": "chat.<workspace>", "data": <ChatEvent>}`. A client that reconnects reads what it missed with
`GET events/{ws}?since=<the last n it saw>`.

body: Each one is used by the others only through its appcomponent (`nuclear check` enforces it). Who depends on whom:
`workspaces` ← `events`, `gifs` ← `messages` ← `channels`, `members`. The members answer by listening to the
events (`listener MemberAnswers` on `chat.event`), so `messages` never depends on `members`.

rows.summary: The components (`nuclear_chat/components/`)
body: | Component | Holds |
| `workspaces` | `WorkspaceRegistry`: the registered projects (in memory: a host registers on start), their channels kept in `channels.json`; `Workspace.chatFile(name)` |

| `channels` | `ListChannels` (unread counts), `CreateChannel` (`Release Plan` → `release-plan`), `ReadChannel` (a closed one opens again), `ChooseAgent` (a direct message's agent), `ChangeChannel` (name, topic, open, closed, archived), `DeleteChannel` (its history moved, `ForgetChannel`) |

| `messages` | `MessageStore`: append, read, fold (edits, reactions, threads), locate a message, unread, search (`from:`, `in:`), a deleted history moved; the use cases of saying, posting, editing, deleting, reacting, GIFs, buttons |
| `members` | `Routing` (who answers), `Responders` (a run per answer, its asks), `AnswerMessage`, `AnswerQuestion` |
| `gifs` | `GifChoice` (the pack, the personality's draw, the one question), `TenorRepository`, `GiphyRepository`, `SearchGifs` |
| `events` | `EventLog` (the last 1000 events of each workspace, numbered), `Emit` (kept, published on `chat.event` and `chat.<workspace>`, which the app's WebSocket pushes to its subscribers) |

rows.title: Overview — What is decided here
rows.summary: Miller's generator: every product under 2^53, exact in every target).
body: - **A GIF's choice is the same on every read**: drawn from the message's id (its rolling sum, then Park and
Miller's generator: every product under 2^53, exact in every target).
- **A responder is never run twice for one message**: a run's id is workspace, member and message.
- **The members' conversation**: a thread's messages, or the channel's messages outside threads, the last 40.
- **Workspaces are not kept by the service**: the host registers its project when it starts (the same folder is
the same id, the channels' last read is kept in the project).

rows.title: The responders — A member's GIF (`GifChoice.pick`)
rows.summary: A `gif` tag in `done` is the member asking for a GIF after their answer; the chat decides, by the personality as a cap: `never` sends none; `sometimes` keeps one ask in two, `often` nine in ten; when the user sent a GIF just before the message answered (their last messages), four in five and always.
body: A `gif` tag in `done` is the member asking for a GIF after their answer; the chat decides, by the personality as a
cap: `never` sends none; `sometimes` keeps one ask in two, `often` nine in ten; when the user sent a GIF just before
the message answered (their last messages), four in five and always. A moment's tag (`failure`, `success`,
`question`) only when the personality's `on` names it. The GIF is one of the pack's with that tag (else a tag that
starts with it), posted as the member's next message; the draws come from the answer's message id, so a history
read again shows the same. A tag that is not a lowercase word is left out. The responder never shows its `gif:`
line as text.
A line that is not JSON is skipped. A command that ends without `done` is told by `system`: `<name> could not
answer: it ended (<code>) without done: <the end of its stderr>`. A command that is not installed is told the same
way (`cannot answer`).

rows.title: The responders — In: one line on stdin
rows.summary: `{"workspace", "root", "member", "channel", "thread", "messages", "said", "lang", "gifTags"?}`.
body: `{"workspace", "root", "member", "channel", "thread", "messages", "said", "lang", "gifTags"?}`. `messages`: the last
40 of the conversation (the thread's, or the channel's outside threads), each `{id, at, author, text, thread, gif}`
(`gif`: its title). `lang`: the member's profile language, else the workspace's: the user's chosen language, which
the member answers in (or in the language the user's message is written in). `gifTags`: every tag of the pack,
only for a member whose personality sends GIFs.

rows.title: The responders — Out: JSON lines on stdout
rows.summary: Out: JSON lines on stdout
body: | Line | What the chat does |
| `{"type": "typing"}` | the event `typing` |
| `{"type": "text-delta", "text"}` | the event `message.delta`: the answer as it is written (optional; the answer is still the `text` lines) |
| `{"type": "text", "text"}` | kept; the texts, joined, are the member's answer |
| `{"type": "tool", …}` | the event `tool` |
| `{"type": "ask", "id", "kind", "question", …}` | the event `ask`; the user's answer (`POST members/{ws}/answers`) is written back on stdin: `{"type": "answer", "id", "answer"}` |

| `{"type": "done", "costUsd", "error"?, "moment"?, "gif"?}` | the end: the answer posted as the member (with `costUsd`; a `moment` or `gif`, a tag of `gifTags`, may bring their GIF); an `error`, posted by `system` |

rows.title: The responders — The money
rows.summary: The chat never spends.
body: The chat never spends. A responder worked by a paid provider asks before it spends (two `ask` of kind `spending`,
spec 011 requirement 16) inside its team's budget, and gives the cost in `done`; the chat shows it on the message.

rows.title: The responders
rows.summary: How a member answers (spec 013, design.md "The responder").
body: How a member answers (spec 013, design.md "The responder"). The chat runs the member's `responder.command`, with
`--events` added when it is missing, once per answer, in the project's folder (`Responders`, `members`).

rows.title: The responders — Which command (`Responder.run`)
rows.summary: A member whose host gave `choices` (requirement 17: the general agent) is answered by the choice its direct message chose (`PUT channels/{ws}/{channel}/agent`), else by the host's `choice`, each only when it is `available`; the choice's `command`, with `--model <model>` added when a model is…
body: A member whose host gave `choices` (requirement 17: the general agent) is answered by the choice its direct message
chose (`PUT channels/{ws}/{channel}/agent`), else by the host's `choice`, each only when it is `available`; the
choice's `command`, with `--model <model>` added when a model is chosen (the conversation's, or the host's `model`
for its default). With no choice, `command` and `paid` as they are. What a choice runs is the host's: the chat only
picks it.

rows.title: The responders — Who answers (`Routing`)
rows.summary: 1. A direct message (`dm-<member>`): its member.
body: 1. A direct message (`dm-<member>`): its member.
2. Each member mentioned, in order: `@<id>`, `@<name>` without spaces, `@<first name>`; then `@<role>` (a member of
the channel's team first, then of the channel, then any).
3. `@<team>` (its id, or its name without spaces): the team's tech lead.
4. In a team's channel (its `team`, or its id is a team's), a message that mentions no member: the tech lead.
5. Nobody else: `#general` without a mention is not answered. A message that starts with `/` is a command (`/poc`
is the host's action). The user's GIFs are not answered.

platform's roadmap): the dialogs and the icon buttons are named by `title`.

- The texts are in one Nuclear model (`shared/models/texts.nuc`): the web platform has no translations yet.
