rows.title: Security
rows.summary: `127.0.0.1` only and every route, and the WebSocket's upgrade, is guarded (ADR-synapsis-0007): the header `X-Chat-Token` must carry the service's token (401), and a request with an `Origin` header (a web page) is refused (403).
body: - **A route can start a command** (a member's responder, given at registration). So the service listens on
`127.0.0.1` only and every route, and the WebSocket's upgrade, is guarded (ADR-synapsis-0007): the header
`X-Chat-Token` must carry the service's token (401), and a request with an `Origin` header (a web page) is refused
(403). Never a query parameter, which reaches the access log. An unset token refuses every request.
- **The service's token** is made once (`secrets`, 32 bytes) by `nuclear-chat serve` and kept in the system's
keyring (service `nuclear-chat`, account `token`), as the Smart Graph keeps its owner token. A machine without a
keyring tool (`secret-tool`, `security`, PowerShell; a server, a container) keeps it in a file only the owner reads:
`$XDG_DATA_HOME/nuclear-chat/.token` (`~/.local/share/nuclear-chat/`, folder `0700`, file `0600`).
`~/.config/nuclearlang/nuclear-chat.json` notes that the keyring keeps it (no secret in it): a keyring closed at
login is waited for (90 s) and then refused, never answered with a second token or with a file, and a keyring
installed later on a machine that kept the file does not take it for a closed one. The service gets it in its
environment (`NUCLEAR_CHAT_TOKEN`); a host gets it from `nuclear-chat connect --json` (the editors' extension host
only).

rows.title: Security
rows.summary: a key.
body: - **A responder runs in the project's folder** with the service's user; the chat gives it the conversation, never
a key. A paid provider's money is the responder's (two confirmations, spec 011).
- **A GIF service's key** is kept in the system's keyring (service `nuclear-chat`, account `tenor` or `giphy`), or
without one in a `0600` file of the same folder (`.tenor`, `.giphy`), read
from stdin by `nuclear-chat gif-key`, never from the command line (but macOS's `security`, a `shortcut:` in
`system/keyring.nuc`). It never reaches a file of the project, an answer or an event. Tenor and Giphy take it as a
query parameter of their own API: a failed search answers `note: "failed"`, never the service's error, which
holds the URL.
- **The search words leave the machine** only when the workspace's setting names a service and the project said
yes once (`gifs.json`).
- **A file name from outside** is never a path: a channel's id is `[a-z0-9][a-z0-9_.-]*`, a pack drawing is
`[a-z0-9-]+.svg` inside the pack.

rows.title: Connect a host — 1. Register the project
rows.summary: curl -s -X POST 127.0.0.1:7880/workspaces -H "X-Chat-Token: $TOKEN" -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{ "root": "/home/me/app", "host": "builder", "lang": "en", "gifs": "pack", "members": [{"id": "ada", "name": "Ada", "role": "architect", "team": "core", "personality": {"gifs": "sometimes",…
body: ```sh
curl -s -X POST 127.0.0.1:7880/workspaces -H "X-Chat-Token: $TOKEN" -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{
"root": "/home/me/app", "host": "builder", "lang": "en", "gifs": "pack",
"members": [{"id": "ada", "name": "Ada", "role": "architect", "team": "core",
"personality": {"gifs": "sometimes", "on": ["failure"]},
"responder": {"command": ["nuclear-builder", "member", "--team", "core", "--role", "architect"]}}],
"teams": [{"id": "core", "name": "Core", "lead": "ada"}],
"channels": [{"id": "core", "name": "core", "team": "core", "members": ["you", "ada"]}]}'
The answer's `id` names the workspace in every route. Register again on every start: the same folder is the same
workspace, and what the project kept (the channels' last read, the user's channels) stays.
A member can be a front for several agents (the general agent): its `responder` carries `choices`, each with the
command that answers as it, and `choice`/`model` the default; the user picks one per direct message (`PUT
channels/{ws}/dm-<member>/agent {"agent", "model"}`) and the chat runs that command
([responders.md](../02-architecture/responders.md)). The Builder's host file gives them from `nuclear-builder agents`.

rows.title: Connect a host — 2. Say, post, read
rows.summary: command runs with the conversation on stdin (responders.md).
body: - The user says: `POST messages/{ws}/core {"text": "how is the run going?"}`. Ada, the tech lead, answers: her
command runs with the conversation on stdin ([responders.md](../02-architecture/responders.md)).
- The host posts a run's station as a member: `POST messages/{ws}/core/post {"author": "ada", "text": "Design
done", "thread": "<the run's message>", "moment": "success"}`.
- What happened is pushed: open `ws://127.0.0.1:7880/ws` with the header, send `{"subscribe": "chat.<ws>"}`, and
each event arrives as `{"event": "chat.<ws>", "data": {…}}` (`message`, `typing`, `ask`, `done`, `action`…).
After a reconnection, `GET events/{ws}?since=<the last n it saw>` gives what was missed.

rows.title: Connect a host — 3. Conversations and the search
rows.summary: Every action of the page is a route a host or an agent calls too (ADR-platform-0009): messages/{ws}/message/<id>` (it shows deleted, its thread stays).
body: Every action of the page is a route a host or an agent calls too (ADR-platform-0009):
- Edit the user's message: `PATCH messages/{ws}/message/<id> {"text": "…"}`; delete any: `DELETE
messages/{ws}/message/<id>` (it shows deleted, its thread stays).
- Close, archive, open again, rename, change the topic: `PATCH channels/{ws}/<channel> {"state": "closed"}` (or
`"archived"`, `"open"`, `{"name": "…"}`, `{"topic": "…"}`); delete: `DELETE channels/{ws}/<channel>` (its history
moved to `.nuclear/chat/deleted/`); make one: `POST channels/{ws} {"name", "topic", "members"}`.
- Search: `GET messages/{ws}/search?words=schema%20from:@ada%20in:%23core`.
- Open the page at a message: mount it on `/<ws>/<channel>?message=<id>&thread=<id>` (VS Code's notifications do).

rows.title: Connect a host — 4. Answer a member's question, take an action
rows.summary: 4. Answer a member's question, take an action
body: - An event `ask` `{id, question, member}`: the user's answer is `POST members/{ws}/answers {"id", "answer"}`.
- An event `action`: a button clicked (`{button, message}`) or `/poc <what>`; what it does is the host's.

rows.title: AGENTS.md — NuclearLang
rows.summary: This project is written in NuclearLang (`.nuc`), dialect `react`.
body: This project is written in NuclearLang (`.nuc`), dialect `react`. Its syntax is not TypeScript, Dart nor Python.
- Before writing code, read the sheet: `nuclear spec --brief --dialect react`.
- After each change: `nuclear check --json` must report no errors; fix exactly what each error says (most carry a `fix`).
- Look up instead of guessing: an API `nuclear defs show <Name> --dialect react`; a kind or decorator
`nuclear help <word> --dialect react` (all: `nuclear help words --dialect react`); a topic `nuclear help <topic>`.
- Create each piece with `nuclear make ...` (`nuclear help`); after `nuclear check`, run `nuclear analyze` and, with tests, `nuclear test`.

- A library the project does not have (npm, PyPI, pub.dev): `nuclear add <package>` installs it and generates its type definitions; then use its names (they are imported for you). Never install it by hand in `build/`.
- Never edit generated code (`build/`): change the `.nuc` files.
- Make it with the tools: `nuclear gen`, `nuclear make`, the MCP server, `nuclear add` for a library. Never write
target code for a feature nor translate TypeScript, Dart or Python into Nuclear by hand; when a tool cannot do
something, say so instead of working around it.

rows.title: Nuclear Smart Graph — Rules
rows.summary: `nuclear build .`, the tests.
body: - **It is written in Nuclear.** The `.nuc` files are the source. After a change: `nuclear check .`,
`nuclear build .`, the tests. What Nuclear cannot express is a finding of the compiler for the language's roadmap
(`../nuclearlang/docs/01-product/roadmap.md`), never a `.py` file written by hand.
- **Never weaken a security rule** (a token on every route, no `Origin`, encryption at rest, only ingest writes the
shelves of the base) to make something easier: build the access the right way (`connect`, a request the user
allows). The exact facts are never written to disk: the database is made in memory from the sealed cards
(`facts.nuc`).
- **The knowledge base is rows, not copied documents.** What has a structured source is generated (the
`extract_*.nuc` modules), never written by hand; what is written by hand names its sources. `shelves.nuc` is the
schema: a new shelf, type or filter is added there, with a test.
- **A question with one right answer** (which, how many, what are) is a row of `data/assets/queries/` over the
views of `facts.nuc`, never a card someone keeps in step by hand: a new kind of fact is a view, a new question a
row with its parameters, and an entry of `data/questions.toml` with `exact = true`.
- **After any change here or in the tree:** `nuclear-graph knowledge build`, `knowledge check`, `ingest`,

rows.title: Nuclear Smart Graph — Stack
rows.summary: writes the Python package `build/nuclear_graph`, which `pyproject.toml` packages (Python 3.12+, uv, hatchling).
body: - **Source:** Nuclear, the `python` dialect (`*.nuc` at the root of this folder, `nuclear.toml`). `nuclear build .`
writes the Python package `build/nuclear_graph`, which `pyproject.toml` packages (Python 3.12+, uv, hatchling).
- **Store:** Chroma, one collection per shelf, documents encrypted (AES-256-GCM); vectors by EmbeddingGemma in ONNX,
run inside the server's process by ONNX Runtime (no Ollama; ADR-graph-0003); the exact facts in SQLite, in memory only.
- **Server:** FastAPI + uvicorn on `127.0.0.1:7878`, a token on every route. The client (`nuclear_graph.client`)
needs only `httpx`.
- **The MCP server** is not here: it is the project [`tools/mcp`](../tools/mcp/AGENTS.md) (command `nuclear-mcp`),
which imports this package; `knowledge build` reads its tools with `nuclear-mcp tools`.

rows.title: Nuclear Smart Graph — Why
rows.summary: Why
body: - Chunked markdown gives the closest pieces, never *all* of something; a model fills the rest from memory.
- Here each card answers one question and links to its neighbours; a question with one right answer gets every row, every run.
- Left out on purpose: not a copy of the docs, not a model (only embeddings are computed), not shared.

rows.title: Glossary

body: | Term | Meaning | Not to be confused with | In the code |
| Shelf | A Chroma collection that answers one kind of question | a folder of documents | `shelves.nuc` (`SHELVES`) |
| Row, card | One entry of a shelf: a card that answers one question. "Row" in the base, "card" when it is read | a piece of a document | `assets.nuc` |
| Id | `<prefix>:<name>` (`error:N0114`, `kind:backend.usecase`). A prefix belongs to one shelf, so an id is read without a search | | `shelfOf` in `shelves.nuc` |
| Keys | The exact names a row is known by, in lower case: what a query may write | tags | a row's `keys` |
| Asks | The questions a row answers, as people write them; each is searched as a question | | a row's `asks`, `facet: ask` |
| Link | A typed pointer `{rel, to}` to a row that must exist | a markdown link | a row's `links` |

| Asset | A file `data/assets/<shelf>/<name>.json`: `{shelf, origin, about, rows}` | | `assets.nuc` |

| Curated row | A row written by hand, which names its `sources` | | `origin: curated` |

rows.title: Vision — Problem
rows.summary: An agent that writes Nuclear guesses what it does not know.
body: An agent that writes Nuclear guesses what it does not know. A knowledge base made by cutting every markdown file of
the tree into pieces does not stop that: a piece knows its file and little else, so nothing says what the ecosystem
is for, what it can and cannot do, which tool does what, how a task is done or what an error has to do with another.
And a search by meaning gives the closest cards, never *all* of something: asked for every tool of the MCP server,
it gives four and a model fills in the rest from memory.
The Smart Graph is the local, private library of everything NuclearLang and Synapsis are. Agents ask it instead of
guessing: what Nuclear is for, how each thing is written, every kind and decorator, every tool, every error and its
fix, what can and cannot be done, how a task is done step by step, and validated code.

rows.title: Vision — What it is not
rows.summary: kind of question, linked to the cards it has to do with.
body: - **Not a copy of the documentation.** It is rows, each one a card that answers one question, on the shelf of its
kind of question, linked to the cards it has to do with.
- **Not a model.** The search, the choice of a strategy and the query planner ask no model; only the embeddings
are computed.
- **Not shared.** It runs on the developer's machine, for one OS user; no program reads it until the user allows it.
- The teaching material (`docs/aprende`) and the pending work of the projects are never part of the base. What
matters of the pending work for a reader of the graph (what cannot be done yet, what was never run for real) is
in `capabilities` rows that name its sections as their sources.

rows.title: Vision — What it must be
rows.summary: cannot do; every error and how errors relate.
body: - A library that knows the theory, the documentation, the rules, the purpose and every tool; what Nuclear can and
cannot do; every error and how errors relate.
- JSON assets with their metadata, in Chroma collections designed for what Chroma can do.
- Versioned, and updated with every feature: the base never stays behind the code.
- Tested with the questions people ask ("how does the MCP work", "what is nuclear", "advantages"), in English and
Spanish.
- Good enough to replace the markdown files one day.
- A question with one right answer (which, how many, what are) gets every row, the same on every run, whatever the
model.

rows.title: Vision — Who reads it
rows.summary: hold no code of a target language.
body: - **Frontier models** (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor) through the MCP server: every row.
- **The local agents** of the Nuclear Developer, over HTTP: only the rows written for them (`agents: true`), which
hold no code of a target language.
- **People**, from a terminal (`nuclear-graph search`, `card`, `answer`, `strategy`) and through Nuclear Atlas of the
editor, whose assistant is one of the local agents.
The Builder of the editors reads it through those two: the Developer and the MCP server.

rows.title: Exact facts and the query planner — Consequences
rows.summary: N0114 mean", "the stages of the Builder" are answered with every row, the same on every run, whatever the model.
body: - "Which tools does the MCP have", "the parameters of `generate_resource`", "how is a use case created", "what does
N0114 mean", "the stages of the Builder" are answered with every row, the same on every run, whatever the model.
- A new kind of fact is a view; a new question is a row of the catalogue with an entry of `questions.toml`
(`exact = true`): no code.
- The facts are only as complete as the structured fields of the generated rows: what only a curated card's prose
says is still found by meaning.
- An answer with exact facts is long: the explanation, then every row.

rows.title: Exact facts and the query planner
rows.summary: A search by meaning gives the closest cards, never *all* of something: asked for every tool of the MCP server, it gives four cards and a model fills in the rest.
body: A search by meaning gives the closest cards, never *all* of something: asked for every tool of the MCP server, it
gives four cards and a model fills in the rest. So the graph also holds **the exact facts** of the base in a
relational database, and a planner that answers from them without a model.

rows.title: Exact facts and the query planner — How an answer reaches a person
rows.summary: The rows reach the reader as they are.
body: The rows reach the reader as they are. The assistant of the Nuclear Developer calls the planner before its model;
its prompt has an "Exact facts" section above the documentation, left out whole when no query ran. The model
explains the rows, and the rows themselves end the answer, put there by code: a list never depends on a model.

rows.title: Exact facts and the query planner — The catalogue: the `queries` shelf
rows.summary: `data/assets/queries/exact.json`, a shelf like every other.
body: `data/assets/queries/exact.json`, a shelf like every other. A row is one question with one right answer
(`query:mcp.tools`, `query:mcp.group`, `query:kind.create`, `query:cli.commands`, `query:diagnostic`...):
- the ways people ask it, in English and Spanish;
- its parameters. Each names the query that lists *what people write* and *the value it means* (`generadores` →
`generate`, `caso de uso` → `usecase`, `generate resource` → `generate_resource`): no word list lives in code;
- its SQL, one `SELECT` over the views, and the heading of each column.
The build runs every query against empty tables and refuses a base whose query does not run, names a parameter it
does not declare, or declares one it never uses.

rows.title: Exact facts and the query planner — The facts
rows.summary: `facts.nuc`.
body: `facts.nuc`. A SQLite database with the rows of the base without their bodies:
| Table | Holds |
| `cards` | id, shelf, type, title, summary |
| `platforms`, `keys`, `links` | a row's platforms, exact names and links |
| `fields`, `items` | every value of a row's `meta` and `data`, flattened |
| `about` | the revision |
One **view** per thing a question can list: `commands`, `mcp_tools`, `mcp_params`, `routes`, `kinds`, `kind_names`,
`decorators`, `plugins`, `dialects`, `generator_pieces`, `layout`, `diagnostics`, `habits`, `library`, `stages`,
`agents`, `components`, `editor_commands`, `editor_settings`, `strategies`, `capabilities`. The generated rows carry
what the views read as structured `data` (a tool's parameters, a command's usage, a generator's pieces).
**The database lives in memory only.** The store's rule is encryption at rest, and a SQLite file would keep names
and summaries in clear. The graph's process makes the database from the cards the store keeps sealed, at the first
question after it starts (a read of every card of the store, once) and again at every ingest, marks it read-only
(`PRAGMA query_only`) and writes nothing of it to disk. It holds no row's body and nothing an agent kept at run
time.

rows.title: Exact facts and the query planner — The planner
rows.summary: It answers `facts` (the rows, whole, with their columns), `knowledge` (the cards) and `needs` (an exact question it is close to that lacks a name).
body: It answers `facts` (the rows, whole, with their columns), `knowledge` (the cards) and `needs` (an exact question it
is close to that lacks a name).

rows.title: Exact facts and the query planner — The planner
rows.summary: `planner.nuc`; `POST /v1/answer`, `nuclear-graph answer "<question>"`, MCP `graph_answer`.
body: `planner.nuc`; `POST /v1/answer`, `nuclear-graph answer "<question>"`, MCP `graph_answer`. It asks no model:
1. It matches the question to the catalogue by meaning (the same embeddings) and by the names it writes. A query
whose parameter the question names is run from further away (`NAMED`) than one it only resembles (`NEAR`); the
thresholds were measured with `questions.toml`.
2. **The shelves decide whether a question is exact at all.** A query runs only when its exact question is closer
to what was asked than the closest card. A name alone is a weak sign, because the things of the ecosystem share
names: "what is nuclear" writes the name of a tool and of a component, and must get the card of the language,
not the commands of the tool. Measured: before this rule 57 of the 107 open questions of `questions.toml` ran a
query; after it 17 (the ones that name one thing, such as a diagnostic's code or where a kind's file goes), and
none of the exact ones lost its query.
3. The question's own words fill the parameters. A follow-up that names nothing ("describe each of them") takes the
names from the user's earlier messages (`history`).
4. A needed parameter no word gives is not guessed: the query is answered under `needs`.
5. What is left of the question is searched in the shelves as always.

| `GET /v1/health` | — | `{status: "ok", version}` |

| `POST /v1/search` | read | `{query, collection \| shelves, k = 5, platform, agents, where, expand}` → `{items: [{id, shelf, text, meta, distance, score, via, card, related}]}`; without a collection, every shelf of the base; `where` filters by metadata (`{"type": "kind"}`, `{"kinds": "usecase"}`) |

rows.summary: command, install it (`installer/install.sh`) before building the base.

command, install it (`installer/install.sh`) before building the base.

The help of every command the build records (`nuclear`, `nuclear-builder`, `nuclear-graph` itself) is

rows.title: The knowledge base: assets, versions, and how it stays current — Retrieval is tested with people's questions
rows.summary: `data/questions.toml` lists questions and the row each must return, and requests with the strategy each must get.
body: `data/questions.toml` lists questions and the row each must return, and requests with the strategy each must get.
`nuclear-graph knowledge ask` runs them against the running graph; a question a change answers is added with the

rows.title: The knowledge base: assets, versions, and how it stays current — The base never stays behind the code
rows.summary: `nuclear-graph knowledge check` fails when a generated file is not what the tree gives now, when a row is invalid, when the manifest is of other rows, when a source of a curated row changed since its review, or when the running graph holds another revision.
body: `nuclear-graph knowledge check` fails when a generated file is not what the tree gives now, when a row is invalid,
when the manifest is of other rows, when a source of a curated row changed since its review, or when the running
graph holds another revision. The end-of-turn hook of the working tree (`.claude/hooks/context-check.sh stop`) runs
it: a session that changed the ecosystem cannot finish while it fails. The procedure is itself a row,
`playbook:update-the-knowledge-base`. A row written by hand is reviewed when it is written or changed.
An ingest embeds again only what changed, removes only the sources of its own roots, and keeps what an agent wrote
at run time.

rows.title: The knowledge base: assets, versions, and how it stays current

rows: `{shelf, origin, about, rows}`. The files of the folder and an example row are in
[`data/README.md`](../../data/README.md); the commands are in
[the runbook](../06-runbooks/update-the-knowledge-base.md).

rows.summary: `nuclear-graph knowledge build` (the `extract*.nuc` modules):

`nuclear-graph knowledge build` (the `extract*.nuc` modules):

rows.title: The knowledge base: assets, versions, and how it stays current — Three kinds of content
rows.summary: the advantages, the concepts and the theory, the questions people ask, what can and cannot be done, the limits of the local agents, the playbooks and the strategies, the roles and skills, the failures of the tools and services, the mistakes small models repeat.
body: | the local agents | their own sources in `nuclear-agents/nuclear_developer/` |
| each component's version (and its repository: `nuclearlang/lang`, the whole tree) | its manifest (`COMPONENTS` in `extract_tools.nuc`) |
| the examples | every `.nuc` of the example projects, by kind and platform |
| the solved tasks | the validated answers of the `train` tasks of the Developer's evaluation, never the held-out ones |

**Curated rows** (`"origin": "curated"`) are written by hand, because no file says it in one place: the purpose and
the advantages, the concepts and the theory, the questions people ask, what can and cannot be done, the limits of
the local agents, the playbooks and the strategies, the roles and skills, the failures of the tools and services,
the mistakes small models repeat. Each names its `sources`: a file, or `file#Heading` for one section.
**Overlays** (`<name>.overlay.json`) add hand-written fields to generated rows by id: which errors come together, a
right example, who reads it.
A new command, MCP tool, kind, decorator, diagnostic, version or example reaches the base by building it. A new
capability, limit, failure or procedure needs its row written by hand.

VS Code Builder tool ──HTTP──┐        nuclear-mcp (tools/mcp) ──► nuclear, nuclear-builder
▼                 │        └─► Nuclear Developer (local 3B agents)
Nuclear Developer ──HTTP──► nuclear-graph serve (127.0.0.1:7878, token)
Chroma: one collection per shelf (encrypted documents) + EmbeddingGemma (Ollama)
One process (`nuclear-graph serve`) opens the store. Everything else reaches it over HTTP with a token:
[integrations.md](integrations.md).

rows.title: Architecture — Quality attributes
rows.summary: Quality attributes
body: | Attribute | How |
| Private | loopback only, a token on every route, documents encrypted at rest: [security](../05-standards/security.md) |
| Never behind the code | `knowledge check` fails when the base is not what the tree gives now; the end-of-turn hook runs it |
| Repeatable answers | the search compares every stored vector (no approximate index); lists come from the exact facts, never from a model |
| Valid or not built | a base with a broken link, a duplicated id or an undocumented diagnostic is refused |

rows.title: Architecture — What the store holds
rows.summary: (exact-facts.md).
body: - **One collection per shelf** of the base ([shelves.md](shelves.md)): the cards, their vectors and their metadata.
- **`prompts`** and **`memory`**: not part of the base.
- **The exact facts**: a SQLite database in the memory of the server's process, made from the sealed cards
([exact-facts.md](exact-facts.md)).
The data folder is `$XDG_DATA_HOME/nuclear-graph` (`NUCLEAR_GRAPH_HOME`), mode `0700`, opened only by the server
process.

rows.title: Architecture — Written in Nuclear
rows.summary: The graph is a Nuclear project of the `python` dialect.
body: The graph is a Nuclear project of the `python` dialect. The `.nuc` files at the root of this folder are the source.
`nuclear build .` writes the Python package `build/nuclear_graph`; `[project] package` of `nuclear.toml` names the
package the files are emitted into (imports between a project's files are relative to it). `pyproject.toml` only
packages that folder: the roles of the software factory, whose skills are the prompts, travel inside the package
(`../nuclear-agents/roles` → `nuclear_graph/roles`; a checkout reads them from `../nuclear-agents/roles/`:
`Paths.roles`), and so does `py.typed` (a project that uses the package is type-checked against it).
`build/` is never edited and never committed. The set-up of the AI services builds before it installs.

rows.title: The search, and the choice of a strategy — A strategy
rows.summary: `strategy:bug-failing-test`...: 31 of them, on the `playbooks` shelf).
body: **A strategy** is the row of one kind of request a user makes (`strategy:resource-db`, `strategy:refactor-rename`,
`strategy:bug-failing-test`...: 31 of them, on the `playbooks` shelf). What a strategy row says and what a run
does with it is `ADR-developer-0001` of the
[Nuclear Developer](../../../nuclear-agents/nuclear_developer/docs/03-adr/0001-a-strategy-for-each-kind-of-request.md).
`POST /v1/strategy` (`nuclear-graph strategy`, MCP `graph_strategy`) says which one a request is, and why:
- An exact sign of the request (`data.signals`: a diagnostic code, a test's output, `rename A to B`, a `GET <url>`
line) outweighs any closeness of meaning.
- Meaning decides between strategies with no exact sign, or the same ones.
- Whether the project has the names the request writes moves the score (`existing`, `new` against the row's
`data.target`).
- A run of the Builder cannot follow a strategy without stages (a question, a command): with `runnable`, such a
strategy comes first only when an exact sign chose it.
- `only` is the strategy a spec names itself (`- Strategy: usecase`).
The answer is at most three strategies, best first, each with the signs that chose it (`why`).

rows.title: The search, and the choice of a strategy — A strategy
rows.summary: nuclear-graph strategy "renombra Book a Title" # → strategy:refactor-rename (it writes "renombra"; ...) nuclear-graph strategy "un CRUD de pedidos" -p backend --full # with the plan of the strategy Limit: the selection reads words.
body: ```sh
nuclear-graph strategy "renombra Book a Title"             # → strategy:refactor-rename (it writes "renombra"; ...)
nuclear-graph strategy "un CRUD de pedidos" -p backend --full   # with the plan of the strategy
Limit: the selection reads words. A request that names its kind in an unusual way is classified by meaning alone,
which a small embedding model does less well than an exact sign; a wrong reading is fixed by a sign or a question
in the row. How it is tested: [testing](../05-standards/testing.md).

rows.title: The search, and the choice of a strategy — Search
rows.summary: (`Store.near`, `Store.measure`); the store's own index (HNSW) is approximate and is not asked.
body: **The search is exact.** The stored vector of every item a filter matches is compared with the query's
(`Store.near`, `Store.measure`); the store's own index (HNSW) is approximate and is not asked. Once rows were
replaced that index did not reach every item it held: after an ingest 3 cards of 2 617 could not be found, and
which ones changed at every start. A shelf holds hundreds of items, so comparing them all costs milliseconds (173
questions in 42 s, the embedding of each included).
A card is read directly by its id, with a line for each card it links to (`GET /v1/cards/{id}`, `nuclear-graph
card`, MCP `graph_card`).
```sh
nuclear-graph search "como funciona el MCP"                # every shelf
nuclear-graph search "how do I declare an entity" -c platforms -p backend --agents
nuclear-graph card error:N0114                             # one card and what it links to
Limit: keys are exact. A name written with a typo is found by meaning only.

rows.title: The search, and the choice of a strategy — Search
rows.summary: one is brought in and moves up: 0.12 for a word, 0.22 for a longer name or a code.
body: **Search** is by meaning and by exact name at once, over several shelves (`retrieve.nuc`):
- The query is embedded once and each shelf asked answers its closest cards.
- The runs of one to four words of the query are looked up in the cards' `keys` (`$contains`). A card that carries
one is brought in and moves up: 0.12 for a word, 0.22 for a longer name or a code. So `N0114`, `gen resource`,
`usecase` or `mcp` reach their card whatever the rest of the sentence says, in any language.
- A card is also found by the questions its author wrote for it (`asks`).
- Entries are ranked together, each card once. A `docs` row yields to a card (0.04), and a document gives at most
two sections.
- `expand` adds to each card the title and summary of the rows it links to.
- Filters: `agents`, `platform`, and any metadata (`type`, `kind`, `code`).
- A result's `distance` is the closest the card came by meaning, by its text or by any question it answers.

rows.title: The search, and the choice of a strategy
rows.summary: Neither asks a model.
rows.body: Neither asks a model. Only the embedding of the query is computed.

rows.title: The search, and the choice of a strategy — What of a spec applies
rows.summary: `POST /v1/applies` answers the `capabilities` rows whose trigger words a text writes (`meta.triggers`): what the platform cannot do yet, limits, parts never run for real.
body: `POST /v1/applies` answers the `capabilities` rows whose trigger words a text writes (`meta.triggers`): what the
platform cannot do yet, limits, parts never run for real. It is exact, never by meaning.

body: `agents: false` marks what only frontier models and people read: the target languages, the dialects underneath, the

rows.title: The library: shelves, cards, links — What agents write at run time
rows.summary: `POST /v1/documents` writes only `memory` and `examples`, as rows of `origin: runtime` that an ingest keeps.
body: `POST /v1/documents` writes only `memory` and `examples`, as rows of `origin: runtime` that an ingest keeps. The
rows of the knowledge base are written by ingest alone: a client cannot plant false documentation.

rows.title: The library: shelves, cards, links — What is stored, and what is embedded
rows.summary: when the row is of every platform: Chroma refuses an empty list), `keys`, `tags`, `links` (the ids it points to, so "who links to X" is a filter), `origin`, `source`, `hash`, `rev`, and the shelf's own filters.
body: - **Metadata**, in clear (as the vectors are): `card`, `facet`, `type`, `title`, `agents`, `platforms` (`["all"]`
when the row is of every platform: Chroma refuses an empty list), `keys`, `tags`, `links` (the ids it points to,
so "who links to X" is a filter), `origin`, `source`, `hash`, `rev`, and the shelf's own filters.
- **The document**, encrypted: the card.
- **What is embedded is not the document.** The title goes in the embedding model's title slot, with the summary
and the first 1200 characters of the body as its text. Each `ask` is one more entry of the collection
(`facet: ask`) that points to its card: a question finds the card whose author wrote that question.
What Chroma gives, and what this design uses of it: collections with their own metadata that survives a restart;
rows with a vector, a document and metadata of texts, numbers, booleans and lists of texts; the filters `$eq $ne
$gt $gte $lt $lte $in $nin $and $or` and, on a list, `$contains`; a query restricted to given ids; lookup by id.
Its full-text filters read the document, which is stored encrypted, so they are of no use here; it has no keyword
index of its own.

rows.title: Security — How it is protected
rows.summary: in constant time, and an allowed request hands its token once.
body: - The server listens on `127.0.0.1` only; a request with an `Origin` header (a web page) is refused.
- Every route but `/v1/health` and the access request needs a token. Tokens are stored as SHA-256 hashes, compared
in constant time, and an allowed request hands its token once.
- Documents are encrypted at rest (AES-256-GCM). The key and the owner token live in the desktop keyring
(`secret-tool`, libsecret), or in `0600` files of the data folder when there is no keyring.
- A graph that starts while its keyring is closed (a service at login) waits for it and never makes a second key or
token.
- The data folder (`$XDG_DATA_HOME/nuclear-graph`, `0700`) is opened only by the server process.
- Only `ingest` writes the shelves of the base: a client writes `memory` and `examples` and cannot plant false
documentation.
- The exact facts are never written to disk: the database is made in memory from the sealed cards, and is
read-only.
- The key of a search engine for the agents (`nuclear-graph web-key brave`) is read from stdin and kept with the
other secrets. The internet tools refuse local addresses.

rows.title: Security — Limits
rows.summary: Protection is per OS user.
body: Protection is per OS user. A program running as you could ask the keyring for the key as the graph does; the graph
stops other users, web pages and programs that only speak HTTP or MCP.

rows.title: Security
rows.summary: Never weaken one of these rules to make something easier: build the access the right way (`connect`, or a request the user allows).
body: Never weaken one of these rules to make something easier: build the access the right way (`connect`, or a request
the user allows).

rows.title: Security — Sensitive data
rows.summary: Sensitive data
body: | Data | Where | How it is protected |
| The text of a card | Chroma, the document | encrypted (AES-256-GCM) |
| The vectors and the metadata (ids, titles, keys) | Chroma | in clear: Chroma searches them. They reveal what a row is about, not its text |
| The documents' key, the owner token, each client's token | the keyring, or `0600` files | per OS user |
| The tokens the server checks | the data folder | SHA-256 hashes |
| The exact facts (names, summaries) | the server's memory | never on disk |

rows.title: Security — Who may read it
rows.summary: Nothing reaches the graph without a token, and no token exists until you allow it.
body: Nothing reaches the graph without a token, and no token exists until you allow it.
| Command | What it does |
| `nuclear-graph connect <client> --scopes read,write` | gives a program access now and keeps its token in your keyring (`--print`: prints the token instead of keeping it) |
| `nuclear-graph requests` | the pending access requests and the allowed clients |
| `nuclear-graph allow <request>` / `deny <request>` | answers a request a program made (`POST /v1/access`) |
| `nuclear-graph revoke <client>` | takes a client's access away (its token stops working at once) |
Scopes: `read` (search, cards, prompts), `write` (remember, add examples), `admin` (ingest, manage: only you, with
the owner token). The two clients of this ecosystem:
```sh
nuclear-graph connect mcp --scopes read,write                 # the MCP server
nuclear-graph connect nuclear-developer --scopes read,write   # the local agents
A program reads its token from `NUCLEAR_GRAPH_TOKEN`, else from the keyring. Without a keyring, `connect` writes
the token to a file of the data folder that only you can read.

rows.title: Testing — What the graph answers
rows.summary: `nuclear-graph knowledge ask [word...]` asks the running graph every entry of `data/questions.toml` (or the ones that contain one of the words) and fails when one does not get what it expects: `exact = true` entry.
body: `nuclear-graph knowledge ask [word...]` asks the running graph every entry of `data/questions.toml` (or the ones
that contain one of the words) and fails when one does not get what it expects:
| Entry | What is asked | It passes when |
| a question | `POST /v1/search` (with its `shelves`, `kind`, `platform`, `agents`) | a row of `expect` is among the first `top` results (3 by default) |
| `exact = true` | `POST /v1/answer` | the planner's first query is the expected one |
| `exact = false` | both | it finds its card, and the planner runs no query: an open question that reads like an exact one ("what is nuclear", "how does the mcp work") |
| `request = true` | `POST /v1/strategy` (with `existing`, `new`) | the first strategy is the expected one |
- `expect` may end in `*`: any row whose id starts with it.
- The questions and requests are in English and Spanish. A request is never one of the `asks` of its row.
- The entries with `says` are also asked to the assistant of the Nuclear Developer (`eval/run.py chat`).
- A question a change answers is added with the change; a new exact question is a row of the catalogue with its
`exact = true` entry.
Measured: the 62 requests all reach their strategy. Of the open questions, the planner runs a query only for the
ones that name one thing ([the roadmap](../01-product/roadmap.md) has what is left).

rows.title: Update the knowledge base — Before building
rows.summary: command, install it (`installer/install.sh`) first.
body: - The help of `nuclear` and `nuclear-builder`, and the tools of `nuclear-mcp`, are read from the installed commands: after changing a
command, install it (`installer/install.sh`) first.
- Run `ingest` for the knowledge folder of this tree. An ingest removes only the sources of its own roots, so one
run for another folder does not empty the graph.

rows.title: Update the knowledge base — Rules
rows.summary: someone keeps in step by hand: a new kind of fact is a view, a new question a row with its parameters.
body: - A generated row is never edited: change its source and build again.
- What is written by hand names its `sources`.
- A new shelf, row type or filter is added in `shelves.nuc`, with a test.
- A question with one right answer is a row of `data/assets/queries/` over the views of `facts.nuc`, never a card
someone keeps in step by hand: a new kind of fact is a view, a new question a row with its parameters.
- What an agent knows is a row of the base, never a text inside the code or a prompt: a new rule, pitfall, limit or
procedure is a row.
- `data/sections.toml` and `data/questions.toml` are edited by hand; `schema.json`, `manifest.json`,
`revisions.json` and `INDEX.md` are written by the build.

rows.title: Update the knowledge base — The commands
rows.summary: `knowledge` takes `--tree` (the working tree; default `$NUCLEAR_ROOT`, else this checkout's) and `--out` (the knowledge folder: `nuclear-graph-storage/data` of the tree).
body: | Command | What it does |
| `nuclear-graph knowledge build` | writes the generated assets, validates the whole base and raises the revision when a row changed |

| `nuclear-graph knowledge check` | fails when an asset is not what the tree gives now, a row is invalid, a curated row's source changed since its review, or the running graph holds another revision |
| `nuclear-graph knowledge review [id...]` | records that curated rows still hold after their sources changed (without ids: every row whose source changed) |
| `nuclear-graph knowledge ask [word...]` | asks the running graph the questions of `questions.toml` and fails when one does not find its row (`exact = true`: its exact query) |
| `nuclear-graph knowledge examples` | compiles every ```` ```nuclear ```` block of the hand-written rows |
| `nuclear-graph ingest [folder]` | makes the folder what the graph knows: only what changed is embedded again; what an agent wrote at run time is kept |
`knowledge` takes `--tree` (the working tree; default `$NUCLEAR_ROOT`, else this checkout's) and `--out` (the
knowledge folder: `nuclear-graph-storage/data` of the tree). `ingest` needs the graph running.

rows.title: Update the knowledge base — The procedure
rows.summary: 1. Build.
body: 1. **Build.** `nuclear-graph knowledge build`. It prints the revision, the rows added, changed and removed, the
size of each shelf, and a `review:` line for each curated row whose source changed. With a problem, nothing is
versioned: fix what each line says.
2. **Review.** For each `review:` line, read the change: update the row, or confirm it with
`nuclear-graph knowledge review <id>` when it still holds.
3. **Write what is new and has no structured source**: a capability, a limit, a failure, a procedure. A new tool,
error, kind or version needs nothing: the build reads it.
4. **Add the question the change answers** to `data/questions.toml` (a question with one right answer: a row of
`data/assets/queries/` and its `exact = true` entry).
5. **Check.** `nuclear-graph knowledge check`.
6. **Ingest.** `nuclear-graph ingest`, then `nuclear-graph stats` shows the revision the graph holds.
7. **Ask.** `nuclear-graph knowledge ask` (every question finds its row) and `nuclear-graph knowledge examples`
(every Nuclear example compiles).

rows.title: Update the knowledge base
rows.summary: working tree (`.claude/hooks/context-check.sh stop`) runs the check and does not let a session finish while the base is behind the tree.
body: **After every change of the ecosystem**: build, review what it names, check, ingest. The end-of-turn hook of the
working tree (`.claude/hooks/context-check.sh stop`) runs the check and does not let a session finish while the
base is behind the tree. The same procedure is a row of the base: `playbook:update-the-knowledge-base`.

rows.title: The Smart Graph — From a program, over HTTP
rows.summary: Every route, and the Python client package (`nuclear_graph.client.GraphClient`, which needs only `httpx`): integrations.
body: Every route, and the Python client package (`nuclear_graph.client.GraphClient`, which needs only `httpx`):
[integrations](../02-architecture/integrations.md). A program needs a token first:
```sh
nuclear-graph connect my-tool --scopes read,write     # with the graph running; the token goes to the keyring
nuclear-graph requests                                # pending requests and the allowed clients
nuclear-graph revoke my-tool                          # take the access away
A program can also ask for access itself (`POST /v1/access`); it gets its token once you `allow` the request.
`--print` prints the token instead of keeping it. Who may read what: [security](../05-standards/security.md).

rows.title: The Smart Graph
rows.summary: The Nuclear Smart Graph is the library of everything NuclearLang and Synapsis are, kept on your machine.
body: The Nuclear Smart Graph is the library of everything NuclearLang and Synapsis are, kept on your machine. An agent
that writes Nuclear asks it instead of guessing: what a kind means, how a task is done step by step, which tool
does it, what an error means and how it is fixed, what the platform cannot do yet.
- **Private and local.** It runs on `127.0.0.1:7878` for one user of the machine. The cards are encrypted at rest,
every route but the health check needs a token, and no program reads it until you allow that program.
- **Cards, not copied pages.** Each row is a card that answers one question, on the shelf of its kind of question,
linked to the cards it has to do with.
- **Exact when the question has one answer.** "Every tool of the MCP server" gives every tool, the same on every
run: those questions are answered from a database of facts, not by a search by meaning. No model is asked.
Why it exists and what it is not: [the vision](../00-context/vision.md).

rows.summary: Every card has an id `<prefix>:<name>` (`error:N0114`, `kind:backend.usecase`, `playbook:add-a-screen`), so one can be fetched without a search.
body: Every card has an id `<prefix>:<name>` (`error:N0114`, `kind:backend.usecase`, `playbook:add-a-screen`), so one
can be fetched without a search. The shelves in full: [shelves](../02-architecture/shelves.md); the words:
[glossary](../00-context/glossary.md).
`nuclear-graph stats` shows how many rows each shelf holds and the revision of the base:

$ nuclear-graph stats

`prompts` (the prompts the models read: the skills of the roles of the software factory) and `memory` (what an agent keeps about a project) are not part of
the base.

rows.title: The Smart Graph — What it holds
rows.summary: What it holds
body: | Shelf | The question it answers | Its rows |
| `concepts` | What is it, why does it exist? | the purpose, the advantages, the theory, the questions people ask |
| `language` | How is it written in Nuclear? | the guide and the rules; the members of each base type |
| `platforms` | What does a platform have, and where does each thing go? | every kind, decorator and plugin of `backend`, `mobile` and `web` |
| `tools` | What can run, and how is it called? | each command of `nuclear`, `nuclear-builder` and `nuclear-graph`, each MCP tool, each HTTP route, the generators |
| `errors` | What went wrong, and how is it fixed? | each diagnostic of the compiler, the failures of the tools, the mistakes small models repeat |
| `capabilities` | Can it be done? | what can be done, what cannot yet, the limits |
| `playbooks` | How is this task done, step by step? | the strategy of each kind of request, the procedure of each use case |
| `examples` | What does the code look like? | the `.nuc` files of the example projects; solved tasks |
| `docs` | What does the full document say? | the long form: dialects, decisions, guides |
| `queries` | Which, how many, what are? | the questions with one right answer and the query that answers each |

rows.title: AGENTS — NuclearLang
rows.summary: This project is written in NuclearLang (`.nuc`), dialect `{dialect}`.
body: This project is written in NuclearLang (`.nuc`), dialect `{dialect}`. Its syntax is not TypeScript, Dart nor Python,
and nothing about it is in your training: learn it from the installation, never from guesses or other folders.
- With the `nuclear` MCP server: call `nuclear_start` first (what Nuclear is, the rules, the work cycle, the atlas of
every topic), then `nuclear_doc(<topic>)`. Without it: `nuclear help start`, `nuclear help atlas`.
- This project's own documents (`docs/README.md`) win over the default way of documenting (`nuclear help context-docs`).
- Before writing code, read the sheet: `nuclear spec --brief --dialect {dialect}`.
- After each change: `{check}` must report no errors; fix exactly what each error says (most carry a `fix`).
- Look up instead of guessing: an API `nuclear defs show <Name> --dialect {dialect}`; a kind or decorator
`nuclear help <word> --dialect {dialect}` (all: `nuclear help words --dialect {dialect}`); a topic `nuclear help <topic>`.
{synapsis}{packages}- Never edit generated code ({generated}): change the `.nuc` files.
- Make it with the tools: `nuclear gen`, `nuclear make`, the MCP server, `nuclear add` for a library. Never write
target code for a feature nor translate TypeScript, Dart or Python into Nuclear by hand; when a tool cannot do
something, say so instead of working around it.
<!-- /nuclearlang -->

rows.title: NuclearLang — 1. Load the sheet (once per task, ~3k tokens)
rows.summary: New to Nuclear: `nuclear help start` (MCP `nuclear_start`) first: what it is, the rules, the cycle; then `nuclear help atlas` lists every topic (the platforms, the dialects, the tools, `example/<name>`).
body: New to Nuclear: `nuclear help start` (MCP `nuclear_start`) first: what it is, the rules, the cycle; then
`nuclear help atlas` lists every topic (the platforms, the dialects, the tools, `example/<name>`).
```sh
nuclear spec --brief --dialect flutter     # Synapsis app (config.nuc + main.nuc, no nuclear.toml)
nuclear spec --brief --dialect <dialect>   # the dialect of config.nuc (fastapi, nestjs) or nuclear.toml (typescript, dart, python)
It says only what changes from TypeScript/Dart. Do not load the full spec (`nuclear spec`) unless the sheet and
`nuclear help <topic>` do not answer.

rows.title: NuclearLang — 2. Work cycle
rows.summary: 1. Synapsis: generate a resource's finished code first (models, repository, a use case per action, the facade, the controller or the screen, tests): `nuclear gen inspect`, then `nuclear gen resource <component> <Name> what is left.
body: 1. Synapsis: generate a resource's finished code first (models, repository, a use case per action, the facade,
the controller or the screen, tests): `nuclear gen inspect`, then `nuclear gen resource <component> <Name>
--from-json <url|file> | --from-spec <spec.md> | --fields "id:int name:string"` (ADR-codegen-0001). Write by hand only
what is left. A use case you wrote is wired by `nuclear gen usecase <component> <Name> [--route "POST
orders/{id}/cancel"]` (its alias in the facade; backend: its route); one that only calls a repository method is
written by it too (`--calls <Repository>.<method>`). With the Nuclear MCP server, call `graph_strategy` first with
the request: it answers which kind of request it is (a resource, one screen, a rename, a failing test...) and the
plan of that kind. Create each other piece with its generator, so it lands in
the right folder with the right kind:
`nuclear make component|screen|usecase|repository|model|event|guard|widget|page|test ...` (`nuclear help`).
2. Write the code following the sheet. Copy the style of the project's existing `.nuc` files.
3. Check until clean, and fix exactly what each error says (most carry a `fix`):
- Synapsis: `nuclear check --json` (must print `[]`), then `nuclear analyze` (no `error •` lines) and, with
tests, `nuclear test`.

rows.title: NuclearLang — 2. Work cycle
rows.summary: then `nuclear build file.nuc --dialect <d> -o file.ts`.
body: - fastapi: `nuclear check . --json`, `nuclear build .`, then in `build/`: `pyright` and `pytest`.
- Other projects: `nuclear check <folder> --json`; a single file: `nuclear check file.nuc --dialect <d> --json`,
then `nuclear build file.nuc --dialect <d> -o file.ts`.
4. Format what you wrote: `nuclear fmt <folder>` (only spacing and indentation; `--check` lists what would change).
5. Never edit generated files (`build/`, `*.g.dart`, the `.ts`/`.dart` output): change the `.nuc` and rebuild.

rows.title: NuclearLang — 3. Look up instead of guessing
rows.summary: `nuclear defs show <Name> --dialect flutter` (or `<Name.member>`); `nuclear defs search <text> --dialect flutter`.
body: - A class, constructor, argument or member of Flutter, Dart or a package:
`nuclear defs show <Name> --dialect flutter` (or `<Name.member>`); `nuclear defs search <text> --dialect flutter`.
Inside the project they also show the packages the project added.
- A library the project does not have (npm, PyPI, pub.dev, for the project's dialect): `nuclear add <package>`
(`<package>@<version>`) installs it, writes it in `config.nuc` and generates its type definitions; then its names are
used directly, without `use` (the import is written for you). `nuclear remove <package>` takes it out. Never
install a package by hand inside `build/`. A package's default export is one name (`dayjs()`, `lodash.chunk(...)`).
- A kind, decorator or header word of the dialect (what it generates, its rules, an example):
`nuclear help <word> --dialect <d>` (`repository`, `@screen`...); every word: `nuclear help words --dialect <d>`; where a kind's file goes: `nuclear help layout --dialect <d>`.
- A language or framework topic: `nuclear help` lists them (`results`, `flutter`, `synapsis`, `tutorial`...).
- A runtime error of the app: `nuclear explain` (reads the error on stdin and points to the `.nuc` line).

rows.title: NuclearLang — 4. Mistakes agents make
rows.summary: sheet's forms (`~x`, `x = 1`, `and`, `not x`, `name = value`).
body: - Writing `return`, `;`, `{ }`, `new`, `await`, `const`/`final`/`var`, `&&`, `!x`, `name: value` arguments: use the
sheet's forms (`~x`, `x = 1`, `and`, `not x`, `name = value`).
- The return type goes after the parameters: `load(id: int) User`.
- Porting TypeScript: `===` and `!==` are `==` and `!=`. Between lists, maps or sets Nuclear's `==` compares what
they hold, not whether they are the same object: check each `===` between arrays or maps the original relied on.
- In Synapsis, a screen calls its `statemanager`, which calls the component's `appcomponent`; only the use case
calls the repository. Another component sees only the `appcomponent`, models, events, guards and screens.
- Real time, guards and a host page are configuration, never hand-written sockets or middleware: a backend's
`WebSocketServer(path = "ws")` and `guards: Guard[] = [NoOrigin(), Token(value = env("T"))]` in its `appConfig`
(`nuclear new -p backend --websocket --token T`); a web app's `WebSocket(url = ...)` connection, `@on("topic")`
repository methods returning `Stream<T>`, `listen(stream, ...)` in a manager; `mount(element, host)` for a host page.
- Texts shown to the user are translation keys: `"component.screen.key".tr()` plus the key in
`assets/i18n/<locale>/<component>.json`.

rows.title: NuclearLang — 4. Mistakes agents make
rows.summary: The compiler catches the habits of TypeScript, Dart and Python (`N0022`, with an exact `fix`), invented classes (`N0220`) and invented named arguments (`N0219`, it lists the real ones).
body: The compiler catches the habits of TypeScript, Dart and Python (`N0022`, with an exact `fix`), invented classes
(`N0220`) and invented named arguments (`N0219`, it lists the real ones). Apply the fix instead of rewriting.

rows.title: NuclearLang
rows.summary: NuclearLang (`.nuc`) is a minimal language transpiled to TypeScript, Dart or Python by declarative dialects.
body: NuclearLang (`.nuc`) is a minimal language transpiled to TypeScript, Dart or Python by declarative dialects. Synapsis
is its framework: three platforms written in Nuclear — `mobile` (dialect `flutter`: the Flutter app is generated in
`build/app`), `backend` (dialects `fastapi` = Python/FastAPI and `nestjs` = TypeScript, built to `build/` by
`nuclear build .`) and `web` (dialect `react` = TypeScript/React). The Nuclear of a platform is the same for every dialect of it; only
the standard library of Nuclear is used on strings, lists and maps (`nuclear help library`), never the target's. Its
syntax is NOT TypeScript, Dart nor Python: read the sheet before writing.
**Make it with the tools.** A product (any software made from Nuclear) is made with the platform's tools:
`nuclear new`, `nuclear gen`, `nuclear make`, the MCP server's tools, `nuclear add` for a library, `nuclear fix`; only
what they leave is written by hand, in Nuclear. Never write target code (`.ts`, `.dart`, `.py`) for a feature, and
never translate React, Node.js, Python or Dart code into Nuclear by hand. Only when strictly necessary, and then say
so: the tool that should have done it is missing something.

rows.title: Start here: NuclearLang for an agent with no context — Rules never broken
rows.summary: 1. Read before writing.
body: 1. **Read before writing.** The syntax sheet of your dialect first (`nuclear spec --brief --dialect <dialect>`,
MCP `nuclear_brief`), then the topic of what you write. Look up a word instead of guessing:
`nuclear help <word> --dialect <dialect>`; a class or member of the target's libraries:
`nuclear defs show <Name> --dialect <dialect>`.
2. **A product is made with the tools.** `nuclear new` creates the project, `nuclear gen` writes finished code of a
resource, `nuclear make` the skeleton of each piece where the platform puts it, `nuclear add` a library. Write by
hand only what they leave, in Nuclear. Never write target code (`.ts`, `.dart`, `.py`) for a feature, never
translate code of another language into Nuclear by hand, never edit `build/`. When a tool cannot do something,
say so.
3. **Nuclear's standard library only** (`nuclear help library`): strings, lists, maps, dates, JSON... never the
target's names in platform code.
4. **Check after every change.** `nuclear check --json` must print `[]`; fix exactly what each error says (most
carry a `fix`, and `nuclear fix` applies them). Then `nuclear test`.
5. **The project documents itself.** Its `AGENTS.md` and `docs/` say what it is and how it is made; keep them true
in the same change (topic `context-docs`). The project's own `docs/README.md` wins over this default.

rows.title: Start here: NuclearLang for an agent with no context — What it is
rows.summary: TypeScript, Dart or Python through dialects (TOML and templates), one way only: the `.nuc` is the source, the target code is generated and never edited.
body: - **NuclearLang** (`.nuc`): a minimal language for AI agents and people. Its transpiler turns `.nuc` into
TypeScript, Dart or Python through **dialects** (TOML and templates), one way only: the `.nuc` is the source, the
target code is generated and never edited.
- **Synapsis**: its framework. Three **platforms**, each written once in Nuclear and built by its dialects:
`mobile` (dialect `flutter`), `backend` (`fastapi` = Python, `nestjs` = TypeScript) and `web` (`react`). The
Nuclear of a platform is the same for every dialect of it: the dialect only changes the language underneath.
- **The golden rule**: generated code as fast as an expert's, instant transpilation, minimal readable Nuclear.

rows.title: The MCP server — Rules
rows.summary: 1. An agent with no context learns Nuclear from this server alone (spec 016, root rule 14): the instructions send it to `nuclear_start`, whose answer and every `nuclear_doc` come from the installed `nuclear` (never a path of the source tree).
body: 1. **An agent with no context learns Nuclear from this server alone** (spec 016, root rule 14): the instructions
send it to `nuclear_start`, whose answer and every `nuclear_doc` come from the installed `nuclear` (never a path
of the source tree). Every project created with Nuclear gets its context documents and an `AGENTS.md` section
that names this server ([the CLI's agent support](../cli/docs/02-architecture/agent-support.md)).
2. **A tool is a method with a comment**: the comment is the description the client reads. A tool added, renamed or
given a parameter is also added to [the guide](docs/08-guides/mcp.md) (a test holds it to the server's list), and
the knowledge base is rebuilt (the graph keeps a row per tool, `mcp:<tool>`, read with `nuclear-mcp tools`).
3. **A generator tool is a `nuclear gen` command**, never its own code: the options and the refusals are the
[code generator's](../code_generator/AGENTS.md).
4. **The `nuclear_project` tool runs only the commands of its list** (`PROJECT_COMMANDS`).
5. **The graph is reached with the token of the client `mcp`**: the user decides whether MCP clients may read it.
Never weaken that to make a tool easier.

body: `nuclear-mcp`: the program an AI client (Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini CLI) starts to work with NuclearLang. It
speaks the Model Context Protocol over stdio and offers the generators, the compiler and the command line, the Smart
Graph, the local developer and the internet as tools. Its instructions tell every client how to work, so they all
behave the same: generate first, let the local developer write the rest, then validate and correct.

rows.title: `nuclear-mcp`, the MCP server — Why
rows.summary: Why
body: - Every client works the same way on a Nuclear project, whatever model is behind it.
- Standard code costs the model no tokens, and it never has to guess an API.
- Safe by default: `nuclear_project` runs only its listed commands; internet text is untrusted.

rows.title: The MCP server: overview — How a tool is declared
rows.summary: tool, and the comment is what the client reads of it.
body: - `McpTools(graph: GraphClient, tools: Toolchain, web: Web)` holds every tool. **Each method with a comment is a
tool, and the comment is what the client reads of it.** The method `graphSearch` is the tool `graph_search`.
- `all()` lists the tools in the order a client sees them: the graph's, the compiler's, `nuclear_project`,
the generators, the internet, the developer's.
- `mcpServer()` makes the server `nuclear` with its instructions and adds each tool of `all()`.
- `mcpTools()` gives the instructions and the tools as data (`{instructions, tools: [{name, description, schema}]}`)
to the knowledge base's build (it runs `nuclear-mcp tools`), so the graph has a row per tool (`mcp:<tool>`) and
answers "which tools" exactly.
- This is the pattern of an MCP server written in Nuclear: the Builder's, `nuclear-builder mcp`, is made the same way
(its own project, [actions.md](../../../../extensions/tools/nuclear-builder/docs/02-architecture/actions.md)).

rows.title: The MCP server: overview — Two modes
rows.summary: The instructions only say where to begin (spec 016: an agent with no context learns Nuclear from this server).
body: The instructions only say where to begin (spec 016: an agent with no context learns Nuclear from this server).
The work cycle is part of `nuclear_start`'s answer: local, `graph_strategy` + `GENERATORS` + `LOCAL` (generate; give
`developer_task` only what is left; wire with `generate_usecase`; validate; correct only what failed;
`developer_review`); remote, `REMOTE_NOTE` + `graph_strategy` + `GENERATORS` + `REMOTE` (generate; the model writes what is left
after reading `nuclear_brief`, the graph and `nuclear_help`; validate and correct). `nuclear_start` itself is `nuclear help start`, that
cycle and `nuclear help atlas`; with a project, `gen inspect` and the brief of its dialect. `nuclear_doc` is `nuclear
help <topic>`. `developer_task` first asks the local developer whether it answers (`developerDown`): when it does
not, it says how to start it and that the model writes the code itself meanwhile. `FIRST` also holds the rule that a
product is made with these tools: no target code for a feature, no native code translated into Nuclear by hand
([ADR-platform-0004](../../../../docs/03-adr/0004-products-are-made-with-the-tools.md)).

rows.title: The MCP server of NuclearLang — 2. How a model works with it
rows.summary: An agent may know nothing about Nuclear: the server's instructions only tell it to call `nuclear_start` before anything about Nuclear.
body: An agent may know nothing about Nuclear: the server's instructions only tell it to call `nuclear_start` before
anything about Nuclear. Its answer is the onboarding (what Nuclear and Synapsis are, the rules never broken, the
work cycle with these tools on this machine) and the atlas of every topic, each read with `nuclear_doc`; with a
project folder, also the project's pieces and the sheet of its dialect. Nothing it reads points into a source tree.
With the local AI services, the cycle then calls `graph_strategy` with the user's own words: it answers which
kind of request it is and the plan of that kind
([the strategies](../../../../extensions/tools/nuclear-builder/docs/08-guides/follow-a-run.md#the-strategy-of-a-request)). For a feature the plan is this order:

rows.title: The MCP server of NuclearLang — 2. How a model works with it
rows.summary: 1. Inspect.
body: 1. **Inspect.** `project_inspect`: what the project already has, so nothing is declared twice.
2. **Generate.** For every resource the spec names (a model and what is done with it), `generate_resource`. Its
fields come from the API's answer (`from_json`; `api_inspect` shows its shape first), from the spec (`from_spec`)
or from `fields`. When neither gives them, the model looks up the API's documentation (`web_search`, `web_read`)
and, if it is still unclear, asks the user: it never guesses. A use case that only calls a repository method is
`generate_usecase` with `calls`.
3. **The local developer writes the rest.** `developer_task` with what the generators did not write (a use case with
its own rules, a view's details): the local agents plan, write the tests first, write the code, run the tests and
the security review, and answer a journal of everything they did.
4. **Wire.** Each use case the local developer wrote, with `generate_usecase` (its alias in the facade, its route).
5. **Validate.** `nuclear_check` of the project must say `ok` and `nuclear test` must pass.
6. **Correct only what failed**, never what passed. Before writing `.nuc` the model reads `nuclear_brief` and
searches the graph. A run that failed for a passing cause is run again with `developer_retry`.

rows.title: The MCP server of NuclearLang — 2. How a model works with it
rows.summary: 7. Review.
body: 7. **Review.** `developer_review` with what was corrected and why: the journal keeps it and the corrected files
become examples the local developer finds next time.
The model writes the code itself only when the local developer is not running, and says so.

rows.title: The MCP server of NuclearLang — Generators
rows.summary: They write finished code that compiles, never a skeleton to fill in.
body: They write finished code that compiles, never a skeleton to fill in. Each is a `nuclear gen` command:
[the generators' guide](../../../../nuclear-synapsis-framework/docs/08-guides/generators.md) has the
options, the examples and what each platform gets.

rows.title: The MCP server of NuclearLang — Generators
rows.summary: generate_resource(project, "orders", "Order", fields="id:int total:double status:string", source="db") generate_usecase(project, "orders", "PageOrders", calls="OrderRepository.page", route="GET orders/pages/{page}") generate_usecase(project, "orders", "CancelOrder", route="POST…
body: | `generate_usecase(project, component, name, calls, route, dry_run)` | a use case wired into its component: its alias in the facade and, with `route` (backend), its route. With `calls` the use case is written too, because it only calls that repository method; without it the use case is one the project already has |
| `generate_screen(project, component, screen, route)` | mobile and web: a screen with its state manager and state model, for a view that is not a resource's list |
| `api_inspect(url, project, component, name)` | the shape of a public API's JSON answer; with a project, the files `generate_resource` would write from it |
generate_resource(project, "orders", "Order", fields="id:int total:double status:string", source="db")
generate_usecase(project, "orders", "PageOrders", calls="OrderRepository.page", route="GET orders/pages/{page}")
generate_usecase(project, "orders", "CancelOrder", route="POST orders/{id}/cancel")   # CancelOrder is in the project
Nothing is overwritten and nothing is declared twice; `dry_run` shows the files first. A generator that cannot write
something finished refuses and says what to do: `generate_usecase` without `calls`, for a use case the project does
not declare, answers where to write it.

rows.title: The MCP server of NuclearLang — Generators
rows.summary: Generators
body: | Tool | What it does |
| `project_inspect(project)` | the project's platform and dialect, its components with their declarations by kind, the generators of its platform |

| `project_monitor(project)` | where the app is slow (Nuclear Monitor): the hot spots and the time, calls, connections and memory of each Nuclear function and method, from the last run with `nuclear run --monitor` |

| `project_run_log(project, lines)` | why the app failed or what it did: the last `lines` (default 200, at most 2000) of the project's `.nuclear/logs/run.log`, which `nuclear run` and the editor's devices write (each step, the build's errors, the server's output, `failed:` and `exited:`); only that file |
| `graph_monitor(project)` | `project_monitor`, and its hot spots kept in the graph (`monitor:<project>`) for the local developer and later sessions |
| `generate_component(project, component)` | a new component with its facade |

| `generate_resource(project, component, name, from_json \| from_spec \| fields, source, path, actions, screen, plural, dry_run)` | a resource: models, repository, a use case per action, the facade's aliases, the controller (backend) or a screen with its state manager (mobile, web), the tests |

rows.title: The MCP server of NuclearLang — The compiler and the command line
rows.summary: The compiler and the command line
body: | Tool | What it does |
| `nuclear_start(project?)` | **first**: what Nuclear is, the rules, the work cycle on this machine, the atlas of every topic; with a project folder, its pieces and the sheet of its dialect |

| `nuclear_doc(topic)` | one topic of the atlas, whole: a guide chapter, `base`, `library`, a platform, a dialect, a tool, `context-docs`, `example/<name>`; a word that is not a topic answers the topics that explain it |
| `nuclear_check(code \| path, dialect)` | `ok`, or one line per error with its fix, for a piece of Nuclear or a whole project |
| `nuclear_build(code, dialect)` | what a piece of Nuclear becomes in the dialect's language |
| `nuclear_fmt(code)` | the piece in the canonical layout |
| `nuclear_help(word, dialect)` | the documentation of a kind, a decorator, a topic or a command |
| `nuclear_brief(dialect)` | the short sheet of Nuclear and a platform: read before writing `.nuc` |

| `nuclear_defs(name, dialect, project?)` | a declaration of the type definitions (a class or `Class.member` of a library); with the project's folder, also of a package the project added (`nuclear_project` with `add`) |

| `nuclear_project(project, command, args)` | `new`, `build`, `install`, `test`, `check`, `analyze`, `make`, `gen`, `migrate`, `add`, `remove`, `explain` in a project (`add` with a name: a package of the target and its type definitions) |

rows.title: The MCP server of NuclearLang — The internet
rows.summary: The internet
body: | Tool | What it does |

| `web_search(query, pages)` | searches the internet and answers the first results with the text of their pages (your own SearXNG with `NUCLEAR_SEARXNG_URL`, Brave with `nuclear-graph web-key brave`, else Wikipedia) |
| `web_read(url)` | the text of a public page, without its code blocks. Local addresses are refused |

rows.title: The MCP server of NuclearLang — The local developer
rows.summary: The local developer
body: | Tool | What it does |

| `developer_task(project, title, description, criteria, use_case)` | **the first step of every task that writes `.nuc`**: the local agents do the whole task in the project (plan, tests first, code, verification, security, artifacts) and answer the run's journal. `use_case`: `feature`, `bug`, `refactor`, `test` |

| `developer_retry(project, run, from_stage, from_step, scratch)` | a run again: from the step that failed, every step that passed kept; the whole of `from_stage`; from one step (`from_step`: its id in the journal, passed or failed) and every step after it; or from scratch (`scratch`: every stage again). What the steps left out wrote is undone first |
| `developer_review(project, run, notes, files)` | **the last step**: the lead's corrections, kept in the journal; each corrected file goes to the graph's examples |
| `developer_code(task, platform, path, kind, context, project)` | one `.nuc` file outside a task, written, checked and repaired by the local model. It returns the file; it does not write it |
| `developer_test(task, code, platform)` | the Nuclear tests of a piece of code |
| `developer_security(code, platform)` | the security findings of a piece of code |

rows.title: The MCP server of NuclearLang — The Smart Graph
rows.summary: The Smart Graph
body: | Tool | What it does |

| `graph_strategy(request, platform)` | **the first call for any request**: which kind of request it is (a whole system, a component, one screen, a use case, a rename, a failing test, a question...), the signs that say so, and the plan of that kind, step by step with the tool of each step |

| `graph_answer(question, platform)` | the exact answer of a question that has one (every command of a tool, the tools of this server and their parameters, the commands that write a kind, a diagnostic by its code, the stages of the Builder, a version...): the rows of the graph's database, whole, never recalled; then the cards the shelves answer by meaning. For "which", "list", "what are the" questions |

| `graph_search(query, shelf, k, platform, kind, type)` | the cards that answer a question, by meaning and by exact name (a diagnostic code, a command, a kind), each with the rows it links to. `shelf`: `concepts`, `language`, `platforms`, `tools`, `errors`, `capabilities`, `playbooks`, `examples`, `docs`, `memory`; empty searches all |
| `graph_card(id)` | one row by its id: `error:N0114`, `kind:backend.usecase`, `tool:nuclear.gen.usecase`, `mcp:generate_usecase`, `playbook:add-a-use-case` |
| `graph_prompt(use_case)` | the validated prompt of `feature`, `refactor`, `bug`, `docs`, `diagram`, `test`, `security`, `piece`, `plan` |

rows.title: The MCP server of NuclearLang — The Smart Graph
rows.summary: The Smart Graph
rows.body: | `graph_remember(id, text, collection, project)` | keeps a decision (`memory`) or a solved example (`examples`) for the local developer and later sessions |

rows.title: The MCP server of NuclearLang — 4. When a tool fails
rows.summary: The graph knows every tool of this page: ask it with `graph_card("mcp:<tool>")`, or ask the editor's chat (`Ctrl+Alt+A`) in your own words.
body: | The tool answers | What to do |

| `the local developer is not running at ...` | `nuclear-builder setup --status` says what is missing; restart it in *Settings and integrations*, or with [the command of your system](../../../../installer/docs/08-guides/ai-setup.md#5-after-the-set-up) |
| the graph refuses the client | `nuclear-graph connect mcp --scopes read,write`, with the graph running |
| `... is not inside a Synapsis project (no config.nuc)` | give the project's folder: `nuclear new <name>` creates one |
| `'<command>' is not allowed here` | the `nuclear_project` tool runs only the commands of its list |
| `'--' is not allowed here` | what follows `--` goes to the target's own tools (a port, a host): an agent never passes it through the MCP server |
| `no run log yet in ...` | the app never ran in that project: run it once (`nuclear run`, or ▷ Run / ▭ Device in the editor), then call `project_run_log` again |
| a generator refuses | its message says what is missing: [when a generator refuses](../../../../nuclear-synapsis-framework/docs/08-guides/generators.md#4-when-a-generator-refuses) |
The graph knows every tool of this page: ask it with `graph_card("mcp:<tool>")`, or ask the editor's chat
(`Ctrl+Alt+A`) in your own words.

rows.title: The MCP server of NuclearLang
rows.summary: MCP is the Model Context Protocol: an AI client (Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini CLI) starts a program and calls the tools it offers.
body: MCP is the **Model Context Protocol**: an AI client (Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini CLI) starts a program and calls
the tools it offers. `nuclear-mcp` is that program for NuclearLang. It speaks MCP over stdio and gives a
frontier model four things: the **generators** that write the standard code, the **local developer** that writes what
is left, the **Smart Graph** to look things up instead of guessing, and the **compiler** to check everything.
The server also tells the model how to work, so every client behaves the same: generate first, let the local
developer write the rest, then validate and correct.
